He then added, "Bhagwan is pulling them."

Swamishri humbly attributes the children's spontaneous devotion not to his own influence, but to the magnetic presence of Bhagwan. This reveals that true spiritual attraction is the work of divine grace.

title: Concentration in Puja
text:
During the Grahan Sabha, a question-and-answer session was held with Swamishri.

Question: "Our minds do not remain focused during puja, so how can we achieve concentration?"

Swamishri: "We have attained the manifest form of Maharaj, and there is nothing superior to Him. Therefore, we must uphold respect for Him. We must mold our lives to be worthy of Him and make Him the center of our existence. One must understand the mahima—that such a Bhagwan has not been attained by anyone else. This is a new endeavor, so initially, the mind may wander in puja, but with time and persistence, it will improve."

Swamishri explained that concentration improves when we prioritize Bhagwan above all else.

title: Daily Spiritual Nourishment
text:
During the Grahan Sabha, a question-and-answer session was held with Swamishri, in which they asked about the ideal amount of daily reading.

Question: "How many Vachanamruts should devotees read?"
Swamishri: "Because they are small or big, counting the pages, one should read two pages."

Question: "How many Swamini Vato should be read?"
Swamishri: "Five."

Question: "How many pages of Jivan Charitra should be read?"
Swamishri: "Three pages."

Swamishri showed that consistency in reading is key to spiritual growth. By dedicating time to read these specific amounts daily, we ensure our minds remain nourished with divine wisdom.

title: A Vision of Divinity
text:
During the Grahan Sabha, a question-and-answer session was held with Swamishri.

Question: "Swami! You have crossed out abhav-avgun (seeing faults in others) many times. Yet, we still end up seeing faults in others. Despite this, your faith in us remains strong. Why doesn't your faith waver?"

Swamishri: "Because I want to make everyone Ekantik."

Question: "If we maintain divyabhav toward some, but not toward others, will you still pass us?"

Swamishri: "One must maintain divyabhav towards everyone and understand each other's greatness. We have to see everyone as divine."

Swamishri's unwavering faith and compassion for us is rooted in his resolve to mold us into Ekantik devotees.

title: Unbreakable Unity
text:
During the Grahan Sabha, a question-and-answer session was held with Swamishri.

Question: "Where do we fall short in maintaining samp (unity)?"

Swamishri: "We fall short in maintaining mutual unity amongst ourselves. [Our unity should be] like broccoli—no matter how much you shake it, the pieces do not separate. We should possess that kind of unity."

True unity means remaining interconnected and inseparable, just like a broccoli floret. Regardless of external turbulence, our bond with one another should remain unbreakable.

title: A New Definition of Unity
text:
After breakfast, during a discussion, Pujya Bhadresh Swami asked Swamishri, "Swami, in your view, what niyam should be kept to maintain samp, suhradbhav, and ekta?"

Swamishri replied, "Everyone should perform tasks together. Any task should be done collectively. If someone is senior to us, we should bow down, and if someone is junior, we should encourage them."

Delighted by this insight, Bhadresh Swami exclaimed, "A whole new definition has been revealed!"

Swamishri offers a practical blueprint for unity that balances humility towards seniors with encouragement for juniors. By emphasizing collective effort over individual ego, he reveals that true harmony is built through mutual respect and shared action.

title: The Ultimate Gift
text:
While doing darshan in the mandir, Swamishri moved from the central shrine toward the main dome. A devotee named Ankur Paladiya was standing there, holding his young son who was dressed in saffron clothes.

Swamishri approached them and compassionately blessed the child. Ankurbhai then pointed to his son and said, "Swami! He was asking me, 'What will Swami give me in my jholi (alms bag)?' I told him, 'Swami will give you the best thing he possesses.' So Swami, what will you give?"

Without a moment's hesitation, Swamishri replied, "Bhagwan!"

Swamishri's instant response reveals that the greatest treasure he possesses and offers is not material, but spiritual. He grants us nothing less than Bhagwan Himself.

title: Unwavering Vicharan
text:
Divyaswarup Swami recounted an incident: "It was around 1975–1976. You were on vicharan near Godhra, in the town of Sahera. While sitting on a cloth seat at Himmatsinh Solanki's home, your finger got jammed between two pieces of wood." Swamishri indicated it was the middle finger of his right hand. Divyaswarup Swami continued, "The flesh of your finger was hanging loose, and there was profuse bleeding."

Swamishri added, "The bleeding was one thing, but the pain was severe—it throbbed intensely."

Swamishri continued, "This happened in Sahera, but later in Baraiya, the pain was excruciating—I couldn't sleep all night."

Uttamyogi Swami asked, "Did you continue your vicharan despite this?" To everyone's astonishment, Swamishri affirmed that he did.

His dedication is defined by the willingness to persevere through hardships.

title: The Joy of Unity
text:
A husband and wife living abroad had been estranged for a long time due to a deep rift.

This evening, as Swamishri returned from the assembly and headed toward the dining hall, an attendant swami handed him a phone. He informed Swamishri that the husband was on the line. The attendant explained, "Because of your words, they have developed deep samp (unity) with one another and have even been blessed with a child."

Hearing this, Swamishri's face lit up with delight. Speaking into the phone, he told the devotee, "I am very happy. This has brought me great joy."

Swamishri's radiant reaction reveals that nothing brings him greater joy than seeing unity restored in a devotee's life, celebrating their harmony as his own.

title: The Art of Care
text:
After lunch, Swamishri called Santcharit Swami over. Gesturing toward the flower pots, he instructed, "If any flowers are on the verge of falling or are damaged, pick those first... take one [from each pot]." He indicated that only a single flower should be plucked from each pot.

When Santcharit Swami asked why, Swamishri explained, "The healthy flowers will sway in the wind (and remain beautiful and can be used in two or three days). But the weaker ones will soon wither, so they should be used first. And take only one flower from each pot, because if you take them all, the plant will look bare."

His specific instructions reveal a divine sensitivity; just as he protects the flowers, he nurtures our souls with the perfect balance of love and wisdom.

title: Seva with Understanding
text:
During an evening discussion, Vednayan Swami asked Swamishri, "In our Satsang, many swamis and devotees, like the Sadguru Swamis, have attained the enlightened state while still on this earth. Please tell us, what did they do to attain such a state?"

Swamishri responded, "They performed seva after understanding the inner wish [of the Satpurush]. We all perform seva, but we must do so by understanding the [Satpurush's] inner wish."

Swamishri clarifies that spiritual elevation is not achieved merely by the quantity of our service, but by the quality of our alignment with the Satpurush. True enlightenment comes when seva is performed with a deep understanding of the Satpurush's inner wish.

title: Every Breath for Bhagwan
text:
After his shower and giving darshan to the swamis, Swamishri rested on his bed. As per his daily routine, his oxygen levels were measured.

The reading showed an impressive 99%. Upon hearing this, Swamishri's face lit up with joy, and he remarked, "I have shaved my head for Akshar-Purushottam; that is why it is 99%!"

Touched by this spontaneous connection, the swamis responded, "Truly, such words only flow if this sentiment is constantly in your heart. Otherwise, such a thought would not even arise."

For Swamishri, even a medical statistic reflects his spiritual dedication, revealing that his existence, down to his very breath, is sustained by his total love for Akshar-Purushottam.

title: The Summit of Knowledge
text:
At 5:35 PM, Swamishri finished his evening walk. At that moment, Atmatrupta Swami requested him to write a motivating message for the students entering the Sanskrit Mahavidyalaya.

Swamishri penned a profound statement: "The knowledge that exists throughout the universe is sattvik and highly sattvik; however, our knowledge of Akshar-Purushottam is beyond all of that. It is gunatit, it is present, and it is embodied."

Swamishri redefines the ultimate goal of education. While worldly knowledge, even at its purest, remains bound by the modes of maya, the knowledge of Akshar-Purushottam transcends them entirely. True knowledge is not merely a subject to be studied in books, but a divine reality to be experienced in the form of the Gunatit Satpurush.

title: An Essential Practice
text:
At 10:20 PM, after his mundan was completed, Swamishri bathed and returned to his room. A swami approached him and asked, "Tomorrow is my diksha anniversary. Do you have any guidance for me?"

Swamishri immediately responded, "Samp (unity). Stay together with harmony and mutual understanding."

In a few words, Swamishri distilled the essence of spiritual life. By identifying samp as an important instruction, he reinforced that true spiritual progress is found not in isolation, but in the harmony and togetherness of the satsang fellowship. Even at night, his brief response underscored that unity, harmony, and mutual understanding are essential practices to be lived every day.

title: The Ultimate Support
text:
Following his morning puja, Swamishri elaborated on Vachanamrut Gadhada II-49: "A Great Difference Exists between God's Form and Māyik Forms; Not Becoming Content with Spiritual Discourses, Devotional Songs, etc."

In his commentary, Swamishri stated with emphasis, "No one can be compared to Maharaj. He is eternally Parabrahma, Purushottam, and Sarvopari. Whose support would He need? Everyone exists because of His support."

Swamishri shifts our focus from our own limited efforts to Bhagwan's limitless power. Recognizing that the One who sustains the entire universe also sustains us frees us from the burden of ego and the anxiety of self-reliance.

title: The Glory of Shastriji Maharaj
text:
Today marked the consecration ceremony of the Johannesburg Mandir. In the evening assembly, Swamishri offered his blessings on the auspicious occasion of Vasant Panchami, the birth anniversary of Brahmaswarup Shastriji Maharaj.

Swamishri recalled, "Today is Shastriji Maharaj's birthday. Shastriji Maharaj used to say, 'This [head] has been shaved solely for the sake of Akshar-Purushottam.' It was clear to him from the very beginning, even during his childhood."

Swamishri continued, "Shastriji Maharaj achieved such a triumph that today we are all content. Even this Mandir we see today is due to the glory of Shastriji Maharaj! Therefore, maintaining such inner strength and bravery, let us not take even a single step back, but instead move forward and forward."

title: The Spirit of True Seva
text:
A few days earlier, Swamishri received a letter from a youth in America asking, "Swami, how can seva be performed correctly?"

Swamishri replied, "When we perform seva, we must do it with pure intentions; we must fully attach our minds [to the seva]. We should perform seva selflessly and maintain the firm conviction that 'Maharaj is true, Swami is true, and Bhagatji Maharaj, Shastriji Maharaj, Yogi Bapa, and Pramukh Swami Maharaj are true.' Otherwise, flaws will cause us to fall back."

Swamishri teaches that the "correctness" of seva is found not in the skill of the hands, but in the heart's purity, selflessness, and unwavering faith.

title: A Unique Friendship
text:
After the night assembly, the swamis engaged in a discussion with Swamishri. During the conversation, a large black ant crawled into Swamishri's dhoti. Shrutipriya Swami immediately tried to remove it, but he could not locate it within the folds.

Unperturbed, Swamishri finished the discussion. Upon returning to his room, Shrutipriya Swami attempted to find the ant again.

Smiling, Swamishri said, "The makodo is a friend!"

Shrutipriya Swami laughed and recalled, "Ants and makodas are your friends! Once, you had brought an ant with you all the way from India to Nairobi. Another time, you saved a makodo from a flower bed."

Where most would react to a biting ant with irritation, Swamishri responds with friendship—a state where love extends compassion to even the smallest of creatures.

title: The Essential Message
text:
Swamishri returned to his room for breakfast. A group of swamis preparing to return to Sarangpur approached him for blessings.

One of them asked, "Swami, do you have any message for the swamis that have come from Sarangpur?"

Swamishri replied, "Samp (unity)... stay together in harmony and with mutual understanding."

Swamishri identifies unity not just as a social virtue, but as the primary instruction for spiritual life. His parting words remind us that before any other seva or achievement, the foundation of our Satsang must be harmony and mutual understanding.

title: True Independence
text:
After breakfast, Swamishri listened to the virtues of various swamis. Afterwards, he entered his room and sat on his bed. Here, Anandpriya Swami requested, "Please stay for another two days."

Swamishri smiled, shook his head, and said, "I have to follow everyone's agna."

Anandpriya Swami responded, "But you are independent!"

Hearing this, Swamishri uttered a profound truth: "Independent from the indriyas (senses)."

Anandpriya Swami persisted, "The tickets could be rescheduled. Ishwarcharan Swami also liked the idea of you staying longer to rest."

Swamishri replied with love, "Instead of having everyone adjust to me, I will adjust."

Swamishri redefines independence not as the authority to command others, but as freedom from the control of the senses.

title: Only What Is Necessary
text:
After his meal, Swamishri began his daily routine of walking one hundred steps inside his room. Noticing the room was dimly lit, an attendant swami said, "Turn on the lights."

The other swamis immediately switched on all the lights.

Swamishri instantly instructed, "Keep only as many lights on as necessary."

Swamishri's instruction highlights a vital spiritual principle: resources should be used with discretion and without waste. Even when comfort is readily available, he chooses the path of karkasar (prudent resource use), reminding us that mindfulness applies to even the smallest act of consumption.

title: Inclination for Austerity
text:
During the Grahan Sabha, a question-and-answer session was held with Swamishri, in which they asked about austerities.

Question: "Why do you like austerity?"

Swamishri: "Shriji Maharaj likes it, so naturally, we should also like it."

Question: "When we perform austerity, we only think about food. So, we feel it would be better not to do it at all. Is that okay?"

Swamishri said no and explained, "We need to cultivate the habit, so one must start it."

Swamishri guides us to embrace austerity simply because it pleases Bhagwan, not for our own comfort. Even if the mind resists, persisting in the practice helps us cultivate the necessary spiritual habit.

title: Reverence for His Guru
text:
Swamishri was engaged in a conversation with a devotee named Harishbhai Bhuptani. During the discussion, Harishbhai presented a brochure for his 'Mama Care Foundation.'

The brochure bore the inscription: 'Inspirer: HDH Pramukh Swami Maharaj.'

Upon seeing this, Swamishri immediately and reverently bowed down to the name printed on the brochure.

For Swamishri, the Guru's name is not merely ink on paper; it is non-different from the Guru himself. This spontaneous gesture reveals the depth of his guru-bhakti, teaching us that true devotion is a constant, living reverence that acknowledges the Guru's presence in every form.

title: 80 Kilometers of Contemplation
text:
In the morning, the swamis and sadhaks residing in Sarangpur benefited from Swamishri's puja darshan and blessings via a live telecast.

After the broadcast, Atmaswarup Swami approached Swamishri and said, "Swami! Just now in your blessings, you mentioned that your reading of the Vachanamrut never truly ends because you get lost in thought. I have witnessed this personally. It was around 1982. We were traveling from Himatnagar to Ahmedabad on a bus, and I sat next to you. You opened the Vachanamrut to read, but after reading just a small section, you closed your eyes. You became so deeply immersed in contemplation that you did not open them until we reached Ahmedabad... You contemplated for a full 80 kilometers!"

For Swamishri, the Vachanamrut is not merely a text to be read, but a reality to be experienced.

title: A Great Vibhuti
text:
During a mulakat, Veljibhai Guniya of Devchadi village came to meet Swamishri. He shared a memory from 1970 when he managed a student hostel in Gondal and would go to Gondal mandir to perform seva.

He recalled an occasion when he was passing the assembly hall, and Yogiji Maharaj called out to him. Pointing toward Mahant Swami, who was resting nearby, Yogiji Maharaj stated, "This is a very great vibhuti (divine personality). Therefore, perform his pradakshina (circumambulations)."

Through his foresight, Yogiji Maharaj highlighted Mahant Swami Maharaj's spiritual greatness long before the world recognized him as the Guru. This confirms that his saintliness is not a product of his position, but his inherent nature—pure and divine from the very beginning.

title: The Birthless One
text:
Santcharit Swami asked Swamishri, "Swami, according to the English calendar, tomorrow is your birthday. Should we celebrate it with nirdoshbuddhi, samp, suhradbhav, or ekta?"

Everyone present anticipated that Swamishri would select one of his favorite virtues.

However, Swamishri smiled and gave an unexpected answer: "The birthdate is of this world. I am birthless. Other souls have taken many births. Your bones are spread everywhere on earth; not one place is left out!"

Swamishri draws a sharp distinction between the bound soul and the Gunatit Satpurush. While ordinary souls are caught in the endless cycle of birth and death, Swamishri reveals his true identity as Aksharbrahma—eternal, divine, and unbound by the limits of time or karma.

title: Wherever I Go…
text:
During lunch, Gnanchintan Swami shared various memories involving Swamishri from the past. He recounted an occasion when Swamishri visited the home of Vineshbhai Patel in Anjangav.

During the visit, the electricity suddenly went out. Vineshbhai felt deeply distressed that such an inconvenience had occurred during Swamishri's presence.

Noticing his discomfort, Swamishri immediately remarked, "Do not worry, this happens wherever I go."

Hearing this lighthearted comment, Vineshbhai's sadness vanished instantly, and he happily resumed serving Swamishri.

Swamishri employs humor not merely for laughter, but as a profound tool of empathy. By playfully taking the "blame" for the power outage upon himself, he instantly absolved the devotee of any guilt or distress, prioritizing the devotee's peace of mind.

title: A Mother's Love
text:
In the evening, Anandjivan Swami, who cherishes many memories of Swamishri's time in Nenpur, had been connected on call with Swamishri. During the call, he recounted a touching incident from the past: "I remember an incident involving Jayesh Mandanka. At the time, he was just a small child and had arrived early for a shibir. You personally spread an asan (mat) for him and seated him for a meal. Then, you sat on the floor right in front of him and remained there until he finished eating. I vividly remember that moment."

This touching memory dissolves the hierarchy between a great Guru and a young child. By personally arranging the mat and waiting patiently while the boy ate, Swamishri demonstrated a love devoid of ego. It reflects a pure, motherly affection, where the comfort of a child takes precedence over his own high status.

title: The Foundational Scripture
text:
After dinner, Swamishri was shown the newly developed 'Swamini Vato' application. Blessing the app, Swamishri emphasized, "Our two main scriptures—the Vachanamrut and Swamini Vato—are the foundation. One must understand this; there is no alternative. Maharaj revealed Swami's form, and Swami revealed Maharaj's form. Thus, these are the talks of Brahma and Parabrahma; there is no scripture greater than these. These two scriptures are the essence of all scriptures. Had we been born 300 years ago, we would not have had his darshan. But we are born in the time of Shriji Maharaj and the Gunatit Guru, reaping this benefit. This is the principal scripture through which we can become brahmarup and ekantik. Therefore, we must read this scripture daily."

Swamishri declares that the Vachanamrut and Swamini Vato are the verbal forms of Brahma and Parabrahma.

title: Unbroken Connection
text:
After his morning walk, Swamishri listens to the biography of Shastriji Maharaj while exercising. Today, the narration had reached a pivotal moment: the pagaran (commencement) of the majestic Sarangpur Mandir. However, in the middle of the account, Uttamyogi Swami paused the recording as the exercise had finished.

Fifteen minutes later, as Swamishri sat down for his meal, his mind remained anchored to that unfinished thought. He asked Uttamyogi Swami, "Three devotees went to Shastriji Maharaj regarding the Sarangpur temple—what did Shastriji Maharaj say next?"

As per his wish, the track was resumed. Shortly after, another swami arrived, and the audio was paused once more. This time, Swamishri expressed his dissatisfaction. Only after listening to the full account with total concentration did he turn to the visitor and his meal.

For him, the biography of Shastriji Maharaj is not mere history—it is a lifeline.

title: The Decision is Yours
text:
After Swamishri's exercise session, Dr. Maheshbhai asked, "Swami, our attainment (prapti) is immense. Yet, if one's base nature (swabhav-prakruti) has not dissolved even after 20 years, what do you think when you see us with such flaws?"

Swamishri replied, "Nothing. Everyone is a mukta (liberated soul). They belong to the brahmakoti."

Dr. Mahendrabhai then asked, "But if one has not become nirvasanik (free from worldly desires), can one attain Akshardham?"

Swamishri answered firmly, "No, they cannot." He added, "If I do not say this, then everything else becomes false. One must become nirvasanik."

Then Swamishri clarified, "Whether a renunciant (tyagi) or a householder (gruhastha), both can become nirvasanik—but only if they choose to do so."

He places the key to spiritual success squarely in the hands of the aspirant.

title: Constant Care
text:
Today marked the Nagar Yatra (city procession) for the Jodhpur Mandir.

Swamishri woke up at 4:00 PM and immediately asked about the procession, "How is it? Is it sunny?"

At 5:00 PM, he asked again, "How is the procession going?"

Then he asked two or three more times, "How is the procession proceeding?" He also inquired specifically, "Are the santos and devotees doing well?"

Seeing Swamishri was worried regarding their well-being, a phone call was made to Santcharit Swami, who was accompanying Shri Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj in the procession. He reported, "The heat has subsided, and it has become cool." Only upon hearing this did Swamishri feel relieved.

Swamishri's repeated inquiries reveal that while he was physically in his room, his heart was walking alongside the devotees in the heat.

title: Servant of Servants
text:
To my dear Pujya Narayanmuni Swami, Pujya Brahmavihari Swami, and all other santos and volunteers,

Jai Swaminarayan from Sadhu Keshavjivandas.

Yesterday's program was wonderful. You all worked exceptionally hard and performed seva despite many hardships, which resulted in a supreme success. However, throughout the entire sabha, the thought kept revolving in my mind that all of this is due to Maharaj and Swami. I am the servant of the servant of the servant of the servant of the servant (das na das...) of Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj, the entire Guru Parampara, and all of you. My only wish is to receive the blessings of everyone.

I ask for forgiveness from the children for the hardships they had to endure. I truly enjoyed meeting all of the children. Truly, the children did wonders!

Thanks to everybody.

Jai Swaminarayan.

title: Thakorji's Comfort
text:
Today, while accompanying Swamishri in the lift for darshan, Vedmangal Swami recalled a memory from Swamishri's visit to Jaipur in 2014.

"The new lift at the Jaipur Mandir was ready for its pujan. When Swamishri returned from lunch, I requested, 'Swami, let us perform the pujan now.' Swamishri politely suggested, 'Would it be alright if we do it at 4:00 PM?' I agreed, though at the time, I did not understand why. However, when Swamishri arrived for his walk at 4:00 PM, the reason became clear. He first instructed me to bring Thakorji down from the mandir. Only then did he perform the ritual. Afterward, I requested photographs, and Swamishri ensured that Thakorji was with him in every single photo."

Had he performed the pujan immediately after lunch, Thakorji would have been resting. Swamishri dictates every schedule around the living presence and comfort of Thakorji.

title: Service Through Study
text:
At 2:15 PM, Swamishri woke from his afternoon rest. After freshening up, he sat on the sofa and gestured for a book with his hands, saying aloud, "HP."

He was asking for a homeopathy book to read and check a specific reference. From 2:30 PM, Swamishri began reading with intense concentration. When Uttamyogi Swami approached at 3:40 PM to retrieve the book, Swamishri simply looked up and gestured that he wished to continue reading.

He read until 3:53 PM, finally calling Uttamyogi Swami to show him the specific reference. Although he had initially intended to only look up one reference, he ended up reading much more. In total, he spent 1 hour and 23 minutes immersed in study.

Swamishri's deep interest in homeopathy is not a mere hobby; it is an extension of his seva, so that he can offer the best guidance to those who seek his help for their ailments.

title: It is Affection
text:
In the evening, Swamishri visited the renovation site of the Bochasan Mandir. As Devkrishna Swami explained the progress, sweat streamed down his face due to the heat. Seeing this, Swamishri instinctively lifted his own gatariyu (upper cloth) and reached out to wipe the sweat from Devkrishna Swami's face. Shocked by this gesture, Devkrishna Swami immediately stepped back, and the other swamis gently stopped Swamishri.

Later in his room, the swamis asked him why he had wiped the sweat. Swamishri answered because he was close. They argued that no one would give their clothes for another's sweat, but Swamishri said, "Affection."

They further asked, "Swami, you are so particular about cleanliness. Didn't you feel any hesitation?"

Swamishri replied with deep emotion, "It is affection and love."

Like a mother who unhesitatingly cleans her child, Swamishri's affection knows no boundaries.

title: The Blossoming Intellect
text:
Swamishri was shown a photograph of Ghanshyambhai and his son, Yogibhai, from Chicago. They explained that every night before bed, they read Satsang books and discuss what they have read.

Swamishri was very pleased to hear this and gave his blessings, saying, "Continue to progress further and further in this way."

Uttamyogi Swami then asked, "What is the benefit of doing this?"

Swamishri replied, "Through this, one gains knowledge of the Sampraday and experiences success in other tasks as well, because once the intellect blossoms, it can be applied everywhere; when the intellect truly flourishes properly, then work can be done."

Swamishri identifies reading and discussions as the catalysts for intellectual growth. Spiritual study is not separate from worldly success; rather, it sharpens the buddhi (intellect).

title: Where the Heart Belongs
text:
Narayanmuni Swami and Brahmavihari Swami had just finished a meeting with Swamishri regarding the upcoming Pramukh Varni Amrut Mahotsav on December 7.

As the discussion ended, Swamishri appeared deep in thought. Noticing this, Brahmavihari Swami asked, "Swami, what are you thinking about?"

Everyone present anticipated a suggestion regarding the festival program or logistics. Instead, Swamishri gently pointed toward a photograph of Tapomurti Shri Nilkanth Varni across the room. Closing his eyes in devotion, he was thinking, "How serene is this murti..."

Though his hands were busy planning a grand festival, his heart did not carry the weight of the work. Like a bird returning to its nest at night, his mind instinctively rushed back to find peace in his beloved, Nilkanth Varni. For him, true rest and uninterrupted bliss are found only in the murti of Bhagwan.

title: Reverence for All
text:
Today, during the sant sabha, Subodhmuni Swami performed the arti of Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj and Swamishri. Afterward, he came forward to offer the arti to Swamishri. At that moment, while still seated, Swamishri leaned forward and reached out to touch Subodhmuni Swami's feet. However, Subodhmuni Swami immediately stopped Swamishri's hand. A brief moment of gentle resistance followed, after which Swamishri said in a slightly raised and firm voice, "I want to touch your feet."

Taken aback, Subodhmuni Swami replied, "You are not supposed to touch [my feet]."

Later, as Swamishri was departing, he was asked, "Swami, why were you trying to touch the feet of this young swami?"

Swamishri replied, "Why not? We have samp, suhradbhav, and ekta. If I touch the feet of one, it is equivalent to touching the feet of all."

His absolute lack of ego drives him to revere all of Bhagwan's devotees.

title: The Three Expectations
text:
In the evening, while Swamishri was engaged in his daily correspondence and reading letters, a swami asked him, "Swami! Which three qualities do you expect from satsangis (devotees)?"

Swamishri concisely replied, "Faith (Nishtha), adherence to moral conduct (Niyam-Dharma), and integrity (Pramanikta)."

By highlighting these three specific virtues, Swamishri provides a clear, actionable blueprint for our daily lives. Nishtha ensures our mind remains anchored in Bhagwan during life's ups and downs. Niyam-Dharma protects our daily spiritual routine. Finally, Pramanikta dictates how we interact with the world—demanding absolute honesty in our workplaces, studies, and relationships. Together, they prove that true devotion is not just what we do in the mandir, but how we live every single day.

title: Unwavering Ahnik
text:
Today, due to a late-running meeting, Swamishri did not sit down for his evening meal until 8:45 PM.

At that moment, Swamishri paused and said, "The arti is still pending."

Uttamyogi Swami informed him, "It is already late, so Thakorji has been put to rest."

However, Swamishri firmly replied, "We will perform it."

With that, Swamishri turned toward the murtis of Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj, Shastriji Maharaj, Yogiji Maharaj, and Pramukh Swami Maharaj displayed on the wall. He performed the entire arti with deep devotion, and only after completing it at 8:50 PM did he finally begin his meal.

This incident is a powerful testament to Swamishri's uncompromising dedication to his ahniks. It serves as a striking reminder that our spiritual observances should never take a backseat to our worldly responsibilities.

title: A Gesture of Care
text:
This afternoon, Swamishri woke up from his rest at 4:30 PM. Immediately, he began moving both of his hands up and down in a rhythmic motion.

Curious, a swami nearby asked, "Swami, what are you trying to say?"

Swamishri simply asked, "Have you done your exercise?"

The swami smiled and replied, "Not yet, but I will do it."

Swamishri's spontaneous inquiry reveals his deep, fatherly concern for the well-being of the swamis. He strongly emphasizes that regular exercise is a vital part of the routine to maintain physical health, as the body is the very instrument we use to serve Bhagwan and others.

title: Performing Mudras
text:
Tonight, before going to sleep, Swamishri spent over half an hour, from 10:22 PM to 10:58 PM, intently reading a book on mudras. Afterward, he sat quietly and performed gnan mudra for 15 minutes.

He then asked for the mudra book once more, reviewing it for another three minutes, before finally retiring to rest at 11:20 PM.

Truly, Swamishri's faith and patience are extraordinary. To sustain such a meticulous, daily practice of mudras late into the night, year after year, requires a level of perseverance that most would find impossible to maintain. Yet, Swamishri performs these mudras not as a chore, but with profound peace and love. Through these simple hand gestures, his mind is not on himself; he is continuously remembering the swamis and devotees, silently praying for the welfare of the entire world.

title: Tireless Dedication
text:
After his evening mandir darshan, Swamishri met with the swamis. Following this, from 6:20 PM to 8:25 PM, he sat for a lengthy and important meeting with Bhaktinandan Swami. During this two-hour meeting, Swamishri was experiencing stomach discomfort and uneasiness, and he had to use the restroom twice.

Despite this physical unease, Swamishri did not let anyone realize the extent of his discomfort. He remained extremely focused, actively participating in the discussion with complete interest and concentration.

From this, we can understand how Swamishri carries out the seva entrusted to him by Pramukh Swami Maharaj. He serves with absolute dedication, completely disregarding his own physical hardships. To witness such profound commitment and tireless service at the age of 92 is truly beyond imagination.

title: The Guarantee of Truth
text:
This evening, yuvaks from North America presented a program before Swamishri during the sabha. Amidst the presentations, a profound question-and-answer session took place.

One of the youths asked, "Swami, when problems arise in life, how can we maintain our courage through the strength of our spiritual attainment (prapti)?"

Swamishri confidently replied, "Keep the firm understanding that Maharaj and Swami are supreme and the all-doers (karta). Move forward with this understanding, because all of this is the absolute truth. If it were false, then take your money back! But it is true, and therefore, wherever you go, you will always emerge victorious."

When we truly understand that the supreme, all-doing Bhagwan is orchestrating our lives, fear dissipates. This conviction becomes our ultimate armor.

title: The Path to Unshakable Faith
text:
As the presentation by the youths from North America continued, another profound question was posed to Swamishri, drawing inspiration from the history of the Sanstha.

A youth asked, "How can we develop the same level of faith (vishwas) that Soma Bhagat had in Shastriji Maharaj?"

Swamishri succinctly replied, "While remaining in agna, firmly uphold agna and upasana, and stay resolute in observing agna."

In his brief answer, Swamishri emphasized the word agna three times. He revealed a beautiful, continuous spiritual cycle: the more we observe our Guru's commands, the deeper our faith grows. Consequently, as our faith becomes more resolute, our commitment to following his commands becomes even firmer. True, unshakable faith is not merely an emotion we wait to feel; it is actively built and sustained through our daily obedience to the Guru.

title: The Ultimate Purpose
text:
As the presentation by the youths from North America continued, a direct and deeply profound question was posed to Swamishri.

A youth asked, "What is the purpose of your birth?"

In response, Swamishri lifted a card that read, "Nishtha Pravartan" (To propagate steadfast faith).

Elaborating on this profound truth, he added, "In nishtha, everything is included."

With this single, powerful gesture, Swamishri revealed the core mission of his life on Earth. His entire existence is dedicated to one subtle yet supreme goal: instilling nishtha, unshakable faith in the supremacy of Bhagwan, within the hearts of devotees. By declaring that "everything is included" in nishtha, he teaches us that once absolute faith is firmly established, all other spiritual virtues like obedience, humility, and unconditional love naturally blossom.

title: The Foundation of Understanding
text:
Based on the afternoon discourse, Adarshjivan Swami sat with Swamishri to delve deeper into the spiritual concepts that had been discussed. He began by asking a fundamental question about recognizing the divine.

Adarshjivan Swami asked, "What should one do to truly understand the [divine] form that is present on Earth?"

Swamishri replied, "Through [following] the niyams given by Maharaj, everything will be understood."

Swamishri immediately establishes that spiritual realization is not merely an intellectual pursuit. Instead, it is a highly practical journey rooted in the foundational disciplines prescribed by Bhagwan Swaminarayan.

title: Bypassing the Intellect
text:
Digging deeper into Swamishri's previous answer, Adarshjivan Swami voiced a common logical doubt regarding the connection between following niyams and understanding the divine form.

Adarshjivan Swami said, "Swami, it doesn't quite settle in the mind that simply by observing niyams, one can recognize the [true] form."

Swamishri responded, "It may not settle in the mind, but if we practice it, the result will surely come."

Swamishri beautifully bypasses human logic. He emphasizes that spiritual truths often transcend our intellectual capacity. However, consistent action and faithful obedience inevitably yield divine results, regardless of whether our mind fully comprehends the process at the start.

title: Understanding the Guru
text:
Continuing with the question-and-answer session, Adarshjivan Swami asked Swamishri about his personal understanding of his own Guru.

He asked, "Swami, how did you understand Yogi Bapa's form?"

Swamishri replied, "In the exact same way as Maharaj resides in Akshardham."

This short answer reveals the depth of Swamishri's absolute spiritual conviction. For him, the Guru on Earth is the exact and present form of Bhagwan, who resides in Akshardham.

title: Faultless Vision
text:
Building on Swamishri's profound understanding of Yogiji Maharaj in the ongoing question-and-answer session, Adarshjivan Swami asked if he ever struggled with human perceptions when observing his Guru's daily, seemingly ordinary actions.

He asked, "While observing Yogi Bapa's [life] incidents, did you ever feel, 'Why did he not take care in this matter?' or 'Why did he appear unaware in this way?'"

Swamishri firmly said no, and added, "There was such absolute innocence (nirdoshbuddhi) that everything appeared entirely divine. Once it is firmly decided that this is the Satpurush, and this form is the very same form as in Akshardham, then no doubts arise. Thereafter, one naturally maintains nirdoshbuddhi."

Swamishri explains that the key to nirdoshbuddhi is making a firm, foundational decision about the Guru's identity.

title: The Master Key of Grace
text:
Understanding that such absolute conviction is rare, Adarshjivan Swami finally asked how a spiritual aspirant can attain this exact state of realization that Swamishri possessed.

Adarshjivan Swami asked, "How does one come to that [firm conviction] even once?"

Swamishri replied, "It happens only if he grants his krupa (grace)."

Immediately, he asked, "Swami, what should we do so that such grace is earned?"

Swamishri said, "Observe niyam-dharma faithfully, loyally, and sincerely—then everything will happen."

The conversation beautifully comes full circle. Ultimate spiritual conviction requires the Guru's krupa, but that krupa is actively earned through our loyalty to niyam-dharma. It is a perfect spiritual cycle: observing niyams earns krupa, krupa grants divine realization, and that realization makes following niyams effortless.

title: Centered Around God
text:
Today, Swamishri performed his morning puja in his room. After completing his puja, he stood up and began to take a brief walk around the room to stretch his legs.

At that time, Thakorji was resting on a stand slightly outside of his walking path. Swamishri gestured for Thakorji to be brought and placed inside the center of the room.

Curious, Shrutipriya Swami asked, "Why did you have Thakorji brought inside?"

Swamishri simply replied, "So I can perform pradakshina (circumambulation) of Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj."

For an ordinary person, a short walk after sitting is merely a physical necessity. However, because Swamishri's mind is constantly anchored in devotion, he instinctively found a way to turn a mundane movement into an act of worship. When Bhagwan is truly at the center of your heart, every ordinary action effortlessly transforms into bhakti.

title: Unshakable Humility
text:
During the question-and-answer session, the following was asked: "Today, devotees from the Mahuva region, the birthplace of Bhagatji Maharaj, have come. Could you please share a special quality of Bhagatji Maharaj that you deeply admire?"

Swamishri replied: "The virtue of Bhagatji Maharaj's nirmanipanu (humility). He endured immense insults and outright humiliation; yet, he never found fault in anyone, not even in the slightest. If it had been anyone else, there would have been fights and brawls. But Bhagatji Maharaj was the Satpurush, so he remained completely unaffected… He roamed in a state of absolute bliss. To endure such hardships and still sing the praises of others is a remarkable trait. Nothing like this has ever occurred in the history of Satsang."

True spiritual strength is not shown by fighting back or defending our ego, but by remaining unaffected by praise or insult.

title: A Resounding Yes
text:
This afternoon, just before the katha, Swamishri experienced physical discomfort and had to clear phlegm from his throat three times.

Despite this unease, if anyone were to ask him about delivering the katha today, he would never refuse. When it comes to katha, Swamishri's answer is always a resounding "yes."

This brief but telling moment reveals Swamishri's profound passion and unwavering devotion toward katha-varta. Even when his physical body is struggling, his spiritual drive to talk about Satsang takes precedence. It is a beautiful reminder that when there is a true, heartfelt eagerness for spiritual discourses, physical excuses naturally fade away.

title: Mutual Divinity
text:
Today marked the first full day of the Yuvak Bharat Yatra. During the introductory sabha, which included the deep pragatya (lamp lighting) ceremony and the welcoming of all the delegates, Swamishri was presented with an official Yatra lanyard.

Taking this opportunity, Swamishri was asked, "What mindset should all the delegates keep in mind throughout this entire trip?"

Without hesitation, Swamishri profoundly replied, "Aras paras divyabhav (Maintain mutual divine vision toward one another)."

Traveling on a long yatra with a large group can naturally bring physical exhaustion, differing opinions, and interpersonal friction. True spirituality is not just about seeing divinity in the Guru or the murti; it is equally about seeing that same divinity in our fellow devotees. When we treat our peers with pure, divine vision, complaints disappear and a physical tour transforms into a spiritual pilgrimage.

title: His Heart's Only Occupants
text:
Tonight, before retiring for the night, Swamishri sat and performed a mudra for 15 minutes. Following this, he spent about 20 minutes intently reading from a book on mudras.

As Swamishri finally prepared to go to sleep, Uttamyogi Swami asked, "While you were performing the mudra just now, what were you thinking about?"

Swamishri simply replied, "I was thinking of Maharaj, Swami, and the devotees."

Even during an activity focused on physical well-being, such as performing a therapeutic mudra late at night, his mind does not wander to worldly matters or even personal relaxation. Instead, his consciousness remains permanently anchored in only thoughts of Bhagwan and His devotees. No matter what action his hands are performing, his heart is exclusively occupied by Maharaj, Swami, and the devotees.

title: Priceless Assets
text:
During his afternoon blessings, Swamishri shared some profoundly practical wisdom. He advised, "We should keep an eye out for the misuse of light (electricity) and other resources. One should not think, 'I will switch off the light tomorrow.' If you notice it, switch off the light immediately. If water is leaking, attention should be drawn to it right away, and arrangements to fix it should be made immediately."

Swamishri then shifted his focus to interpersonal relationships, stating, "Maintaining atmiyata (spiritual harmony and closeness) with everyone is a priceless asset worth millions of dollars."

Finally, on personal spiritual growth, he added, "In satsang, we should never harbor the attitude that we know everything. If we maintain the understanding that we know nothing, only then will something truly meaningful come into our hands."

title: A Midnight Reminder
text:
In the middle of the night, Swamishri woke up to use the bathroom. At 2:40 AM, he returned to his bed to lie down again. At this time, he looked at a half-asleep Uttamyogi Swami, and said, "Prapti!"

Through this single, powerful utterance, Swamishri was conveying a profound message: having attained the supreme Bhagwan and Guru, one should constantly remain in a state of immense joy. It brings to mind the beautiful sentiment, "Piya paaya to phir kya sona..." (When the Beloved has been attained, what need is there to sleep?).

To offer such a deep spiritual teaching in the dead of the night is truly extraordinary. Swamishri's joy and spiritual conviction are not bound by time, physical fatigue, or the hour of the day. Because his heart is constantly awake in the bliss of Bhagwan, he reminds us that the awareness of our spiritual attainment should never sleep.

title: The Color of Faith
text:
Following his daily routine after dinner, Swamishri went for darshan at the sacred rooms of the Gurus. As he was returning from the sabha hall after performing darshan, the sadhaks assisted him in putting on his sandals.

Seizing the moment, one of the sadhaks asked, "Swami! During the Fuldol festival, you completely drenched us in the color of nishtha (firm faith). What must we do to ensure that this color only continues to deepen?"

Swamishri immediately replied, "Agna ([following] commands)!"

In just one word, Swamishri revealed the profound and direct relationship between faith and obedience. Spiritual conviction is not just a passive emotion or a temporary high experienced during a grand festival. Swamishri makes it clear that the more strictly we follow the Guru's commands in our daily lives, the deeper and more permanent the "color" of our faith becomes.

title: No Excuse for Cheshta
text:
On December 13, 2024, Swamishri began an international vicharan tour at the age of 91. Over 107 days, he travelled across two continents, covering around 32,000 kilometres by air, visiting devotees in Africa and Australia before landing back in Surat on April 3, 2025.

Today, after his evening meal, Swamishri's eyelids grew heavy. The jet lag from his recent tour was evident.

Seeing this, one swami began to sing: "Podho podho Sahajānand Swāmi... akhiyā mā nindra bharāni re!" (Sleep now, Sahajanand Swami... your eyes are filled with sleep.)

Hearing these words, Swamishri looked up in surprise. Sitting up straight, he firmly said, "We still need to recite the cheshta. Why are you even talking about sleep?"

Even when truly exhausted, Swamishri's determination was unmistakable: the cheshta must be recited daily.

title: Darshan Before Sleep
text:
"Please turn my chair to face Shastriji Maharaj."

As he did every night, Swamishri enjoyed sitting before the painting on the wall. The artwork depicted a pivotal moment in BAPS history: Shastriji Maharaj meeting his guru, Bhagatji Maharaj, for the first time. Bhagatji Maharaj delivers a discourse while sewing, as young Shastriji Maharaj approaches with eyes shining with awe.

Swamishri fixed his gaze on the painting and recited the cheshta, immersing himself in devotion. After nearly half an hour, the singing came to a close.

Then Swamishri rose from his seat. Everyone expected him to continue with his nightly routine. Instead, he paused. His eyes returned to the painting, studying it as if to take in every brushstroke. After some time, Swamishri explained: "Our last darshan of the night should be of Bhagatji Maharaj and Shastriji Maharaj."

Bhagwan and Guru belong at the very center of our lives.

title: Using Time for Seva
text:
After singing the cheshta, Swamishri approached his bed to lie down. But he suddenly caught sight of the clock. It was 9:40 p.m. Instinctively, he paused, turned back, and began, "It's still..."

"Swami! Please go to bed," the attendant urged, hoping Swamishri might rest earlier that night.

But Swamishri had already moved with determination. "No, bring some letters," he said.

"There are no letters," the attendant replied.

He explained, "All these sadhus are waiting just to have your final darshan. If you rest now, they can leave and take their meal."

Swamishri's voice grew firmer. "I will get up again," he said.

Prabhucharan Swami tried once more. "Swami! You can't read much in five minutes."

But Swamishri insisted, "In five minutes, I can read a lot."

His witty response filled the room with laughter. Swamishri instead spent the time meeting sadhus and devotees one by one, finally lying down at 10:14 p.m.

title: Serving Tirelessly
text:
After a full year of intense preparation, one of the most significant festivals in BAPS history was nearing its start: the centenary celebrations honouring the life and legacy of Pramukh Swami Maharaj. With less than two weeks remaining, every hour felt critical.

The day had been long and demanding. Early in the morning, Swamishri personally toured the vast 600-acre celebration site, listening with full attention as department heads presented their progress and challenges. By evening, he had also performed pujan ceremonies for the murtis of 25 mandirs. Even after taking his evening meal and reciting the cheshta, 89-year-old Swamishri continued blessing and guiding people over the phone, one call after another.

title: Desire to Read
text:
Swamishri was about to retire for the night, but he glanced at the clock, 9:48 p.m., and decided firmly, "It's still early." He expressed a desire to read Purushottam Bolya Prite. However, he also noted, "It will be difficult to read; I will need my glasses."

"Shall we leave it for now?" Uttamyogi Swami suggested, after noticing Swamishri's fatigue from the long day.

Swamishri immediately replied with a solution: "You can read it out loud."

Uttamyogi Swami countered, "Since it will take time for you to bathe before sleeping, perhaps we can read afterwards."

But Swamishri was insistent: "We will do all that later."

"We can read for five minutes," Vinaypriya Swami suggested, trying to find a middle ground.

At once, Swamishri stretched out his hand towards him, gesturing, "What do you mean, just five minutes?"

Accepting Swamishri's wish, they took out the Purushottam Bolya Prite.

title: Read it again
text:
They began to read from Purushottam Bolya Prite: "In Gadhpur, Shri Hari (Bhagwan Swaminarayan) said: I have immense love for one who sees and speaks of sadhus and devotees as nirdosh (pure-hearted and divine)."

Then Swamishri shared his thoughts: "This alone is what we must do. What a beautiful teaching. You don't have to give or take anything, not even a penny, and yet the gain is immense. Read it again."

The passage was read a second time, and Swamishri explained, "What [spiritual] wealth! Such immense affection! Shriji Maharaj has the highest love for such a person. Is that any small matter? Such immense affection... for whom? Read it again."

Vinaypriya Swami read the passage for a third and fourth time, upon Swamishri's request.

title: Read it again
text:
After Vinaypriya Swami finished reading, Swamishri said, "If you so much as look at faults, everything gets cancelled. Maharaj speaks directly: 'You must see them as nirdosh.' That is the starting point."

With that, Swamishri began reciting the teaching himself for the fifth time, then explaining: "He says to speak about them as nirdosh. Someone may see virtues yet still go around talking about faults. But that is just worthless chatter, rubbish, nonsense. Maharaj says it plainly and completely clear. His words are straight and direct like an airport runway."

"But because people lack maturity inside, they don't understand this. So all kinds of long, complicated ideas appear, and the simple, runway-like clarity disappears. What can you do?"

"We have to see everyone as nirdosh," the attendants affirmed.

Swamishri replied, "Good. Read it again." He paused and then exclaimed, "Read it ten more times!"

title: Read it again
text:
Everyone laughed as Swamishri's genuine joy became contagious.

The momentum grew as the passage was read and discussed ten more times, until everyone could recall it from memory.

On the fifteenth reading, Swamishri again poured out his feelings: "Immense affection! When a child clings to you, you feel so much love for them. In the same way, if we live by this teaching, Shriji Maharaj will cling to us. What more could be said? But we don't think about it. We just read it and move on. We should reflect on it a little. Not even much, just a little. Even if you read it twice, that is enough. Read it again."

title: What can we do?
text:
Vinaypriya Swami read the passage for the sixteenth time. Then Swamishri emphasized, "This is the teaching worth practising. Look at the difference: where is Shriji Maharaj and where are we? We are like bacteria. And yet he has such immense love for us. Just hold on to this, only this, and drink it in, sip by sip."

With that, the explanation seemed complete, but then, as if another wave rose in his heart, Swamishri said, "Maharaj has given us heaps of this, but none of it really sinks in... Now what can we do?"

In response, Uttamyogi Swami recited the passage for the seventeenth time.

Only then did Swamishri feel fully satisfied. After completing his nightly routine, he finally lay down to rest at 11:00 p.m.

After a gruelling day of serving others, Swamishri still made time to reflect on God's wisdom. Genuine service draws its strength from personal devotion.

title: Not Just a Routine
text:
Tonight, Swamishri was scheduled for an eye check-up after completing his nightly routine. During the recitation of the cheshta, the optician entered the room to administer eye drops in preparation.

Once the cheshta concluded, Swamishri went for the examination. Afterwards, he returned to his room and prepared to rest. As he was about to lie down, he said, "I want to recite the cheshta."

The attendant replied, "We have already recited it."

Swamishri explained, "While it was being recited, my eyes were uncomfortable and I was distracted. I could not recite it properly. So, I want to do it again."

title: Not Just a Routine
text:
Thinking that Swamishri was repeating it for his sake, perhaps because he had not been fully attentive, the attendant humbly offered, "I will recite it again."

But Swamishri insisted, "I want to recite it myself."

The attendant reassured him, "I give you my word, I will recite the whole cheshta again."

Still, Swamishri was resolute, "But I still want to recite it again. Whether you do it or not, I will recite it."

Hearing this, the attendant could not hold back and finally said, "There is no need for you to do it again."

Swamishri grew serious. "I will not break my niyam," he said firmly. "Look, it will only take half an hour, and I will be awake anyway." Hearing the conviction in his tone and seeing the sternness on his face, the attendant at once understood.

title: Not Just a Routine
text:
With that, Swamishri began reciting the entire cheshta once more. He sang softly, savouring each moment and revelling in bliss as if the world had slipped away.

When the recitation was complete, the clock reached precisely 11:11:11 p.m. Seeing the time, Swamishri beamed with joy and concluded, "Purna Purushottam Narayan Shri Swaminarayan Bhagwan ni Jay," and then lay down to rest.

For Swamishri, following a niyam like the cheshta is never about merely checking off a box before bed. It requires genuine focus, devotion, and attention. His firmness to re-recite it completely demonstrates that true spirituality is not about rushing through our daily observances, but doing them with absolute presence of mind and love for Bhagwan.

title: Kāle, Kāle, Kāle
text:
At night, Swamishri joined the cheshta recitation. His voice was soft yet steady, his presence filling the room.

When it ended, Santcharit Swami said with concern, "Bapa, you've done so much today!"

"Why?" Swamishri asked, looking mildly surprised.

"You still have a cold, yet you met devotees, gave samip darshan, offered blessings... Now it's time to rest."

"I still have to write letters," Swamishri replied firmly.

The illness showed in his face and voice. So, Uttamyogi Swami suggested, "Write them tomorrow."

"Kāle, kāle, kāle – always tomorrow!" Swamishri responded, his tone showing his dislike for delaying seva.

title: Kāle, Kāle, Kāle
text:
"It's not urgent," the attendant reasoned.

"It is urgent," Swamishri insisted, his words now heavier.

Others joined in, appealing with care: "Bapa, tomorrow you will have time during the day. If you rest tonight, your cold will recover sooner. Doctors advise, 'The more you sleep, the quicker you heal.'"

But Swamishri stayed seated, resolute. Finally, in a slow, deliberate voice, he repeated, "I have to write the letters."

"We'll do it tomorrow, after your morning rest," said one attendant a little more firmly.

Still, Swamishri insisted.

title: Kāle, Kāle, Kāle
text:
At that moment, Shrutipriya Swami entered carrying the bag of letters. "Swami, honestly, there's nothing urgent right now," he said, his tone persuasive. "You need rest. Please sleep."

This time, Swamishri agreed and lay down.

The attendants stood in awe. At 89, even when ill, Swamishri's spirit to serve still shone: steadfast, selfless, and sincere. His sharp rejection of "kāle" (tomorrow) is a powerful reminder that when it comes to serving Bhagwan and His devotees, there is no time better than the present.

title: Eight Interruptions
text:
In 2008, Swamishri, at the age of 74, pressed on with his vicharan at a tireless pace. On April 18, he travelled from Kolkata to Mumbai and onward to South Gujarat, moving through the tribal villages of Navsari, Bilimora, Dharampuri, and Vaghai, before arriving in Saputara to serve in the Dang district.

One night during his stay, around 10 p.m., Swamishri sat down to recite the cheshta.

Not long after he began, someone approached seeking guidance. Swamishri paused, listened patiently, and offered his advice and prayers before restarting the cheshta from the beginning. A little later, the same person returned with another matter. Once again, Swamishri gave him his full attention, resolved the concern, and began the cheshta anew.

This happened four times. The same person returned again and again with fresh issues. Swamishri never grew frustrated, nor did he brush him aside.

title: Eight Interruptions
text:
Others also came forward with their questions and tasks. Swamishri could easily have asked them to wait; it would have been perfectly reasonable, but he never did. Instead, he placed their needs before his own, listening to each person in turn before resuming his devotion.

In all, the cheshta was interrupted eight times. Yet never once did he show haste or irritation. Patient and unhurried, he began again and again, until, after an hour and a half, the cheshta was finally completed.

That night in Saputara revealed more than Swamishri's patience; it showed where his heart truly rested. He never sought to be understood, only to understand. He gave without expectation, wholeheartedly and without burden, and each time he returned to Bhagwan's remembrance with the same freshness.

title: Love for Nilkanth Varni
text:
This morning, Swamishri arrived to perform the pratishtha (consecration) ceremony of the grand Tapomurti Nilkanth Varni. Elevated by a crane, he reached directly in front of the magnificent murti.

During the ceremony, Shrutipriya Swami asked a few questions, to which Swamishri's heartfelt sentiments flowed naturally.

Swamishri said, "This murti is immensely grand, divine, and extraordinary! Whoever does darshan of this murti will attain Akshardham, and their pure desires will be fulfilled. May Nilkanth Varni bless everyone with divine happiness, and may no one harbor worldly desires... Bhagwan wants a pure heart. Therefore, we should pray to Bhagwan with a pure heart."

Swamishri's love for Bhagwan overflowed in this divine moment. It illustrates that his entire life is fundamentally God-centric and every quality he possesses is rooted in nothing but his singular devotion to Bhagwan.

title: The Inspiration of Austerity
text:
Later, Swamishri was requested to share his blessings. He began with a resounding "Tapomurti Nilkanth Varni Maharaj ni... Jay!" and shared the following:

"Upon doing darshan of this Tapomurti, the mind becomes completely still. Looking at it, we should reflect on Nilkanth Varni—what an extraordinary Bhagwan He is! He performed immense, astonishing austerities (tap). He remained on freezing ice for six months, surviving only on air. Even with today's modern equipment, one could not perform such austerities. And Maharaj fearlessly wandered through dense jungles among wild animals, simply for the kalyan of all. What selfish motive did He have? Absolutely nothing.

"May everyone be inspired to perform austerities. We must do at least a little bit of tap. Do not just keep eating constantly."

By practicing self-control with a pure heart, we honor Bhagwan Swaminarayan's life.

title: Naturally Woven Smruti
text:
Once in Nenpur, Swamishri was asked about how he stays connected to his gurus through smruti (remembrance), and how he reinforced that habit at night:

"How do you do smruti?"

Swamishri replied, "While brushing, I remember Yogi Bapa using a datan (a twig used as a natural toothbrush). When I sit down to eat, I recall, 'How would Yogi Bapa eat?' In this way, I've organized my mind to connect those memories naturally with my daily routine."

Then Swamishri paused and shared a cherished memory:

"Once, Yogi Bapa had injured his hand. While washing his hands, he needed my assistance. That moment comes to mind vividly. I remember him naturally, not just by a fixed method or place. But yes, smruti is incredibly valuable."

title: Naturally Woven Remembrance
text:
Swamishri was asked, "Did you reflect upon those moments on the day of the event?"

"Usually, during the night goshthi (around 10:00 p.m.) each person shares what they learnt and experienced that day. So yes, that very day."

"Do you recall everything or only specific moments?"

"Specific moments."

"And with what mindset do you recall these moments?"

"Āpana dhanya-bhāgya chhe - we are fortunate to have met such a guru."

Swamishri reveals that true smruti is not merely a scheduled activity, but a continuous state of mind seamlessly woven into daily life. By intentionally linking ordinary, everyday actions, like brushing teeth or eating a meal, to memories of his Guru, he maintains an unbroken connection to the divine. Ultimately, this natural remembrance is driven by an overwhelming sense of gratitude for having attained such an extraordinary Guru.

title: Directly In Front of Me
text:
Swamishri was asked, "In 1997, when you were doing vicharan in Australia and New Zealand, every night before going to sleep, you would gather the sadhus and ask, 'Where do you think Pramukh Swami Maharaj is today?' Then you would recall memories of him. So, along with all your daily activities, it is clear that the remembrance and connection to the Satpurush have always been central to your life."

Swamishri replied, "Yes... I remember him as if he were here before me, directly in front of me."

For Swamishri, recalling his Guru isn't merely an exercise in nostalgia; it is a vivid, living reality. By keeping Pramukh Swami Maharaj constantly in his thoughts, Swamishri experiences his Guru's presence directly in front of him, proving that physical distance is meaningless when a spiritual connection is absolute.

title: Dedication to Seva
text:
After completing the recitation of the cheshta, Swamishri expressed a wish to spend some time writing letters. Settling himself in place, ready with pen and paper, he began his work.

But almost immediately, he gave a big yawn, and then yawned again. One attendant, noticing, teased: "Akhiyā mā nindrā bharāni re... – Your eyes are filled with sleep."

Swamishri looked up, dismissing the call of sleep, and replied in kind, "Tamāre bharāni – yours are filled with sleep."

In truth, Swamishri must have been tired; the day had been long. But he brushed it aside and continued with his task. For the next 43 minutes he gave his full attention to the letters, replying with the same care and thoughtfulness as always. Only when the work was done did he sleep.

For him, correspondence was never routine paperwork—it was a way to bless and uplift hearts, one message at a time.

title: Six Hours of Reflection
text:
One attendant described Swamishri's deep and meticulous method of studying the shastras.

"Swamishri has been reading Purushottam Bolya Prite for many years, but he's only gotten through sixty pages - because he reflects on each word deeply.

"Once, while travelling together, we read a single passage from the Vachanamrut, and then Swami closed the book, shut his eyes, and remained immersed in thought for six hours."

This instance highlights Swamishri's profound dedication to spiritual study and his ability to find spiritual bliss even in the midst of a demanding schedule.

title: It's Still Early…
text:
Today, Swamishri was experiencing a slight cold. Even while meeting devotees, the discomfort continued to trouble him. By the time he had finished reciting the cheshta and completing his nightly routine, it was already 10:15 p.m.

It would have been perfectly reasonable for Swamishri to rest. Instead, he looked up at the clock and said with determination, "It's still early... I'd like to read Prakash."

Honoring his wish, the attendant picked up the Swaminarayan Prakash magazine and began reading aloud an article entitled 'Prayer'. Swamishri listened attentively, his face calm and absorbed, taking in every word with genuine focus.

Only once the reading had concluded did he rest, content at having squeezed in a little more satsang into his day.

title: Freezing in the Desert
text:
When Swamishri retired for the night, the attendant asked, "Swami, what would you like to cover yourself with – a shawl or a blanket?"

Smiling as a memory surfaced, Swamishri said, "Once in Muscat, in the desert, I actually felt cold. They had turned the AC up so high! I was freezing, right there in the middle of the desert."

"So you were freezing in the midst of the burning desert!" one of the sadhus exclaimed, amused by the irony.

Swamishri nodded. "Yes."

title: Freezing in the Desert
text:
Vednayan Swami grew curious. "But didn't you have the AC switched off?"

"I didn't know how to, and it was central AC. Everyone had gone downstairs."

"Was it a night stay at someone's home?" Brahmavatsal Swami asked.

"Yes, at the home of one of the volunteers."

"If you were so cold, what did you do? Just tolerate it?"

"Yes."

title: Freezing in the Desert
text:
"Were you able to sleep?"

"No."

"You just stayed awake?"

"Yes."

Silence fell. The sadhus knew this Swamishri well, yet each time they were struck anew. Time and again, they had seen him endure heat, cold, illness, and hardship without complaint. If it meant sparing others inconvenience, he would simply remain silent.

title: Freezing in the Desert
text:
Then one sadhu enquired further, "What were you doing while awake all night? Were you remembering God?"

"Yes... I did what I needed to do," Swamishri admitted.

His thoughts rested on God, never straying to his discomfort. Instead, he simply smiled: a calm, unassuming smile. In that one expression, they saw what it truly meant to live for others.

In this incident, Swamishri's profound sahan-shilata shone through. Instead of waking up his hosts to adjust the AC, he chose to silently endure a freezing, sleepless night so they could rest. More remarkably, he didn't spend the night dwelling on his physical discomfort; he used the quiet hours to connect with God. His unassuming smile years later reveals that for him, sacrificing his own comfort to spare others is not a burden, but a natural expression of selfless love.

title: Straight from the Heart
text:
It was 10:29 p.m., and Swamishri was preparing to rest for the night. Just then, Shrutipriya Swami informed him about a student in London who had not been accepted to the University of Cambridge for his master's degree.

Swamishri had taken a keen interest in this student's progress. The youth simply wanted to share the news and hadn't expected anything more. Shrutipriya Swami, too, intended only to pass on the message.

But the moment Swamishri heard the news, he said at once, "Phone him."

Shrutipriya Swami tried to reassure him that it was late and the day had been long, and that he could speak to the youth another time. It was not urgent.

Yet, Swamishri was insistent. "No, phone him now."

The call was placed, but the youth did not pick up. He was on an underground train with no reception. A message was left. Within minutes, he stepped onto the platform, and when he phoned back, the first voice he heard was Swamishri's.

title: Straight from the Heart
text:
Normally, Swamishri would listen first, allowing the other person to speak. But this time, before the youth could say a word, Swamishri spoke straight from the heart:

"Something good must be meant to happen in the future. We just can't see it yet. God is never against his devotee. Whatever he does will always be for the best. You must not feel disheartened. God is looking after your moksha. He weighs everything in terms of satsang and moksha, and whatever he does, it is always for our good. Sometimes we feel, 'This didn't happen' or 'That didn't work out,' but Shriji Maharaj takes everything into account for our liberation, and for satsang, and places things exactly as they need to be. So even though we may be intelligent or capable, if we still don't get something, that too is God's doing. We should simply remain content."

title: Straight from the Heart
text:
Swamishri continued guiding the student, giving him hope and strength. Then, summarizing his words of encouragement, he concluded softly, "Āpde rāji rahevu, Bhagwān je kare e, ha – whatever Bhagwan does, we should remain happy."

Swamishri's words were filled with profound wisdom, yet his tone was that of a loving father. The youth became emotional on hearing such care. In that one call, he was struck by how Swamishri placed the needs of others above his own. When no one had asked him to, when he could so easily have rested, when the youth never expected it, Swamishri still chose to give, and he gave straight from the heart.

title: Eager for the Morning
text:
After performing the Bharuch patotsav, Swamishri travelled to Saring village for a murti-pratishtha. By the time he returned to Bharuch that night, it was already 11 p.m. Seeing his exhaustion, Anirdesh Swami said, "Swami, today has been a long and gruelling day. Tomorrow, please begin only after having a full rest."

But Swamishri smiled and replied, "I am eagerly waiting for the morning."

Puzzled, Anirdesh Swami asked, "Why are you so eager for the morning?"

He answered with joy, "So I can read the Vachanamrut! Even at night, I look forward to holding it in my hands the next morning. It brings me such joy and interest."

title: Eager for the Morning
text:
In 2025, Adarshjivan Swami reminded Swamishri of this moment. Once again, Swamishri's face lit up as he shared his approach to studying shastras:

"When I start reading the Vachanamrut, I read just one segment, and rarely finish it in a single sitting. For three or four days, I keep reflecting on it. Now, if someone simply reads through it quickly, nothing really stays with them. But the deeper you go, the more you ruminate and reflect, the more joy you experience. Even now, new insights keep emerging all the time."

Hearing Swamishri's enthusiasm, Adarshjivan Swami remarked: "That's why you are truly a devoted student of the Vachanamrut."

By reflecting slowly on passages over several days, he teaches that spiritual joy stems from deep digestion and rumination rather than speed.

title: Prayers for the Voiceless
text:
After Swamishri finished his evening meal, Vimalseva Swami and Adarshmuni Swami shared a detailed report about the ravaging bushfires in Australia. "Because of the fires, already more than half a billion animals and birds have perished."

Swamishri's heart dropped. "It has to rain," he whispered. "That is the only solution. Bhagwan's wish will prevail."

Although Swamishri continued with his routine, his mind remained absorbed in thoughts of the fires. Halfway through the recitation of cheshta, the attendant placed an ice pack on his right foot to soothe Swamishri's foot pain.

When the cheshta concluded, Swamishri looked over as the ice pack was removed and asked, "Was that on my foot?"

The attendant replied, "Yes, Swami."

"I didn't even realize…" Swamishri said softly.

title: Prayers for the Voiceless
text:
Immediately, the attendant touched Swamishri's foot to check whether the ice pack was still cold. The area was chilled through, showing that the ice pack had been cold the entire time. He guided Swamishri's hand to feel it. Swamishri expressed his surprise, "Yes, it's very cold!" Then, again, he repeated, "But I didn't feel it at all."

Rahulbhai, who was assisting with Swamishri's physiotherapy, observed, "Swami, you normally don't like the cold, not even for a second, and yet you didn't notice this! It's really astonishing…"

Later, Uttamyogi Swami asked Swamishri, "Why didn't you feel the ice pack on your foot?"

Swamishri replied, "While reciting cheshta, I was also praying for Australia."

Everyone was stunned. Swamishri had become so immersed in prayer that he felt no sensation from the ice pack.

title: Prayers for the Voiceless
text:
After giving darshan to the sadhus, Swamishri lay down to rest at 10:20 p.m. But at 10:53 p.m., he looked up and requested his mala with a gesture. While turning the mala, he prayed continuously until 11:32 p.m.

In those 39 minutes, bead by bead, Swamishri turned his mala. Each moment was a prayer for the voiceless, an offering for those who could not ask for help, yet were carried tenderly in the heart of a sant thousands of miles away.

His prayers did not remain as thoughts alone. Under Swamishri's guidance, volunteers mobilized to bring relief to the stricken areas, transforming his compassion into organized service.

While physically in Surat, his heart was entirely with the suffering animals in Australia. His empathy was so profound that his prayers completely overrode his physical senses. True spiritual leadership combines heartfelt prayer with practical, organized relief for all living beings.

title: Clockwork Devotion
text:
Swamishri recited the cheshta as part of his nightly routine and then listened to the biography of Pramukh Swami Maharaj. After taking a bath, he returned to his room. The time was around 11:01 p.m., and when he glanced at the clock, a wide smile appeared on his face.

On 22 May 2020, Swamishri began a thoughtful and endearing habit, inspired by the symmetrical patterns on his digital clock. When a sequence like 11:11:11 appeared, he would treat it as a reminder to remember God and joyfully offer a devotional "Jay!"

title: Clockwork Devotion
text:
He had even created a unique expression for each time:

1:11:11 or 11:11:11 – "Purna Purushottam Narayan Shri Swaminarayan Bhagwan ni Jay!" or "Sahajanand Swami Maharaj ni Jay!"

2:22:22 – "Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj ni Jay!"

3:33:33 – "Dhām, Dhāmi, Mukta ni Jay!"

4:44:44 – "Dhām, Dhāmi, Mukta ne Haribhakta ni Jay!"

5:55:55 – "Panch Tattva ni Jay!"

For the past three weeks, the attendants had watched Swamishri anticipate these moments with joy. His delight became theirs too, and the experience left an impression on everyone present.

title: Clockwork Devotion
text:
That evening, as the hour neared again, Swamishri looked at the clock and said with childlike enthusiasm, "Last night, I caught them all: one, two, three, four, and five!"

An attendant replied with a grin, "Swami, that's not something to be proud of. It just means you haven't been sleeping! You're staying awake for those numbers."

Swamishri remained silent, but the knowing smile on his face said it all.

Another attendant teased, "We're thinking of changing the clock. Let's replace the digital one with an analogue clock. That way, maybe you'll actually get some rest!"

Laughing, Swamishri lay back on his bed. The time was 11:08 p.m. Only a few minutes remained.

Turning to Uttamyogi Swami, he requested, "Until then, recall some Swamini Vato."

title: Clockwork Devotion
text:
Uttamyogi Swami began to recite the sayings of Gunatitanand Swami. He shared one after another, his voice filling the room. By the time he had reached the tenth, the clock read 11:11:06.

Swamishri fixed his gaze on the numbers, watching them inch closer with expectation. The moment the digits aligned – 11:11:11 – he raised his hand and joyfully proclaimed, "Sahajanand Swami Maharaj ni Jay!"

Swamishri's endearing engagement with a simple digital clock reveals a profound spiritual truth: a true devotee will find any excuse to remember God. What an attendant jokingly pointed out as a reason for lost sleep was, for Swamishri, a cherished opportunity to express his devotion. By filling even the few waiting minutes with spiritual discourses, he demonstrates how to turn mundane, everyday moments into continuous joy and remembrance.

title: Waiting for the Satpurush
text:
As part of his regular routine, Swamishri recited the cheshta and listened to the biography of Pramukh Swami Maharaj. He then went for his nightly bath, returned, and lay down. The attendants were hoping Swamishri would fall straight to sleep.

But, as he had done in recent days, Swamishri looked at the clock. It was 11:02 p.m. With a tinge of concern, he asked, "Did it pass?"

One attendant replied, "No, Swami, there are still nine minutes left... there's plenty of time. So please rest."

Swamishri said, "My eyes are closed, but my mind is still there!"
