title: Waiting for the Satpurush
text:
The attendants laughed and asked, "So shall we wait and see, and then sleep?"

Swamishri replied, "Yes."

Even so, thinking Swamishri might eventually drift off, the attendants turned off the lights. Swamishri closed his eyes but remained fully awake. From time to time, he would open one eye and glance at the clock. It was now certain: Swamishri would not sleep without seeing 11:11:11.

To help pass the time, the attendants recited a few poems. Swamishri was pleased and shared his own wordplay: "Three lions!"

title: Waiting for the Satpurush
text:
One attendant looked puzzled and asked, "What does that mean?"

Uttamyogi Swami laughed and explained: "Earlier, we were talking about how doing one Ekadashi is worth trillions in blessings."

Then Swamishri broke the word trillions into two parts:

tri (pronounced like three)

lions

So, 'trillions' became 'three lions'! Swamishri said that to complete a waterless fast on Ekadashi and stay awake until midnight, you need the bravery of three lions.

Everyone was delighted by Swamishri's clever and playful wisdom.

title: Waiting for the Satpurush
text:
At 11:10 p.m., Swamishri grew a little eager. To an attendant standing nearby, he said, "Please move aside, I want to see the clock."

Then Swamishri asked, "One minute left?"

"Yes, Swami. Just one minute."

Swamishri then remarked, "One must wait like this... for the Satpurush!"

The attendant responded in awe. Once again, Swamishri had drawn out an enigmatic insight from something so simple!

title: Waiting for the Satpurush
text:
On the wall clock, 11:11:01 appeared. Swamishri raised his hands, took a deep breath, and readied himself.

Tick, tick, tick...

At 11:11:11, he joyfully proclaimed, "Purna Purushottam Narayan Shri Swaminarayan Bhagwan ni Jay!"

The attendants burst out laughing.

Swamishri's gaze now turned to the second clock in the room, which ran about thirty seconds behind. He squinted with one eye, focused intently, and as soon as it showed 11:11:01, he again joyfully declared, "Purna Purushottam Narayan Shri Swaminarayan Bhagwan ni Jay!"

The attendants, laughing, said, "Swami! There's still time... slowly... slowly…"

Swamishri simply raised his hands. Another wave of laughter rippled through the room.

title: Enough! Enough!
text:
The following night, on 17 June, at 10:58 p.m., Swamishri glanced at the clock as the attendants anticipated what would come next. But to their surprise...

Swamishri raised his hand and said, "Yes. Enough! Enough!" He then made an 'X' sign in the air, as if to close the chapter.

The attendants were stunned. Just that afternoon, Swamishri had still shown so much interest, and now, just like that...

One swami asked, "Is this practice finished now?"

Swamishri replied firmly, "Yes."

At the request of Shrutipriya Swami, Swamishri chose to stop staying awake to watch the clock. He let go of the habit with remarkable ease. He had begun on May 22, 2020 and concluded on June 17, 2020. For 27 days, he created joyful memories for those around him, all centred on remembering God.

Though he no longer stayed up, now and again, if the numbers aligned, he would still call out 'Jay!', lighting up the room with joy.

title: Moved to Respond
text:
In 2015, Mahant Swami Maharaj visited the UK for vicharan. At the close of this visit, the female volunteers of the national Yuvak-Yuvati (youth) Mandal prepared a brief two-page report on behalf of the whole mandal, summarizing their recent activities. Anandpriya Swami, the lead sadhu of the Yuvak Mandal, presented it to Swamishri, making it clear that no reply was necessary. Yet, after reading it, Swamishri was moved to respond with a letter.

He was especially pleased to see volunteers from every mandal and department come together nationally to make two major festivals a success, reflecting an enthusiasm and spiritual maturity that sustained their satsang duties amid personal, professional, and family demands.

This letter was written on the night before his departure for India. Though tired and knowing he would rise early for a 7:15 a.m. flight, he began writing at 11:25 p.m. and finished at 12:10 a.m.

title: Fostering Harmony
text:
During a question-and-answer session, Swamishri was asked about his practice of reciting the cheshta.

A question was posed: "Why do you always insist on reciting the cheshta together as a group?"

Swamishri explained with conviction, "When everyone gathers, it increases samp and suhradbhav. Reciting together rather than individually fosters a spirit of harmony."

Ultimately, Swamishri shows that fostering harmony among devotees is the highest aim, transforming even the nightly cheshta into a moment of shared spiritual unity.

title: No Compromises
text:
It was 8:30 p.m. Swamishri was about to begin dinner. The preparatory period of the lunar eclipse would begin in just thirty minutes. As per the observances prescribed by Hindu shastras, one should refrain from eating for a set period before and during an eclipse, and remain awake during the eclipse to engage in devotional practices.

Swamishri had followed these observances his whole life. Casually, he asked, "Is everyone going to stay awake tonight?"

"Yes, Swami, it's a full-night eclipse," the attendant replied.

"In that case, I should eat less…" Swamishri said to himself.

The attendants paused in surprise. They suddenly realized he fully intended to observe the eclipse, even at his advanced age.

"Swami, you should rest. You are 90 years old and have already endured so much," they urged.

"Why? It's an eclipse! One must stay awake during an eclipse," he replied matter-of-factly, his face beginning to show resolve.

title: No Compromises
text:
"But you've already observed plenty of eclipses," the attendants reasoned.

At this, Swamishri's expression changed. He was visibly displeased, even trembling slightly. Nothing unsettled him more than compromising religious observances. However, the sadhus, knowing that shastras exempt anyone over 80 from certain duties, were only concerned for his health.

Swamishri respected the exemptions for the elderly. Yet for himself, he felt satisfaction in following Bhagwan Swaminarayan's instructions, not in seeking an easier path. That night, he ate only 30-40% of his already small dinner portion, resolute to observe the eclipse with everyone else.

When the eclipse began at 11:30 p.m., Swamishri went straight to recite the cheshta. The attendants offered him a sofa, but he declined with a smile: "I'll fall asleep in that!" Determined to remain alert, he sat on a simple chair and sang with complete devotion until 3:00 a.m.

title: #No Compromises
text:
Then at 3:05 a.m., Swamishri entered the assembly hall. Instantly, the atmosphere shifted; faces lit up and fatigue melted away. "Swamishri," Apurvamuni Swami teased, "we've been keeping everyone awake with presentations and kirtans, but with your arrival, no one feels sleepy!"

From 3:05 to 3:30 a.m., as photos and videos played, Adarshjivan Swami and Vedchintan Swami drew Swamishri into memories of landmark festivals of the last six decades where he served at the forefront.

Recalling the 1981 Bicentenary Celebration of Bhagwan Swaminarayan, Swamishri shared how, despite being unwell, he had tirelessly served each day under the blazing sun, working on the landscape decorations. Asked what kept him going, he said simply, "For one's guru, what would you not do?" When asked why he did the seva himself, he replied, "If it's for the guru, I must do it myself; just ordering others is not enough."

title: No Compromises
text:
Later, given the mic to bless the gathering, he said, "One must observe the eclipse properly. Yogi Bapa has taught us this: no compromises."

At 90, Mahant Swami had done just that, spending the four-and-a-half-hour eclipse in spiritual discussion, devotion, and seva without a trace of drowsiness. Serving tirelessly under the sun in 1981 and observing the eclipse in full this very night embodied the same sentiment: to personally offer devotion to God and guru with perfection.

At 4:00 a.m., as the eclipse drew to a close, Apurvamuni Swami requested, "Bhagwan Swaminarayan would personally embrace all those who stayed awake during an eclipse. If you embrace us all, it will make this night truly fruitful."

Swamishri stretched his arms wide without hesitation, as if embracing everyone present. Then everyone began chanting the Swaminarayan mantra, and Swamishri closed his eyes in deep devotion as the eclipse came to an end.

title: No Compromises
text:
At 4:15 a.m., he left for his accommodation and yawned for the first time all night. Shrutipriya Swami suggested that, in the future, Swamishri should extend his arms a little less when embracing large groups to ease the strain.

Swamishri disagreed: "It must be done! [Because of] Love!"

"But it causes you pain," responded Shrutipriya Swami.

"That's fine, it only hurts for half an hour!" Swamishri said casually.

It struck everyone present: nobody had known that embracing devotees in this way caused him pain, and it left the sadhus wondering how many such 'half-hours of pain' Swamishri had borne over the decades, all for the joy of others.

When dawn broke at 5:00 a.m, his daily program continued as normal: he sought no extra rest, lessened no devotion, and missed no moment to serve or inspire. He stepped into the new day exactly as he had lived at night.

title: I Belong to Whoever Wants Me
text:
At 12:30 p.m., Swamishri sat down for his meal. Digantbhai Sadhak approached him to get a signature to keep as a smruti. However, the paper was blank. Because of this, Digantbhai started joking with Swamishri: "You are signing a blank piece of paper. So now, whatever I write on it, you will have to give it to me."

Swamishri gently replied, "Yes."

Digantbhai then said, "In that case, let me write down 'Akshardham'."

Swamishri, with a generous heart, said, "Granted."

Feeling even more playful, Digantbhai asked, "What if I ask for even more than that?" He clarified his wish: "I will write down [your name]... You will have to come with me."

Swamishri gave a profound reply: "I belong to whoever wants me…"

Anyone who has a true desire for liberation and his presence will have that wish granted. The Satpurush is bound not by conditions, but purely by the spiritual longing of the devotee.

title: A Midnight Surprise
text:
Swamishri suddenly sat up in bed and began repeating, "Goshthi, goshthi, goshthi…"

"What do you mean, Swami?" Uttamyogi Swami asked.

Swamishri reached out and gave the attendant a light tap on the head. "Silly," he said softly, then repeated more firmly, "Goshthi!"

"But we haven't planned a goshthi."

"I want to go there and have a goshthi," Swamishri explained, pointing towards the letter-writing office.

Uttamyogi Swami hesitated. "Everyone is already awake and engaged in their own activities," he said gently.

title: A Midnight Surprise
text:
Swamishri remained resolute. "What about online? Let's do an online goshthi."

"It only works if everyone has planned to join."

"If we start a goshthi, everyone else will join," he insisted.

"If you want, I'll contact everyone by phone."

Swamishri nodded. Uttamyogi Swami sent out the messages, and Swamishri walked to the correspondence room as everyone slowly began to gather.

It was Ekadashi, and at Swamishri's encouragement, all had stayed awake until midnight to observe a waterless fast, a tradition that blended fasting with late-night devotion as an act of spiritual discipline.

title: A Midnight Surprise
text:
One by one, the swamis trickled into the room, slightly anxious. They sat cross-legged on the floor like students before their headmaster, eyes fixed on Swamishri. What could be so urgent that he had called a meeting at such a late hour?

Then, with a smile, Swamishri broke the tension with a simple explanation:

"I just wanted to see if you were awake."

Laughter and smiles spread across every face, the mood lifted in an instant.

With that, Swamishri steered the gathering into a discussion on Yogiji Maharaj's teachings from the Yogi Gita.

In this lighthearted and endearing moment, Swamishri demonstrates his profound ability to blend strict spiritual discipline with playful affection. He shows that true spiritual vigilance is sustained not just by strict adherence, but by joy, unity, and a loving connection with the Satpurush.

title: The Simplest Path
text:
Swamishri gave the ninth lesson of Brahmavidya (divine knowledge): "The simple means of becoming Brahmarup is Satsang activity."

Explaining this further, he said: "Becoming Brahmarup and becoming an Ekantik devotee is our only goal. Keeping the mind engaged in Satsang activities is the simplest way to become Brahmarup."

This teaching emphasizes that spiritual liberation isn't found through complex rituals alone, but through active participation in Satsang activities. By keeping the mind focused on these tasks, a person naturally evolves toward a divine state.

title: The True Knowledge
text:
In the evening, Swamishri was engaged in his daily routine of reading and replying to letters. During this time, he encountered a letter posing a profound theological question.

The devotee had written: "Jai Swaminarayan Mahant Swami Maharaj. A question always remains in my mind: Are you and the Guru-parampara Aksharbrahman or Aksharmukta? Please give the true knowledge to me and others like me."

Without hesitation, Swamishri penned a definitive response: "Bhagatji Maharaj, Shastriji Maharaj, Yogiji Maharaj, and Pramukh Swami Maharaj are all Aksharbrahman themselves. Jai Swaminarayan from Sadhu Keshavjivandas." He noted that this same divine tradition continues today.

By explicitly identifying the lineage as Aksharbrahman, Swamishri reaffirms the absolute core of the Akshar-Purushottam Darshan. The Guru is the living embodiment of Aksharbrahman and the ultimate bridge to God.

title: The Good of Others
text:
After Swamishri's breakfast, Gunvatsal Swami spoke about the new charitra Swamishri had performed and said, "Today, whatever is given - khichu, upma, shiro - Swamishri takes from his hand and straight to his mouth." Everyone else also took note of this. Gunvatsal Swami then asked Swamishri, "Why like this?"

Swamishri responded, "What is the reason for wasting a clean spoon?"

Gunvatsal Swami further added, "If you use it, then it will not be considered a waste; rather, it will become prasadi."

Swamishri then responded, "Do what will not cause a waste."

While eating the different dishes prepared by the swamis, Swamishri remembers all of them and wishes for the good of all. Expanding on this, Swamishri said, "If we think that good happens to all, then we will get infinitely many blessings."

Even while eating, his thoughts were with others, praying for their well-being and happiness.

title: Deeply Immersed
text:
After his walk, Swamishri would listen to the biography of Shastriji Maharaj while doing his exercises. Once his exercise routine was finished, Uttamyogi Swami paused the audio. At that exact moment, the narration was describing the early beginnings of the large mandir in Sarangpur, and the audio was stopped right after the phrase: "Three devotees went to Shastriji Maharaj..."

Fifteen minutes later, as Swamishri sat down for his meal, he turned to Uttamyogi Swami and asked, "Three devotees went to Shastriji Maharaj for the Sarangpur mandir... then what did Shastriji Maharaj say?"

Uttamyogi Swami didn't know the answer, but he was amazed by Swamishri's sharp attentiveness. For fifteen straight minutes, Swamishri had been eagerly wondering what Shastriji Maharaj might have told those devotees.

title: Deeply Immersed
text:
At Swamishri's request, the track was resumed from where it had been paused. Swamishri began listening with deep concentration. Right in the middle of the narration, a swami came to meet Swamishri, prompting Uttamyogi Swami to pause the audio once more.

Swamishri did not like this at all and clearly expressed his displeasure at the interruption. The biography was immediately resumed. Swamishri felt satisfied only after listening to the entire incident. Once the narrative was complete, he finally met with the visiting swami and began his lunch.

This incident beautifully illustrates how completely absorbed Swamishri becomes when listening to the life and work of his Gurus. His profound eagerness and curiosity to hear their charitras (life events) are so intense that they take precedence over everything else—even his meals and meetings.

title: Swamishri's Research
text:
While having breakfast at the Delhi mandir from the annakut (sacred offering of food), Swamishri tasted a tiny pinch of a penda (a milk-based sweet). He immediately remarked, "This will spoil in one or two days."

The swamis witnessed a glimpse of his remarkable discernment—recognizing the exact state of the food from just a single taste, much like Pramukh Swami Maharaj used to do. With folded hands, they reassured him, "Swami! The pendas are completely fresh."

Explaining his reasoning, Swamishri said, "Because the sugar content is low, it will spoil in two to three days. In a traditional Khambhati penda, the sugar is balanced equally, so it stays good for up to six months."

Munichintan Swami quickly affirmed, "That is true, Swami. Sugar acts as a natural preservative." The Satpurush is fully present, with a wisdom that seamlessly bridges the divine and the mundane.

title: Samp in Satsang
text:
During the evening session of the youth shibir, the kishores (youths) asked Swamishri a vital question: "Swami, how can we keep samp (unity)?"

Swamishri replied, "Pramukh Swami Maharaj has said, 'Even [at the expense of] ingesting poison, unity must be maintained.' Ingesting poison symbolizes the importance of maintaining samp until our 'last moment'. To [sustain] dāsbhāv (a feeling of servitude) and mahimā (understanding each other's spiritual glory), samp is 'very important'. Even if it falls upon us to ingest poison, samp should not be broken. [While some prioritize wealth over unity,] Yogi Bapa has said, 'We do not need money; we need samp.'…If we maintain samp from our end, then the results will speak for themselves.'"

Swamishri emphasizes that true unity requires immense personal sacrifice—swallowing our own pride, ego, and grievances for the greater good of satsang.

title: Rajipo on Satsang Activities
text:
Swamishri imparted the twenty-first lesson of Brahmavidya (divine knowledge), stating: "Bhagwan is a thousand percent pleased with those who perform Satsang activities."

To emphasize the magnitude of this statement, he clarified, "Not 100%, not 200%, but 1000% pleased!"

By declaring that Bhagwan's rajipo is magnified a thousandfold for those who commit themselves to these endeavors, he highlights that sincere, active participation in Satsang activities is a direct way to earn Bhagwan's favor.

title: Progressing in Satsang
text:
In the evening, Swamishri sat down to write replies to letters. Among them was a heartfelt letter from a devotee who asked: "Swami! What should I do to progress further in Satsang? Which rules (niyams) should I follow so that your divine form remains in my mind for 24 hours, I can focus during my daily worship (puja), and all worldly (mayik) thoughts cease?"

Swamishri wrote back the answer: "Follow the code of conduct (dharma-niyams) given by Maharaj."

We often look for complex secrets to achieve spiritual milestones, but Swamishri reminds us that by simply and sincerely following the fundamental rules of conduct prescribed by Bhagwan Swaminarayan, a devotee naturally attains deep focus in worship, overcomes worldly distractions, and maintains a constant connection with Bhagwan.

title: Finding Time For Prayer
text:
During a conversation, Swamishri was asked about his personal approach to prayer.

Question: "Why do you prefer to pray at night?"

Swamishri: "During the day, I have no time. And even if I do, it's filled with interruptions. But at night, everything is quiet, and I can pray in peace, free from disturbance. We should offer God our very best, choosing the time when our prayer can reach him in the most heartfelt way. It's like giving to charity: we give the best we have. In the same way, our prayers should be our finest offering."

In this profound response, Swamishri reveals the depth of his devotion and highlights the importance of the quality of our spiritual practices. He reminds us that our time and attention given to God shouldn't simply be whatever is leftover in our busy schedules, but rather our most peaceful, uninterrupted, and finest offering.

title: Praying during a Storm
text:
The shilanyas (foundation stone-laying) rituals for the new mandir in Dhule were scheduled for the next day. At Pramukh Swami Maharaj's request, Mahant Swami and Kothari Bhaktipriya Swami were to lead the ceremonies before 65 swamis and over 6,500 devotees.

However, the evening before, heavy rain began to fall and would not stop. Tents and decorations were soaked, and many arrangements were on the verge of being ruined. As the night wore on, the situation only grew more uncertain.

Seeing the disaster unfold, Anandjivan Swami became deeply concerned. At 12:30 a.m., he went to Mahant Swami's room, woke him, and explained what was happening outside.

Without hesitation, Mahant Swami rose and began to pray. For over ninety minutes, he chanted 'Swaminarayan, Swaminarayan...' with unbroken concentration.

By morning, the rain had eased and the weather settled completely. The ceremony went ahead joyously as planned.

title: Prayer with Joy
text:
Reflecting on the 2013 shilanyas ceremony in Dhule, swamis recalled how Swamishri rose at 12:30 a.m. during a storm to pray for over ninety minutes.

They then asked him, "You woke up at 12:30 a.m. and prayed for a long time. Don't you ever get frustrated by these disturbances?"

Swamishri smiled and replied, "If satsang keeps growing, you never feel frustration, only joy."

This beautiful reflection reveals the profound depth of Swamishri's selflessness. While most people would feel annoyed or burdened by having their sleep interrupted to solve a crisis, Swamishri viewed it entirely differently. Because his sole focus is the spiritual growth of the devotees and the expansion of Satsang, any personal sacrifice made for their growth is experienced not as a hardship, but as a source of genuine joy.

title: Silent Prayers for Others
text:
It was 12:45 a.m., and Swamishri was slowly turning his mala. Intrigued, Uttamyogi Swami wondered whose prayers were on his lips…

On August 16, a few swamis entered the room after Swamishri completed his evening meal. They were to present questions on behalf of devotees. Swamishri listened attentively and responded to each question with wisdom and clarity.

As the session concluded, an attendant began to speak. "Swami! A request has come from Sarangpur…" He stopped mid-sentence, his voice trailing off.

Swamishri looked up, with curiosity in his eyes. A few weeks earlier, he had received news of a drought and had been asked to pray for rain. Now, once again, his thoughts returned to the farmers and their welfare.

title: Silent Prayers for Others
text:
With a wry smile, the attendant completed the request: "…Please pray that the rains stop now!"

Everyone in the room chuckled at the unexpected turn of events. With a big smile, Swamishri joined them before replying, "Three days of mala."

The room grew quiet, the humour giving way to intrigue.

Sitting nearby, Uttamyogi Swami began to share the story behind those words, explaining how Swamishri had been praying for rain to end the drought: "For three consecutive nights, 1st, 2nd, and 3rd August, Swami turned his mala for over an hour each night. He wouldn't say anything. After getting up to use the bathroom, he would quietly sit down again and begin doing mala. I once asked, 'Swami, why are you doing mala right now?' But he wouldn't answer… He just said, 'You go to sleep. I'm doing mala.'"

title: Silent Prayers for Others
text:
Uttamyogi Swami shared the narrative behind Swamishri's silent vigil, revealing the depth of his concern for those suffering through the drought: "I had a feeling something was on his mind. Days later, I asked again. This time, Swami admitted: 'There was no rain in some areas… so I was doing mala that rain might come.'"

Uttamyogi Swami noted each moment as Swamishri sat in silent prayer for the parched land and its farmers:

August 1, 2020 – 12:45 a.m. to 1:47 a.m. – mala for 1 hour and 2 minutes
August 2, 2020 – 12:58 a.m. to 2:12 a.m. – mala for 1 hour and 14 minutes
August 3, 2020 – 2:45 a.m. to 3:55 a.m. – mala for 1 hour and 10 minutes

title: Carrying the Pain
text:
At around 12:50 a.m., Swamishri awoke to receive an urgent message from Houston. Jaiminbhai's ten-year-old son, Aryan, had been in a terrible accident and had to be hospitalized immediately. The entire family was extremely worried and overwhelmed with fear. The child was also in severe pain.

The attendant shared everything with Swamishri. Offering blessings, Swamishri sent a voice message to the child: "Aryan, everything will be alright. Be strong and brave."

Then he lay down again. But his compassionate nature would not allow his mind to settle. He kept thinking about the boy. Unable to sleep, at 1:12 a.m., he pressed the pager. When the attendant arrived, Swamishri began asking questions.

"Where is this child from?"

"From America."

"Was the child hurt badly?"

"Yes."

title: Carrying the Pain
text:
Swamishri continued asking about the boy, "When is the operation?"

"In five or six hours."

"Oh dear!" Swamishri exclaimed, as if he were personally feeling the child's pain. "What will happen to this child until then?"

The attendant said, "You have sent your blessings, so he will find strength."

Swamishri remained deeply concerned. "For five to six hours… he will be in so much pain. He must be suffering a lot."

Even in the stillness of the night, Swamishri's heart did not rest. His thoughts and prayers remained with the child, carrying the boy's pain as if it were his own. Such tender empathy and tireless prayer revealed the depth of his compassion: a love that reached far beyond time zones and distances, bringing comfort and strength to a child and his family when they needed it most.

title: Understanding the Sentiment
text:
When Swamishri arrived at the mandir, Abhayswarup Swami and other swamis showed him a beautiful inlay design created on the stone located on the central pathway. They mentioned, "The artisans who created this had a deep desire for you to cast your sight upon it." For this reason, the carpet on Swamishri's walking path had been laid out starting a short distance away from that specific area.

Upon hearing about the artisans' heartfelt sentiment, Swamishri immediately stepped off the warm carpet and walked onto the bare stone to get closer to the design.

The swamis quickly tried to stop him, warning, "Swami! It is cold…"

Unfazed, Swamishri calmly observed the intricate design, sanctified it with his touch, and only then moved forward. By understanding the pure sentiments of others, he happily withstood the cold stone beneath his bare feet to fulfill the artisans' wish.

title: The Source of Energy
text:
Seeing Swamishri's intense schedule at almost ninety years old, a swami was curious about how he manages to dedicate his sleeping hours to prayer.

Question: "You have said you pray and do malas at night because it is a peaceful time. But during the day, you are deeply engaged in so much seva – caring for the Sanstha, guiding others, and meeting people. You have even remarked, 'I am tired 24 hours a day,' and during the Pramukh Swami Maharaj Centenary Celebrations, you said, 'Everything runs through atma-nishtha.' So, the body gets tired and has its limits. Yet, even at a time when most would rest, you stay awake and pray. Where does that energy come from?"

Swamishri: "We pray to Purna Purushottam Narayan, that is where the energy comes from!"

By rooting his life in prayer and reliance on Bhagwan, Swamishri shows us that when we anchor our actions in faith, Bhagwan Himself sustains us.

title: True Humility
text:
Swamishri woke up and, after returning from the washroom, sat on his bed. Then, quite suddenly, he bent down to the floor and touched his attendant's feet in reverence. Instinctively, the attendant stepped back, his face flushed with embarrassment.

It was Ekadashi, and Swamishri was pleased to see the sevak awake past midnight. Smiling, he mimed filling a bag, expressing a sentiment he often shared with those who kept a midnight fast: "You have bagged trillions and trillions of dollars' worth of God's blessings."

Moved by Swamishri's enthusiasm, the attendant expressed his gratitude but humbly pleaded, "You should not bow to my feet."

"Why not? Is there a rule against it?" Swamishri asked.

"Yes! Seniors should not bow to juniors."

Revealing his heartfelt humility, Swamishri confessed, "Hu nāno j chhu – I am still junior."

title: Caring Like a Father
text:
Shrijiswarup Swami and Bhaktinandan Swami revisited their early days in the 1970s when they were young sadhus training in Mumbai. Swamishri listened intently as they described how he had guided and cared for them as the head of the sadhus' ashram, even into the late hours of the night.

Shrijiswarup Swami recalled, "At that time, we did not even use blankets. On cold nights, we would curl up in a thin sheet and try to sleep. But you always noticed. If we were shivering, you would cover us with your own shawl or gatariyu. Many times, even at 1:00 a.m., you would quietly climb two or three storeys to search for a quilt somewhere. Once you found one, you would bring it back and cover us while we were still asleep."

Bhaktinandan Swami added, "You did that so many times. We did not realize until later that you had sacrificed your own rest and warmth just to make sure we were comfortable."

title: Caring Like a Father
text:
Their memories then broadened. "This was our initial training," one of them said. "We had grown up and studied outside India, so we could not even read or write Gujarati. You taught us everything; you made sure we were fed and you cared for us like a father."

Shrijiswarup Swami smiled and added, "If someone prepared juice for you, you would take only a little and give the rest to us. For us, that was a special treat."

Bhaktinandan Swami concluded, "You cared for us with such kindness while at the same time firmly guiding us in our niyam-dharma and personal discipline. Yet never once did we feel you were upset or angry. Everything you said came from the heart. We may not have had formal swami training in Sarangpur, but the memories with you are securely treasured in our hearts."

Swamishri's life shows that true leadership is rooted in sacrifice and pure love.

title: The Purest Resolve
text:
On February 2nd, during Swamishri's Janma Jayanti celebrations, Swamishri graced all the bal and balika vidwans with samip darshan.

The following day, the swamis from the Bal Pravrutti Central Office asked Swamishri, "Swamibapa, during the samip darshan, as all the children came before you and you looked upon each of them, what were you thinking? What sankalp (resolve) did you make at that time?"

Swamishri simply replied, "Only that they all become ekantik."

Swamishri's response highlights his vision: leading everyone toward becoming an ekantik bhakta. While we enjoy the physical darshan, his gaze focuses on our spiritual destiny. By prioritizing our eternal perfection over temporary happiness, he teaches us to align our aspirations with the goal of pleasing Bhagwan.

title: Unrelenting Dedication
text:
This evening, Swamishri was writing English sentences and phrases for the text 350 Insights from Satsang Diksha. Suddenly as he was writing, his hand began to cramp. Every time he tried to write, the cramp would return. When he paused, the tension eased, but as soon as he resumed, the cramping started again.

Seeing his discomfort, Shrutipriya Swami humbly suggested, "Shall we take a little rest and then continue writing?"

Swamishri declined and pressed on. He managed to write a little more despite the recurring cramps. He still genuinely wished to continue, but the attendant swamis eventually had to gently insist that he stop and rest.

At ninety-three years of age, when rest is expected and well-deserved, his drive to serve and share spiritual wisdom remains completely undiminished. When our actions are fueled by a pure desire to please Bhagwan, temporary physical discomforts are easily overshadowed.

title: His Problem is My Problem
text:
A devotee had fallen into serious financial difficulty. The matter was discussed with Swamishri during the day, and even at 1:00 a.m., when he awoke, his thoughts remained with that devotee's struggles.

At 4:00 a.m., as Swamishri rose to start his day, he expressed his deep concern: "The worry stays on my mind. How can we help solve his problem?"

He then added, "I cannot stop thinking about it, because emno problem chhe e amāro j problem chhe (his problem is my problem)."

For many, empathy is a passing feeling. But for Swamishri, it was a responsibility he chose to carry; another's pain became his own. His love was not distant or symbolic, but practical and deeply personal.

title: The All-Doer's Will
text:
During a conversation in London, a swami asked Swamishri about his method of praying for those in need.

Question: "Swami, you do not pray for yourself, but you pray when people share their troubles. What exactly do you pray for?"

Swamishri: "First of all, God is the all-doer; he does everything. Even a dry leaf cannot move on its own. You may think, if God has such complete doership, what remains for us? Still, we pray and share in the joys and sorrows of others - that remains naturally."

Swamishri reveals that true prayer is not about trying to change God's will, but about aligning our hearts with His wish and praying for the welfare of others.

title: Empathy as Bhakti
text:
Continuing the conversation in London regarding the nature of prayer, a swami asked Swamishri a profound follow-up question.

Question: "If God is the all-doer, then why is there any need to pray?"

Swamishri thoughtfully replied, "We should pray to God with humility and as our support. Without that, mala, chanting, penance, and all forms of devotion will fade away. Since Bhagwan is present before us, our prayers should reflect that. As a bhakta, we hold the sentiment that 'Bhagwānnā bhaktanā dukhe dukhiyā, sukhe sukhiyā – one should be pained by a devotee's pain and joyous in a devotee's joy.'"

For Swamishri, prayer is a genuine offering of humility and compassion before God: an embrace of his will, and a sharing in the joys and sorrows of others. In such prayer, empathy blossoms into bhakti.

title: A Silent, Unseen Prayer
text:
At 1:03 a.m., Swamishri woke up to use the bathroom.

While bathing, he recited the ashray diksha mantra aloud three times:

"Dhanyo'smi purna-kāmo'smi nishpāpo nirbhayah sukhi; Akshara-guru-yogena Swāminārāyan-āshrayat."

The mantra affirms the blessing, fulfilment, purity, courage, and bliss found through refuge in Bhagwan Swaminarayan and personal engagement with the Aksharbrahma Guru.

It was a mantra that Swamishri encouraged everyone to meditate on daily.

Afterwards, as he prepared to rest again, Swamishri remained thoughtful about the bushfires in Australia.

He asked Uttamyogi Swami, "What time is it in Australia?"

Checking his phone, Uttamyogi Swami replied, "7:01 a.m."

Swamishri requested, "Phone the sadhus in Sydney and ask for an update on the rainfall."

title: A Silent, Unseen Prayer
text:
Uttamyogi Swami tried calling the swamis in Australia as Swamishri had instructed, but there was no response.

"They're not answering at the moment," he explained. "I'll leave a message and let you know as soon as they reply. Please try to sleep."

Around 1:40 a.m., Swamishri was still lying awake, silently praying.

Moments later, Brahmasmaran Swami phoned Uttamyogi Swami from Sydney. "There's been no new update since Priyachintan Swami last spoke to you," he said.

At 1:45 a.m., Uttamyogi Swami checked if Swamishri had fallen asleep. Seeing Swamishri's eyes open, he relayed Brahmasmaran Swami's message.

Swamishri's wakefulness was not restlessness; it was compassion. A silent, unseen prayer of a guru who carries the world lovingly within his heart.

title: The Joy of Prapti
text:
In a question-and-answer session, Swamishri explained how we can nurture our prapti in the same way that enabled him to remain joyful even in the late hours of the night.

Question: "How can we keep the joy of prapti alive in our hearts every moment of the day, all 24 hours?"

Swamishri: "We live in unsettled times, so it is natural for the mind to waver. Yet if we persist, step by step, we will continue to move forward. This is sadhana, dedicated spiritual practice, it is not a game. We must be strong and keep unflinching faith. Our efforts cannot remain on the surface; we need to go deep if we truly wish to attain it. Only then will we grasp the real meaning of prapti. Wisdom does not simply fall into place. The great Paramhansas worked tirelessly; such insight never comes without effort. But only by living sadhana will we taste its reality, just as you know the sweetness of a mango only by eating it."

title: The Constant Joy of Prapti
text:
At around 1:20 a.m., Swamishri woke up, walked a little, and noticed that the attendant was awake.

"Smile!" Swamishri warmly reminded him.

Later, as the attendant assisted him to lie back down on the bed, Swamishri spoke in English: "Bhagatji... despite all difficulties, he smiled. Is that right?"

The attendant replied, "Yes!"

It was a small moment, but its message deeply resonated with the attendant: just like Bhagatji Maharaj, Swamishri constantly enjoys the bliss of Bhagwan.

The joy of prapti, after all, is available to everyone, at all times and in every circumstance.

title: A Smile a Mile Away
text:
Swamishri always encourages others to remember how fortunate they are to have found God, wanting everyone to feel the joy of that prapti (attainment) and always hold on to that bliss.

Sometimes, when waking up in the middle of the night, Swamishri would ask people to smile.

At that time, most people are still sleepy, but Swamishri would be wide awake and radiant, his mind full of thoughts of God.

At 1:10 a.m., Swamishri woke up and took a short walk between rooms.

He saw the attendant awake and called out, "Smile!"

The attendant gave a sleepy grin. When Swamishri saw his weak attempt, he let out a friendly laugh and joked in English: "Moodless. Your smile is a mile away."

Through this lighthearted late-night interaction, Swamishri reveals that true joy is not dependent on the time of day or our physical energy levels. A genuine smile is the natural byproduct of holding onto the bliss of our spiritual attainment.

title: Prapti Every Second
text:
Continuing his late-night conversation, Swamishri wanted to explain why we should wake up with a smile.

He asked the attendant, "Do you feel the joy of prapti every second, or only once every fifteen days?"

The attendant honestly replied, "Well... not every second."

Swamishri snapped his fingers and said, "Not every second?! It should be there every second."

He then quoted a famous devotional verse: "Piya paya to phir kya sona." (If you have attained God, then why would you want to sleep?)

Swamishri asked, "Is God present?"
"Yes."
"Then why do you still feel sleepy? If you have truly attained God, you should feel only joy!"

Swamishri challenges our complacency by reminding us that the realization of God's presence should be an overwhelming source of constant happiness. When we deeply understand the magnitude of what we have attained, lethargy is replaced by an unshakeable, 24/7 bliss.

title: The Resident of the Heart
text:
Deep in the quiet hours of the morning, the attendant asked, "Swami, how can we stay connected to prapti for 24 hours?"

Swamishri profoundly replied, "Why? Does Maharaj only visit once every fifteen days? He is always here. Every second, there is a connection. If that connection breaks, even for one moment, we are lost. God lives in our hearts. If he left even for one second, we could not live. God is always present inside you. Akhand biraja chhe (He is eternally present). Both Aksharbrahma and Parabrahma. God lives in your heart. He is... He is... He simply is."

It was late, so the attendant suggested: "Swami, let's sleep now."

Swamishri smiled: "I'll sleep. Both waking and sleeping will continue. The body may rest, but Maharaj and Swami are always present in the heart."

The attendant summarized, "Bhagwan is the resident, and we are the home." Swamishri was very pleased and blessed his head three times.

title: An Unsleeping Joy
text:
The attendant slept, but Swamishri remained awake, deeply immersed in thoughts of prapti and feeling divine joy.

At exactly 2:22 a.m., Swamishri suddenly sat up, smiled brightly, and proclaimed, "Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj ni Jay!"

Then he lay down again.

At 4:00 a.m., Swamishri woke up to start his day.

Still carrying the thoughts from the night, he reminded the attendant, "This is the body. Inside the body lives the jiva (soul). And inside the jiva, lives God. If he is always present, then the joy of prapti should be felt every second, not just once every fifteen days."

Swamishri's spontaneous proclamation of victory in the middle of the night demonstrates a state of ultimate spiritual absorption. While the physical body requires rest, the soul that is deeply aware of God's presence rejoices continuously.

title: Prayer Amid the Storm
text:
Cyclone Gita was battering New Zealand. Torrential rain pounded the ground. Gale-force winds whipped the trees.

Surging waves bashed the coast. Several regions were already under a state of emergency: flooding, fallen trees, and power outages were sweeping across the country.

That night, before sleeping, Swamishri had stood quietly at the doorway watching the rain pour down.

Long after the rest of the household had gone to sleep, he woke again, around 1:30 a.m., his thoughts turned immediately to the storm raging outside.

He rose from his bed and walked to the window. Outside, the trees bent and strained in the wind; the rain struck hard against the glass. In the dim light of the room he stood motionless, his gaze steady on the scene beyond.

In that solitary moment, Swamishri prayed not for himself but for the cyclone to ease and for everyone's safety.

title: Intentional Interactions
text:
A special spiritual conference had been organized for an international group of young, dedicated BAPS volunteers.

The initial sessions were to be held in Mumbai and included interactive learning with Swamishri.

Next, the group was to travel to Sarangpur for the second phase of the conference, where they would receive guidance from the resident scholarly swamis.

But unexpectedly, Swamishri expressed his wish to go to Surat for the Jholi Utsav festival instead of remaining in Mumbai.

Since several sessions with him were already scheduled in Mumbai, the organizers asked what they should do.

Swamishri suggested, "Come with me to Surat. There we will have even more opportunities to interact."

title: Care Beyond Convenience
text:
No arrangements had been made for the young volunteers in Surat.

So, in a matter of hours, the organizers had to book flights, find accommodation, and reserve spaces for the sessions.

With all the preparations complete, they made their way to Surat.

Swamishri soon arrived. At the first opportunity, he arranged a meeting with the group who had travelled there with him.

They sat under the mandir podium, where Swamishri delivered a 52-minute discourse, elaborating from his handwritten letters.

The attendant later noted that it was the longest address he had given since becoming Guru.

Over the next few days, Swamishri remained attentive to every detail.

He asked about their travel, their meals, and even how they had enjoyed their time in devotion during the eclipse.

He wanted to be sure everyone was comfortable and cared for.

title: Care Beyond Convenience
text:
When the group prepared to continue to Sarangpur as planned, he asked again, "When are you leaving? How will you get there? How long will it take?"

That night, the volunteers boarded the coach and began their overnight journey.

A few hours later, around 1:45 a.m., Swamishri woke up.

He sat on the bed for a moment and spontaneously said, "Sarangpur."

Then he called the swami and asked, "Kyã pohchyã hashe? – Where must they have reached by now?"

The swami replied, "They are meant to reach by six in the morning. I'm not sure exactly where they are now."

Swamishri paused and said thoughtfully, "They must be halfway there by now."

Even long after the program had ended, as the young volunteers slept in the coach, Swamishri's thoughts remained with them. It was a small glimpse of his constant care, for worry is, after all, an expression of love.

title: Prayers for All
text:
Swamishri called Paramchintan Swami and shared his prayers: "I woke up at 1:30 a.m. last night. I prayed to Maharaj and Swami for all the devotees in Melbourne to become settled and happy, and for all their challenges to be resolved."

Over the years, during his visits across Australia, Swamishri had personally met countless individuals and received thousands of letters.

He had listened attentively to their concerns, some of whom were living on work permits or student visas, unsure of their long-term future.

Their concerns became his prayers.

Then, after a pause, he continued: "But then another thought came to me: What about those who are not devotees? I then prayed that all those who have visited the Swaminarayan Nagar may also be happy, be comfortable and settled."

title: Prayers for All
text:
The Swaminarayan Nagar was a large festival campus created during Swamishri's stay in Melbourne, which welcomed thousands of visitors from across Australia, not all of whom were devotees.

Continuing on his call with Paramchintan Swami, Swamishri said, "Then I thought... What about those who have never visited the Swaminarayan Nagar? I prayed that they, too, may be happy. And then I prayed even more widely, that all the citizens of Australia may experience happiness, stability, and calm."

In the middle of the night, Swamishri's prayers began with those who had sought his guidance, but then widened to embrace strangers, and finally, all people of the nation.

His mind and heart eventually embraced all, with an openness that was sincere and filled with goodwill.

title: The Ultimate Expectation
text:
After dinner, Swamishri was asked, "Swami, what expectation do you have of us?"

Swamishri replied, "Become Ekantik, everyone! An Ekantik devotee... Ekantik devotion... that is what is immensely dear to Maharaj. It is for this very reason that Maharaj came; before his arrival, Ekantik devotion existed only in talks, but it had never been put into practice. It was only after Shriji Maharaj came that the propagation of Ekantik devotion took place and thousands became Ekantik devotees. Therefore, for everyone to become an Ekantik devotee, that itself is the expectation. Everything is included in that!"

Swamishri clarifies that his ultimate expectation for us does not revolve around worldly milestones, but rather mastering Ekantik Dharma. Attaining this state of pure devotion fulfills the very purpose of our spiritual journey.

title: The Joy of the Vachanamrut
text:
Adarshjivan Swami reminded Swamishri of a moment from Dallas in 2011, when he had diligently read two Vachanamruts before retiring for sleep.

"At that time, you were 78," he continued, "yet you showed such enthusiasm for reading the shastras. You have often mentioned that you still discover new insights in the Vachanamrut. Could you share how you approach it?"

Swamishri replied, "It is divine. Maharaj and Swami's entire form is divine, even down to the smallest particle. In that way, I realize the whole murti as divine."

"Why does reading the Vachanamrut bring you such joy?"

"It is divine speech because they are Maharaj's own words."

The eternal bliss Swamishri finds in the Vachanamrut comes from his deep-seated conviction that these are the direct, sacred words of Maharaj.

title: The Joy of the Vachanamrut
text:
Then Uttamyogi Swami asked, "When we read the Vachanamrut, we don't feel the same level of enthusiasm. How can we develop the kind of interest you have, so that even in the middle of the night we feel inspired to read it?"

Swamishri replied, "Through mahima, a genuine appreciation of Bhagwan Swaminarayan's greatness. There is no one beyond him. He is the ultimate. Divine. That is why there is such bliss. We have attained the supreme."

Swamishri's profound reverence for the Vachanamrut is inherent. His unbroken enthusiasm for reading the scriptures does not stem only from mere academic interest, but from a deeply realized understanding of God's greatness (mahima).

Swamishri beautifully teaches us that to truly find joy and inspiration in our daily spiritual reading, we must first cultivate a heartfelt awareness of the supreme divinity we have attained.

title: Praying in the Night
text:
Swamishri awoke in the middle of the night once again.

It was 2:02 a.m. He sat up with purpose, took a mala into his hand, and began to chant softly, "Swaminarayan, Swaminarayan..."

It was almost a month after the delta variant of the Covid-19 pandemic started.

Each day, Swamishri was on the phone, counseling, consoling, and organizing as needed.

Under his guidance, BAPS Charities and the worldwide BAPS community would go on to launch large-scale relief work: distributing millions of meals, essential supplies, and medical equipment to vulnerable communities across continents.

Yet even with much happening during the day, Swamishri would regularly immerse himself in prayer for those suffering.

Over the past few nights, he had rested less, spending time turning his mala at night. His quiet, purposeful chanting in the early hours revealed his heart's love and prayers for the well-being of others.

title: Praying in the Night
text:
Even with his immense daytime responsibilities during the pandemic, Swamishri would regularly immerse himself in prayer for those suffering.

Over just a few nights, he chose to rest less, sacrificing his sleep to spend time turning his mala for the world's well-being.

Here are the details of his silent, late-night prayers:

April 4, 2021: 11:09 p.m. to 12:25 a.m. (1 hour and 16 minutes)
April 6, 2021: 1:45 a.m. to 2:50 a.m. (1 hour and 5 minutes)
April 7, 2021: 2:02 a.m. to 3:03 a.m. (1 hour and 1 minute)

Across those nights alone, Swamishri prayed for 3 hours and 22 minutes.

Swamishri's recorded hours of midnight prayers demonstrate a staggering level of empathy. When the world slept, he sacrificed his physical rest to spiritually uplift and protect humanity. Our prayers for others should not be an afterthought; they should be intentional, consistent, and driven by selfless love.

title: Overjoyed by the Satsang Diksha
text:
It was the night of Guru Punam. Swamishri had just found out that the Satsang Diksha had been successfully published online, just two minutes before midnight.

Though he had been already asleep, a simple note left by Shrutipriya Swami in the bathroom informed him at 2:10 a.m.

When Swamishri read it, his face lit up with joy.

He had wished for the teachings of Satsang Diksha to be published quickly, but the challenges of Covid-19 made printing difficult.

Now, seeing it released online, Swamishri expressed his delight.

"Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj ni Jay! Jay Swaminarayan! Satsang Diksha ni Jay Jay Jay!"

Uttamyogi Swami joined him in celebration. What followed was a heartfelt conversation that revealed Swamishri's growing joy and satisfaction for what had been accomplished.

title: The Satsang Diksha's Glory
text:
Uttamyogi Swami asked, "Swami, what benefit will everyone experience from the Satsang Diksha?"

"They'll benefit a lot! Many children, teenagers, and adults will learn the shloks. There will be immense joy!"

"Will they memorize it?"

"Yes, and they will gain the knowledge of the Satsang Diksha."

"And that knowledge takes the clearest and most powerful form, through the wisdom of Akshar-Purushottam."

"Exactly. The principles of agna and upasana are clearly written. Whatever was in Maharaj's and the Gunatit Gurus' minds has been expressed step by step."

"So now, the path to Akshardham is…"

"...completely straightforward!" said Swamishri, completing Uttamyogi Swami's sentence.

title: Embracing the Satsang Diksha
text:
Although it was well past midnight, Swamishri's enthusiasm only deepened.

While his body rested, his mind remained alert, immersed in the anticipation of how this knowledge would transform lives.

At 2:44 a.m., he spoke again: "I want to embrace the Satsang Diksha!"

Swamishri took the large book, held it close to his chest, and voiced his feelings: "I am embracing the personified form of Shriji Maharaj, the Guru Parampara, and the Siddhant."

Later, he shared another wish: "At the speed of an aeroplane, everyone should memorize this scripture."

At 4:08 a.m., Swamishri awoke once more and mentally offered a variety of flowers to Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj while chanting, "Akshar-Purushottamāy Namah."

title: No Half-Hearted Effort
text:
In the morning, Swamishri was unable to complete his usual stretching exercises on his bed because a meeting ran late.

Later in the evening, an attendant asked him, "Would you like to do your exercises while lying down?"

Swamishri agreed and then firmly added, "Do not do it 'half-hearted'. Do it fully. Only do it if we are going to do the 'full' [amount]."

Sometimes, due to a lack of time, attendants halve exercise counts. However, Swamishri insisted on finishing the full routine.

Unlike others who might appreciate a shorter workout, Swamishri's commitment to proper exercise at his age demonstrates exceptional dedication. His rejection of "half-hearted" efforts reflects his lifelong principle of khatko—a drive for perfection and discipline.

title: A Timeless Roadmap
text:
Question: What quality of Neelkanth Varni do you admire the most?
Swamishri: "Bhakti! Doing bhakti."

Question: Which murti of Neelkanth Varni do you meditate on?
Swamishri: "The one where He is standing on one leg with His arms stretched out, performing tap. I really like that one."

Question: What inspiration should kishores take from His life?
Swamishri: "Live a disciplined and austere life. When the senses and mind are under control and paired with satsang, we can truly offer sincere bhakti."

Question: How did He spread the true siddhant?
Swamishri: "Through His pure character and upasana. He never forgot Bhagwan even for a second. Unless you live your words, they don't truly impact others."

Question: "What did Nilkanth Varni dislike?"
Swamishri: "Worldly gossip, and actions that waste our time."

Question: "And what did he like?"
Swamishri: "Spiritual discourses and kirtans."

title: Effortless Smruti
text:
During lunch this afternoon, Swamishri had to wait briefly for his chaas (buttermilk).

In that small amount of time, he naturally folded his hands and closed his eyes.

When he opened his eyes a few moments later, his gaze fell upon the murtis of Shri Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj, Shastriji Maharaj, and Yogiji Maharaj on the wall opposite him.

He bowed his head slightly in reverence before accepting the chaas.

This simple incident reveals a profound secret to continuous devotion.

We often feel we lack the time for prayer or smruti (remembrance of God) amidst our busy schedules.

However, Swamishri demonstrates that devotion does not always require hours of isolation. It can be effortlessly woven into the natural, idle pauses of our day. By filling our empty gaps with remembrance, we can transform ordinary waiting time into a continuous divine connection.

title: Anchored in the Murti
text:
During the singing of the cheshta today, Swamishri was seated facing the murtis of Shastriji Maharaj, Yogiji Maharaj, and Pramukh Swami Maharaj displayed on the wall. Throughout the cheshta, his gaze remained warmly fixed upon them. At one point, he affectionately remarked that Yogiji Maharaj had a large chandlo on his forehead. With his hand, he made a wide, circular gesture to trace its size, his face lighting up with pure joy.

Once the cheshta concluded, some recent news was briefly shared with Swamishri. Then, when it was time for him to stand up, he rose and immediately turned his attention right back to Yogiji Maharaj's murti. He playfully repeated the same gesture of the large chandlo, smiling with the exact same delight as before.

The attendant swamis were left in awe. Their own minds were still lingering on the worldly news, yet Swamishri's mind had instantly and effortlessly returned to the murti.

title: Lifelong Humility
text:
This evening, Swamishri was looking through a photo album of Yogiji Maharaj alongside Viveksagar Swami and Atmatrupt Swami.

As he turned the pages, Swamishri fondly recounted many beautiful memories of Yogiji Maharaj. In one particular photograph, Yogiji Maharaj was seen meeting Ranchhodji Maharaj. A large group had gathered around them, but Mahant Swami was nowhere to be seen in the frame. Nevertheless, Swamishri vividly remembered the entire occasion.

Noticing his absence, it was casually stated, "Swami, you are not visible in this photograph."

With his natural simplicity, Swamishri replied, "I was present, but it was never my nature to push my way to the front. I would just stay in the background."

His life is a powerful reminder that true devotion is not about being seen or recognized by others, but about quietly and sincerely maintaining our connection with Bhagwan and our gurus.

title: The Fruits of Mukhpath
text:
This morning, child scholars living abroad gave a presentation during Swamishri's puja.

Blessing them, Swamishri said, "It can be difficult for children living overseas to do mukhpath, but because you had the deep desire to please Bhagwan and the Sant, you succeeded. The impact of this mukhpath will help in your studies, and you will continue to progress immensely. Through this mukhpath, everything will be accomplished."

Swamishri then advised, "You must keep revising what you have memorized; otherwise, it will be forgotten. If you revise regularly, it will always remain fresh."

He further added, "Through this mukhpath, an atmosphere of unity has been created. Now, you must continue to expand this unity and make the circle of samp bigger." Swamishri even made a wide, circular gesture with his hands.

Finally, Swamishri shared, "As you dive deeper into this, your conviction and joy will grow."

title: Golden Muktos
text:
Today, instead of the usual afternoon discourse, Swamishri wished to meet the swamis personally. One by one, they approached to offer charansparsh. Afterward, Anandpriya Swami engaged everyone in a lighthearted session, during which Swamishri shared some profound teachings.

"Under no circumstances should we look at the faults of others," Swamishri instructed. He then added affectionately, "We will take everyone to Akshardham, carrying them on our shoulders."

Continuing, Swamishri urged, "No matter what happens, put a complete cross over abhav-avgun. All of these are golden muktos." He emphasized, "Always maintain divyabhav."

After the curtains closed, Uttamyogi Swami casually mentioned how Swamishri had just spoken about avoiding abhav-avgun. Hearing this, Swamishri's mood instantly shifted. Firmly pushing the attendant's hand away, he spoke with intense gravity: "Abhav-avgun ruins everything."

title: The Heart of a Servant
text:
Swamis from abroad had traveled to Delhi, and Swamishri was spending time in meetings with them. During one of these meetings, a swami affectionately remarked, "Swami, you are now seated as the Guru, so you should only be giving orders."

The moment the words were spoken, Swamishri immediately shook his head and declined the thought. "No orders," he replied softly.

Then, folding his hands and gently bowing his head, he spoke with absolute sincerity, "I am a das (servant), so I cannot give orders."

Although Swamishri sits upon the highest spiritual pedestal and is revered by millions, his heart remains entirely untouched by the authority or ego of his position. His response reveals how he breathes pure dasbhav every second of the day, teaching us that true greatness is never found in wielding authority, but in joyfully remaining a selfless servant to all.

title: A Light Night Call
text:
Swamishri woke up. Moments later, as the clock reached 2:22:22 a.m., Swamishri exclaimed, "Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj ni Jay!"

Then, Swamishri told Uttamyogi Swami, "We need to call Krishnaprem Swami."

"Why?" he replied curiously.

Swamishri replied, "No particular reason... I just remembered him." He then asked, "What time must it be there?"

Uttamyogi Swami checked the world clock and responded, "It's 3:50 p.m. in Houston."

Swamishri immediately said, "Then let's call him!"

Swamishri sat on his bed, and the call was connected.

"Jay Swaminarayan," said Swamishri.

Krishnaprem Swami was stunned. It was the first time he had received a call from India at such an hour.

title: A Light Night Call
text:
Krishnaprem Swami said in an emotional tone, "Bapa! Dandvat pranam. Jay Swaminarayan."

Swamishri smiled and said, "Ha... I simply wanted to say Jay Swaminarayan, so I called."

After the brief conversation, Swamishri said, "Now connect a call to Anandpriya Swami in London."

Once again, he offered his Jay Swaminarayan and spoke warmly, not out of formality but out of spontaneous affection.

Later, Krishnaprem Swami reflected:

"Swamishri often remembers people like this. It's an expression of his care. There are many instances where he has made phone calls or left voice messages just to let people know he had them on his mind. Even when it's very early in India, he has called at 2:30, 2:48... once, at 2:13 a.m. It's deeply comforting. It's a blessing to have a guru who cares so much."

title: Bearing the Unbearable
text:
This afternoon, following lunch, Swamishri held a meeting with leading volunteers from the Ahmedabad region. During the session, one of the volunteers fondly recalled a striking memory of Swamishri's dedication.

"You have done extensive vicharan in the rural areas of Ahmedabad," the volunteer shared. "You visited 28 villages in just seven days. One night, as you lay down to rest and the sadhus were massaging your head, you mentioned, 'It feels as though hammers are striking my head.' You were in such intense pain, yet throughout the entire day, you had done padhramanis, addressed assemblies, and carried out every activity without saying a single word about your discomfort. It is impossible to even imagine how much you must have silently endured."

This memory offers a humbling glimpse into the immense physical toll Swamishri willingly accepts for the spiritual upliftment of his devotees.

title: The Greatest Honor
text:
Gnanvatsal Swami asked, "What thoughts were going through your mind while you were seated in the Bhakti Tula?"

Swamishri replied simply, "No new thoughts. Only the thoughts of Shastriji Maharaj, Yogiji Maharaj, and Pramukh Swami Maharaj."

He then added, "All these honors that take place... I am not even aware of them. Everything simply continues on its own."

Struck by this profound detachment, Gnanvatsal Swami remarked, "That is an extraordinary state. Whether you are sitting in a Bal Sabha or in a Bhakti Tula, for you, it is all exactly the same."

Swamishri offered a beautiful insight: "In the end, everything merges into Maharaj and Swami."

title: The Greatest Honor
text:
Gnanvatsal Swami then recalled, "Before, when you were a sadguru, you would often say, 'The One who is beyond the counting of countless universes—we have merely come into his sight, that itself is an incredibly great attainment.'"

Hearing this, Swamishri enthusiastically agreed, "That is absolutely true. 'Great, great, great!'"

Finally, Swamishri explained a deep theological truth, "Maharaj deliberately retains certain human traits so that we may slowly understand who God truly is- so we should realize Bhagwan's true divine nature."

While thousands gathered to honor him, his thoughts rested exclusively on his gurus. Swamishri reveals the essence of true equanimity: when the heart is completely absorbed in the glory of God, worldly praise and grand ceremonies lose all their weight.

title: Conduct Speaks
text:
This evening, Swamishri gave blessings to the karyakars (volunteers) involved in the BST (Bal-Balika Sevak Training) and KST (Kishore-Kishori Sevak Training) programs currently taking place in North America.

Offering his heartfelt guidance and blessings, Swamishri shared a profound message: "All of you are highly capable and strong, so move forward by maintaining firm conviction (nishtha) and strictly following the commands (agna). Vartan vatu kare chhe (conduct speaks)! Right from the time of Shriji Maharaj, the greatest emphasis has been placed on pure conduct (vartan). Conduct is everything. No matter how much you do, without proper conduct, it all amounts to zero. Therefore, conduct is paramount; always maintain pure conduct."

Swamishri shifts our focus from simply doing good work to genuinely living a pure, spiritually aligned life every single day.

title: Nurturing Talent
text:
Swamishri gazed firmly at the clock. Minutes moved, seconds spun, and then... at precisely 2:22:22 a.m., Swamishri announced, "Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj ni Jay!"

His thoughts then turned to a former student of BAPS Swaminarayan Vidyamandir, Gondal, a residential school in Gujarat. Swamishri recalled how, many years ago, the boy used to sing with extraordinary devotion; his voice was so remarkable that professional producers had approached him to record songs for their albums. At the time, the boy humbly replied, "I have learnt to sing only to please Pramukh Swami Maharaj. I do not wish to sing for anyone else, nor for money."

Moved by the memory, Swamishri said, "Find the boy's current location and contact number. Ask the sadhus at Gondal Gurukul."

title: Nurturing Talent
text:
Later that morning, while exercising, Swamishri followed up with keen interest, "Have you enquired about that boy?"

The attendant replied, "Yes, Swami. We have spoken with the sadhus at Gondal Gurukul. They are looking into it and will share his details."

By the late afternoon, the boy's details had come through. He had grown into a young man, now married and living in Ahmedabad. Immediately, they placed a call. When Swamishri spoke with him over the phone, he was deeply pleased by the young man's sincerity.

Then, Swamishri enquired, "Are you still singing?"

The young man admitted that he was not.

Swamishri encouraged him warmly, "You should continue learning music. Keep singing."

Then, turning to those around him, he said with earnest care, "We should stay in touch and encourage talented children and youngsters like him. Their abilities should be nurtured so they progress further."

title: Taking the Blame
text:
Before departing from the assembly, a group of devotees from Charlotte had gathered for the shilapujan ceremony of their new mandir. Just before the curtains were closed, Swamishri noticed one of them stretching his legs, clearly finding it difficult to sit cross-legged on the floor. Swamishri immediately perceived his discomfort.

As the attendant swamis began drawing the curtains, Swamishri gestured to share a thought. Uttamyogi Swami leaned in closer, and Swamishri told him, "We should ask for forgiveness from these devotees. They had difficulty sitting; they should have been provided with chairs."

Uttamyogi Swami relayed this to Shrijikirtan Swami, who then announced that Swamishri was asking for their forgiveness, adding, "This was a flaw in our arrangements, and we will be far more mindful of this."

His sensitivity demonstrates that true greatness means silently absorbing blame to prioritize the care of others.

title: Foresight in the Flow
text:
After dinner, the swamis responsible for assembly arrangements approached Swamishri to seek his guidance on managing the massive crowd flow for the upcoming Fuldol festival. The plan was to have eight lines on the left and eight on the right, allowing sixteen lines to move simultaneously.

The swamis asked, "Swami, during the last Fuldol, we reserved four lines specifically for the volunteers. Should we keep volunteer lines this time? The crowd seemed to move smoothly even without them."

Swamishri replied firmly, "Volunteers must be kept."

They then asked, "Should we dedicate four lines or two lines for them?"

"Keep two lines," Swamishri answered.

Curious, the swamis asked his reasoning. Swamishri explained, "If an emergency occurs, it would take too long for volunteers to reach the middle from the outer edges. If there is a dedicated line in the middle, they can provide immediate assistance whenever needed."

title: The True Charioteer
text:
This evening, during the Rath Yatra assembly, Swamishri shared his blessings.

"Today is the sacred day of Rath Yatra, and a divine memory of Yogiji Maharaj comes to mind," Swamishri began. "In 1970, we were in London with Yogi Bapa during the Rath Yatra festival. Yogi Bapa instructed Ishwarcharan Swami and me to make all the arrangements."

Swamishri continued with a smile, "We went out to get the horses. The horses were very large, and the chariot was quite small. But because Yogi Bapa had given the command, we did it. During the procession, the reins were placed directly into the hands of Shriji Maharaj. Seeing this, Yogi Bapa was incredibly pleased. He said, 'When the reins are in Maharaj's hands, He is the one steering our chariot. He has become our charioteer, and He will accomplish everything.'"

The moment we place the reins of our lives in Bhagwan's hands, our inadequacy is replaced by His omnipotence.

title: Unyielding Discipline
text:
Swamishri was about to retire for the night when he suddenly remembered that his Gnan Mudra exercise was still pending. Knowing how late it was, Uttamyogi Swami suggested, "We can do it while you are lying down."

However, Swamishri firmly declined the compromise. Instead, he sat upright in his chair, perfectly performed the Gnan Mudra, and only then, at 11:30 p.m., retired for rest.

Despite his advanced age and the sheer exhaustion from the heavy schedule of the Fuldol festival, Swamishri refused to take the easy way out. His strict adherence to his daily discipline teaches us a profound lesson in spiritual fortitude. True devotion is not just found in the enthusiasm of grand festivals, but in the quiet, unseen moments when we are tired and tempted to skip our daily practices.

title: The Habit of Humility
text:
The swamis mentioned to Swamishri, "The day after tomorrow is the Sant Shibir, and all the swamis are seated here, fully prepared."

Hearing this, Swamishri naturally folded his hands in reverence.

Noticing this, Narayanmuni Swami asked, "They are simply sitting prepared. Why did you fold your hands?"

Swamishri replied with total simplicity, "My hands just fold automatically. It has become a habit."

Throughout our lives, we unconsciously develop countless habits, but rarely do we cultivate the reflex of folding our hands in pure humility. Swamishri's automatic response reveals the astonishing depth of his dasbhav (servitude). He does not need to pause and remind himself to be humble; respect and reverence for everyone have become his very nature.

title: The Joy of Smruti
text:
After waking up this afternoon, an album was brought to Swamishri. It had been compiled by Bhudarjibhai Maru, the father of Bharatbhai Maru, who had personally taken the photographs of Yogiji Maharaj. Bharatbhai had carefully preserved this album for years.

Because the album was quite large, only a few pages were shown to Swamishri initially before it was placed on his bed. However, it seemed Swamishri's mind remained fixed on those images. After some time, he gestured toward the album and expressed his desire to see it. When he repeated this request two or three times, Uttamyogi Swami gently noted, "You have already seen this album before."

Hearing this, Swamishri became deeply immersed in a divine mood and replied, "Even if we see it 17 times, it is still not enough."

The memories of our Guru are living fountains of divine joy that only get sweeter with time.

title: The Guru's Care
text:
After lunch, when the swamis came to offer charansparsh, Kaivalyamurti Swami approached. Swamishri gestured and asked him, "How is your back now?"

About two months prior, Kaivalyamurti Swami had sought blessings for this in Ahmedabad. Swamishri had remembered that detail exactly. In the two months since, Swamishri had encountered countless visitors, attended numerous programs, and held endless meetings.

Even at age 93, Swamishri's ability to remember minor details reflects his selfless love and silent watchfulness over everyone's well-being. His memory expresses a heart that holds every devotee and cares for their individual struggles. This watchful compassion reminds us that to the Satpurush, no detail is too small and no devotee is ever forgotten.

title: Thoughtful Sensitivity
text:
After dinner tonight, a green laser pointer was left on the table. Swamishri picked it up and attempted to turn it on; seeing this, Uttamyogi Swami switched it on for him. Swamishri then aimed the beam toward him and asked, "Does it feel warm?"

When Uttamyogi Swami replied that it did not, Swamishri smiled.

Later, Uttamyogi Swami realized that during the evening program, Swamishri had been asked to use that laser to point toward certain swamis. Initially, he had pointed it upward. When he was prompted, "Swami, please point it toward the sadhus," he complied, but there was a visible hesitation. It seemed he was thinking, "If I point this at them, will it feel warm or cause them any discomfort?"

His hesitation reveals a deeply compassionate heart, sensitive to the discomfort of others even in trivial matters.

title: The Divine Vision
text:
Late tonight, as Swamishri was resting, he suddenly said, "Call Brahmavihari Swami."

As the call was being connected, Swamishri kept his hands folded in prayer. Intrigued, one of the swamis gently asked, "Swami, to whom are you folding your hands?"

Swamishri replied, "To Maharaj."

The swamis looked around and asked, "Where is Maharaj? We cannot see Him."

Swamishri gestured, but since there was nothing there, the swamis asked again, "Where is Maharaj?"

Swamishri then moved his right index finger in a slow circle, encompassing the entire room, and said, "Maharaj is everywhere."

For Swamishri, seeing Bhagwan everywhere is a living reality, not just a philosophy. This moment revealed his vision is fully anchored in that divine state, reminding us that Bhagwan is omnipresent.

title: The Spirit of a Youth
text:
This evening, the attendant swamis spoke to Swamishri regarding the upcoming consecration of the Nilkanth Varni murti. They explained, "The crane basket arranged for the installation is quite small and narrow, making it very difficult to sit in and ascend." They showed him photographs, hoping to suggest an alternative: "We will perform all the rituals at the feet of Nilkanth Varni on the ground. Would that be acceptable?"

Swamishri immediately signaled his clear preference. "We must go up to perform the consecration rituals." Then, he gestured the motion of applying a chandlo and said, "We must go up to perform the pujan and archan."

When he added, "We have done this everywhere else," the swamis expressed concern about the 108-foot height, the swaying, and the wind. "A young person could easily climb, but…"

Before they could finish, Swamishri interjected with remarkable fervor, "I will climb! I will climb!"

title: A Determined Path
text:
The attendants humbly persisted, "From a safety perspective, it would be better if we did not go up."

Yet, Swamishri remained resolute. He emphasized the purpose of the journey, saying, "We have traveled all the way from Gujarat for this—specifically for this consecration. If not for this, we could have done it in Gujarat. There would have been no need to come here."

Again, he made the gesture of applying a chandlo, clarifying that the entire purpose of the trip was to perform the pujan and archan of Nilkanth Varni from above. He insisted that the rituals must take place at the murti's level, not merely at the charanarvind (divine feet) below.

Seeing his clear, firm intent, everyone realized that Swamishri's courage transcends his physical age. He does not settle for the easy path; he seeks the most perfect way to honor Bhagwan.

title: The Inner Compass of Peace
text:
During today's evening assembly for the Akshardham volunteers, there was a question-and-answer session held with Swamishri.

Question: "How did you know when your Guru was truly pleased with your seva?"

Swamishri: "There was always a sense of peace within; that is how I knew the Guru was pleased."

Question: "You served alongside people with difficult or different natures. What mindset allowed you to serve joyfully with those individuals despite their natures?"

Swamishri: "I considered everyone to be muktas (liberated souls) and greater than myself. When you serve with the understanding that others are muktas, no obstacles can arise."

His life teaches us that the ultimate indicator of a Guru's pleasure is not external recognition, but the deep, unshakable peace that settles in our hearts.

title: The Selfless Servant
text:
After breakfast this morning, an urgent and important meeting was arranged, which concluded at 9:40 a.m. Swamishri was scheduled to retire for rest, but instead, he remarked, "I need to go for a bath. I have been feeling the need for quite some time, but I have been holding it back." Saying this, he proceeded to bathe.

In this way, Swamishri continues to carry out the work of the organization without a single thought for his own body. He ignored his designated rest time and suppressed his own physical needs to remain seated throughout the meeting.

He finally retired at 10:30 a.m.—which was actually his usual time to wake up—yet he did not offer a single complaint, nor did he suggest that meetings should not be scheduled at such hours.

Swamishri always endures personal inconvenience so the work of Bhagwan and the Guru continues uninterrupted.

title: Worrying about Thakorji
text:
Swamishri woke up. Although he lay back down, he did not fall asleep.

At 2:25 a.m., he pressed the pager for Uttamyogi Swami.

"Have Maharaj-Swami been covered warmly?" Swamishri asked, referring to Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj, the murtis embodying the living presence of Bhagwan Swaminarayan and Gunatitanand Swami.

"I could call Santcharit Swami," Uttamyogi Swami suggested, referring to the pujari of the murtis, "but he might be asleep…"

"Yes, go ahead and call," Swamishri said.

Even in the midst of the night, despite being tired and cold, his first thoughts trailed to making sure Thakorji was taken care of.

title: Worrying about Thakorji
text:
