Swamishri had Uttamyogi Swami call Santcharit Swami. To their surprise, Santcharit Swami answered the phone. As per Swamishri's instruction, he immediately went to the mandir and warmly covered the murtis of Maharaj-Swami.

Santcharit Swami then reported back, knowing Swamishri would be waiting, "Maharaj and Swami already had separate covers, and over that, a shared blanket. But since Swamishri specifically said 'warm,' I added an extra layer over the blanket as well."

Smiling, Uttamyogi Swami explained, "This all started because Swamishri woke up and felt cold."

"That's why Maharaj-Swami came to mind," Swamishri added.

For Swamishri, personal comfort has never taken precedence over his bhakti towards Thakorji. Even at this age, he continues to serve and care for the murtis with utmost devotion.

title: Writing the Satsang Diksha
text:
The Satsang Diksha is no ordinary text.

Composed by hand over 64 days, the Satsang Diksha was Swamishri's heartfelt offering to his guru, Pramukh Swami Maharaj, during his centenary celebrations. He began writing on Vasant Panchami, January 30, 2020, and completed it on Swaminarayan Jayanti, April 2, 2020. Each day, he wrote with devotion and discipline, 1.5 to 2 hours at a time, not just as an author, but as a humble channel for Bhagwan's will.

Its 315 Sanskrit shloks express the essence of the Vachanamrut and Swamini Vato in a format that is profound, concise, and accessible.

Swamishri longed for this wisdom to reach the masses. In a letter to devotees, he once wrote: "It is my deep wish to personally visit each and every home and explain these teachings one-to-one. But due to many limitations, this is not possible. However, as this text has reached your home, I feel the visit has been fulfilled."

title: Writing the Satsang Diksha
text:
This is why, on Guru Punam, Swamishri had one simple but heartfelt wish: the Satsang Diksha must be published online before the day ended. At 11:58 p.m., after final reviews by the publishing team, that wish was fulfilled. Swamishri was overjoyed.

Since then, the Satsang Diksha has been translated into over 14 languages and embraced around the world. Devotees have read, reflected upon, and memorized the verses. Scholars have written papers. Poets have composed kirtans. Thousands of children, many of whom had never studied Sanskrit before, have studied and memorized all 315 shloks.

More than just a text, the Satsang Diksha has become a vehicle of spiritual transformation: cultivating understanding, compassion, moral awareness, family unity, and devotion. It has empowered individuals intellectually and spiritually, helping them live as more conscious, caring, and principled human beings.

title: Dreaming of Devotees
text:
On this day, as per the doctors' advice, Swamishri began walking on a treadmill.

Since it was his first day using it, the speed was set to 2.7 km/h, and Swamishri occasionally sat in a chair to rest between sessions.

While walking, Swamishri said: "Today, in my dream, I saw myself meeting devotees. But here, because of my slight cold, they (pointing to the swamis) have recommended no personal meetings for now. Yet still, I meet them all in my dreams."

Swamishri's love for his devotees knows no limits—even asleep, he finds them in his dreams, showing the depth of his bond. His life is a testament to this selfless devotion; he prays, remembers, and guides them constantly, quietly bearing his own struggles so that he may nurture and uplift those who are his entire world.

title: Remembering Akshar-Purushottam
text:
Today was the start of Swamishri's 87th birthday celebrations. He woke up at 1:53 a.m. When the clock struck exactly 2:22:22 a.m., he called out, "Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj ni Jay!"

With delight, he said, "The birthday has begun with the jay of Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj!"

Then he offered prayers: "May Akshar-Purushottam nishtha spread throughout the world. May all the sadhus and devotees remain in good health and help in spreading this nishtha everywhere. These sankalps were made at exactly 2:22 a.m."

Swamishri returned to his room and lay down, but his eyes remained open and thoughts of God continued to flow. At 2:35 a.m., he added another prayer: "May no satsangi be harmed by the coronavirus. May no one at all be affected."

He sank again into contemplation.

title: Remembering Akshar-Purushottam
text:
At 2:47 a.m. on his 87th birthday, Swamishri said, "People can celebrate any birthday in any way, but if we share our nishtha in Akshar-Purushottam, if that devotion flourishes, then life is truly fulfilled."

Then he said, "Alright, let's sleep now."

The attendant requested, "Please bless all the sadhus and devotees so that Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj becomes the center of our lives."

Swamishri replied, "It will happen... it will happen."

At 2:55 a.m., he said, "Apart from Akshar-Purushottam, Brahma and Parabrahma, what else is there? They are the essence, the essence of all essences. And we have attained them — Brahma and Parabrahma! What great fortune…"

Then he said, "Now I must sleep…"

In Swamishri's life, nothing exists outside the divine focus of Akshar-Purushottam.

title: Remembering Akshar-Purushottam
text:
At 3:02 a.m. on his 87th birthday, Swamishri continued sharing his divine thoughts: "The essence of all the shastras is Brahma and Parabrahma! Without them, there is only confusion. These two are the essence!"

Swamishri smiled and asked, "What time is it?"

The attendant replied, "3:04... Swami, please try to sleep now."

"Alright."

"If you keep thinking, you won't fall asleep... try not to think."

Swamishri smiled faintly in agreement.

At 3:14 a.m., he said, "The splendour of countless universes is nothing without Akshar-Purushottam. Without them, nothing can be attained."

title: Remembering Akshar-Purushottam
text:
Again, at 3:20 a.m. on his 87th birthday, he said, "In the assembly hall, there is the murti of Neelkanth Varni performing penance. I always liked it, but somehow it never felt complete. But when Akshar was placed there, then everything matched perfectly. The connection was made. Without Akshar, worshipping Purushottam is impossible. When the principle of Akshar appears, everything falls into place."

He laughed softly and said, "Alright, let's sleep now."

At 3:33:33 a.m., he called out, "Dhām, Dhāmi, Mukta ni Jay!"

Swamishri rested for just a short while, and by 4:05 a.m., he was fully awake again. When he emerged from his room in the early morning, his face shone with the same serene freshness as always.

Regardless of occasion or time, his spiritual fervor for Akshar-Purushottam remains constant.

title: Dreaming of Neelkanth Varni
text:
On April 30, Swamishri watched the fourth part of the Shri Swaminarayan Charitra animation series, titled: Neelkanth and the Snows of the Himalayas. The film's stunning visuals of young Neelkanth Varni traversing India's scenic landscapes left a deep and lasting impression on him.

That night at 12:45 a.m., Swamishri woke from a dream, his face beaming with joy.

"I had the darshan of Neelkanth Varni walking," he said softly. "His walk was royal."

By the following morning, the memory was still vivid, and he shared more with eager delight: "He just kept walking and walking... There was no background, only the open sky! And he looked exactly like the Neelkanth Varni from the animation, just as I had hoped: royal, saiyami, and tapasvi. Shriji (Shrijiswarup Swami) created the animation perfectly, exactly how I envisioned it."

Thoughts of Bhagwan stay with him even in his dreams.

title: Dreaming of Neelkanth Varni
text:
Swamishri was narrating his dream of Neelkanth Varni and his sentiments behind the divine darshan.

Uttamyogi Swami, listening carefully, added: "In Swamishri's dream, there was another murti, a silhouette of Neelkanth Varni, sitting in a meditative pose."

Swamishri corrected him: "Not meditating! His leg was stretched out, resting on a stone — like this."

Then he extended his leg to demonstrate the exact posture he had seen in the dream. Then, laughing heartily, he said: "Those scenes went on all night... and even now, they continue in my mind."

While this dream brought a memory into being, it also revealed the presence of God that remained at the forefront of Swamishri's mind. Just as in the dream, Neelkanth Varni continued to walk unceasingly through his thoughts, beneath an open sky, vivid and alive.

title: Seva While Dreaming
text:
It was the sixth day of Swamishri's stay in Ahmedabad. After completing his morning puja, he folded his hands, meeting every person's gaze with affection, before returning to his room. Later, he walked to the dining hall, where sunlight streamed through open windows and a cool breeze carried freshness into the morning calm. A few swamis sat nearby; the serene atmosphere was perfect for correspondence work.

While seated there, Swamishri called everyone closer and shared a dream he had experienced earlier that morning: "Pramukh Swami Maharaj came into my dream," Swamishri revealed. "He said that he wanted to eat capsicum. The thought came immediately: 'this is my rare chance to serve him personally.'"

Swamishri continuously seeks opportunities to serve his guru, even within his dreams. He views any task as a precious opportunity to earn his rajipo.

title: Seva While Dreaming
text:
Swamishri narrated his dream from the night before to the swamis seated around him.

In the dream, Swamishri rushed to the kitchen. The capsicums were ready to be chopped, the pan was heating on the stove, and the spices were neatly arranged. His hands worked quickly, eager to prepare the food for his guru. But suddenly, flames leapt from the stove, smoke filling the kitchen. Overwhelmed, Swamishri called out, "Uttam, you take care of it now!" Uttamyogi Swami stepped in, and at that very moment, the dream ended.

Swamishri's voice softened as he reflected: "I wasn't able to serve Pramukh Swami…"

The swamis listened intently, smiling at the innocence of the dream. It was only a dream, yet even there Swamishri's heart revealed its devotion: a deep eagerness to serve his guru, and a sadness when it seemed he could not, even through the simplest act of cooking a meal.

title: A Borderless Akshar Deri
text:
A meeting had just finished, and Swamishri sat down for lunch. But today, he wanted to share something exciting. With a sparkle in his eyes, he said, "I had a dream…"

The swamis sitting nearby leaned in eagerly. "Tell us, Swami!"

Swamishri began describing it, his voice light and happy: "I saw the Akshar Deri, but it had no borders — no pillars, no walls, nothing to restrict it. Everyone was freely doing pradakshina, moving around in devotion."

The Akshar Deri is a sacred shrine in Gondal, built at the cremation site of Gunatitanand Swami. But what Swamishri saw was beyond even that: a shrine without edges, open and infinite, almost like Akshardham itself.

Swamishri continued while smiling: "There was G.D. Kaka, A.P. Kaka, Manibhai Saladwala, and so many devotees. Everyone was doing pradakshina freely, and yet no one bumped into each other. It was beautiful... peaceful... perfect."

title: A Borderless Akshar Deri
text:
Hearing Swamishri's dream about the Akshar Deri, one attendant asked curiously, "So, Swami, what were you doing?"

Swamishri laughed: "I was in space."

The swamis looked at each other, amazed. "In space? Watching from above?"

"Yes," Swamishri replied with a grin. "From there, I could see everyone. I was doing their darshan."

Another attendant asked, "Were there sadhus in the dream too?"

Swamishri nodded. "Yes, all of them. And all the foundational devotees I had met throughout my life."

As Swamishri shared the vision, his face glowed with bliss. In his dream, the Akshar Deri was a limitless haven of devotion, where devotees of past and present moved freely in prayer without limitations of time and space. For those listening, it revealed Swamishri's deep love for the Akshar Deri and his wish for samp amongst all.

title: Twenty-Three Dandvats
text:
It was very early in the morning, around 2:15 a.m., and most of Sarangpur was fast asleep. But Swamishri was awake. He later revealed the reason:

"I had a dream... I saw Doctor Swami sitting peacefully in the sun. And, I thought to myself, 'This is the perfect chance to do dandvats!'

So I slowly approached from behind, and then bowed by laying flat on the ground — one dandvat. Doctor Swami didn't even notice!

'No one is here to stop me,' I thought. 'I can make the most of this opportunity!'

So I bowed again: two dandvats, three, four... and I kept going.

I wanted to keep doing dandvats for as long as I could. But when I reached 23 dandvats, I suddenly heard a noise and thought, 'Oh no, someone is coming and will see me!' So I stopped."

Upon hearing Swamishri's dream, everyone smiled. Even in his dreams, Swamishri shows deep respect and love for senior swamis.

title: It Is My Bhakti
text:
During a conversation, Swamishri was asked about his dedication to letter writing amid the intense travel and challenges of vicharan.

"Swamishri, in Ghoghamba, you wrote a letter at 3:30 in the afternoon. From Khajurdi village, you wrote another at 2:30 in the early hours of the morning. While in Panchmahal, one of your fingers got caught in a chair."

Swamishri smiled as he held up the affected finger.

"Yes, so you had to eat using a spoon with your left hand. Despite the pain, you continued writing letters. One letter you completed only after finishing your vicharan in three different places.

Whether short on time, in discomfort, or faced with other challenges, you never stopped writing letters. What gives you the strength to endure such pressure?"

Swamishri replied, "I have given everything to Shriji Maharaj; he is the one who does it all."

"But with what mindset do you bear such hardship?"

"It is my bhakti!"

title: The Pragat Form
text:
In the evening session of the ongoing shibir, many questions were asked to Swamishri.

One of the questions asked was as follows: "How should we understand that you [Mahant Swami Maharaj] and Swami Bapa [Pramukh Swami Maharaj] are one?"

Swamishri replied, "[In the way that] Bapa has written in the letter."

Swamishri's answer highlights the importance of unwavering faith in the Satpurush's words. It reminds us to internalize the profound lesson taught by Shastriji Maharaj upon Bhagatji Maharaj's return to Akshardham: that the Satpurush never leaves this Earth. Recognizing this oneness allows us to experience their constant presence and guidance.

title: A World Without Negativity
text:
It was the Covid lockdown, and Swamishri had already spent almost 200 days in the peaceful village of Nenpur. This beautiful land had been blessed by Bhagwan Swaminarayan, and even today, it was full of nature, wildlife, and prayer.

One morning, after puja, Swamishri shared a special dream.

In the dream, Swamishri stood in Banyan Tree Square, the open space at the heart of Nenpur. But it looked very different. There were huge boards standing everywhere, each taller than a person. On them were the words: 'No Abhav-Avgun!' – meaning 'No Negativity' – written in Hindi, Gujarati, and Marathi.

Above them, a giant green X stretched across the sky from the banyan tree to the garden near the Sarvasva building.

His subconscious focus on avoiding abhav-avgun demonstrates that his commitment to remaining free of negativity is a deep, internal immersion that continues even while he rests.

title: A World Without Negativity
text:
Swamishri's dream in the Banyan Tree Square in Nenpur continued:

All around, senior sadhus were teaching about living without complaint and without negativity. Respected teachers – the sadguru santo, Gnaneshwar Swami, Narayanmuni Swami, Adarshjivan Swami, and others – spoke to big groups. Swamishri walked around, guiding and checking every detail.

The square was full of energy; hundreds of thousands of devotees buzzed in and out. They greeted each other by making an X sign in the air with their finger and happily calling, "No Abhav-Avgun! No Abhav-Avgun!" In another corner, Bhadresh Swami led the Marathi section.

People kept coming and returning again and again. In total, one hundred speakers shared the same positive message, their voices joined together like one big song of unity.

His singular desire is to foster a global community where negativity is absent and divine positivity flourishes in every heart.

title: A World Without Negativity
text:
Later in the day, Swamishri went for his usual short walk on the path near Sarvasva and then stepped into Banyan Tree Square. He smiled and pointed to the exact places from his dream: the coconut tree by the dining hall where the giant X began, the corner of the garden with the weaverbird's nest where the X ended, and the place in the sky where he had seen Shastriji Maharaj and Yogiji Maharaj, faint and glowing, watching with warm smiles.

"The X wasn't red," he remembered. "It was green, full of life."

For those listening, the dream felt like an optimistic vision of the future. For Swamishri, it was already real — alive with love, harmony, and happy hearts — it was a world he lived out every day and invited everyone to join.

title: Dandvats to His Attendants
text:
After reciting the cheshta, Swamishri followed his nightly routine and took a bath. When he returned to his room, something unusual awaited him: all the attendants stood in a perfect line, like soldiers ready to welcome their commander-in-chief.

This fun moment had started earlier that morning when Swamishri shared a dream: "In my dream," he said, "I lined up all the sevaks and told them, 'I need to scold you today.' And then I shouted, 'Attention!'"

Everyone stood perfectly: chin up, chest out, shoulders back, stomach in, arms at their sides. Completely still.

But instead of scolding anyone, Swamishri bowed down and offered dandvats to all the attendants.

"These two wrestlers rushed to stop me," Swamishri said, playfully referring to Santcharit Swami and Uttamyogi Swami. "But as they ran toward me, I shouted, 'STOP!' and they froze like statues. Then I finished all my dandvats without interruption."

title: Dandvats to His Attendants
text:
After hearing Swamishri's dream, the attendants later got together and hatched a plan: "It doesn't feel right for Swamishri to bow to us," they agreed. "Tonight, we'll turn it around and bow to him instead!"

That evening, when Swamishri entered his room, the attendants stood in formation like soldiers. One attendant called out, "Together now... Daaaandvats!"

All of them bowed down at once before Swamishri, laughing as they stood back up.

Swamishri looked at them in surprise, then his confused expression spread into a wide smile: "What's all this?" he asked.

They explained, "In your dream, you bowed to us. Now we are bowing to you…"

Then the attendants made a request, "Swami, in the dream you wanted to scold us. So please, scold us now!"

Swamishri shook his head and replied in English, "No, no... I cannot dare to do that!"

title: Dandvats to His Attendants
text:
The attendants persisted: "We don't mean a harsh scolding, Swami. Just give us one piece of advice, anything we should improve on."

But instead of scolding them, Swamishri praised them: "Tame badhā mukto chho – you are all liberated souls."

Still, they pleaded: "Just one point, Swami. Don't call it a scolding, call it loving advice."

Smiling, Swamishri said, "You already have everything you need in your lives…"

Tyagratna Swami then shared what was in Swamishri's heart: "His only intention was to bow down to us, not to scold us. That's why, in his dream, he said 'Attention!' and had everyone stand in line."

Swamishri agreed, "If I hadn't made you stand in line, none of you would have allowed me to do it. After I said 'STOP!' no one moved, so I could finish all my dandvats."

The joy of being able to offer dandvats to the attendants, even in a dream, was visible on Swamishri's face.

title: They Are All Mukto
text:
Swamishri awoke at 3:30 a.m. Everyone was still sleeping, so Swamishri tiptoed his way to the bathroom. On his return, he paused in the faint light before the murti of Shastriji Maharaj, Yogiji Maharaj, and Pramukh Swami Maharaj, gazing at them in silence. Then he lay down once more and had a beautiful dream.

Just days earlier, from March 7 to 9, 2017, Swamishri had traveled more than 200 kilometers to Mount Abu to spend three days with the children of the BAPS Swaminarayan Vidyamandir, a residential school founded by Pramukh Swami Maharaj.

During that visit, Swamishri interacted with the students, played games with them, fed them tasty snacks, and watched proudly as they displayed their talents — ranging from acrobatics to painting. He had taught them to wake up early, study honestly, pray to Bhagwan, and be brave. Truly, he had become their favorite teacher and trusted friend.

title: They Are All Mukto
text:
In his dream, Swamishri once again visited the school, but this time, he was accompanied by Shastriji Maharaj, Yogiji Maharaj, and Pramukh Swami Maharaj.

Pramukh Swami Maharaj looked at the rows of children and said, "All these children are divya (divine)."

Swamishri replied joyfully, "They are 100% divya!"

Looking towards Shastriji Maharaj, Swamishri thought, "How wonderful, at such a young age, these children have grasped the importance of Akshar! Truly, they are mukto."

Just then, the smell and sound of food being served filled the air. Yogiji Maharaj always loved cooking and feeding others like a doting mother, and here he served and fed the children as they sat neatly in rows. Halfway through, Yogiji Maharaj called Swamishri to join him.

Pramukh Swami Maharaj began joyfully serving the children and said, "They are all mukto." The atmosphere was filled with love and devotion.

title: The Guru That Bows
text:
After a light meal, Swamishri returned to his room to rest in the morning. One attendant, seizing a quiet moment, ventured a question that had been on his mind for some time.

"Swami," he began, "many times you've mentioned dreams, but some are still left untold."

Swamishri's face lit up. "Well," he said, smiling to himself, "in most of my dreams, I'm simply offering dandvats to everyone. Really, I should be doing it one by one, but most of the time, I bow to everyone together."

It was an image both surprising and endearing: the guru, even in his dreams, bowing humbly to all.

Hearing this, the attendant couldn't help but laugh. "Ā to avli Gangā thai!" he exclaimed. The Gujarati phrase literally means, "The Ganga has started flowing in reverse," used when something happens opposite to what's expected.

Swamishri only smiled and replied, "That's how it is most of the time… so there's hardly a need to mention it."

title: Dreaming of Gurus
text:
During the first twelve days of his vicharan in Dar es Salaam, Swamishri stayed where youth and children's conferences were being held.

This morning, Swamishri sat in an electric shuttle. As he was driven towards the conference hall, he blessed all those attending the conference, and shared something special with Uttamyogi Swami.

"I walked with Yogi Bapa along the seashore... holding his hand. Pramukh Swami Maharaj was walking with us."

"In a dream?"

"Yes."

title: Dreaming of Gurus
text:
Two nights later he mentioned his initial dream, the same experience returned.

Around 2:30 a.m., Swamishri awoke to bathe, the dream still vivid: he was walking along the seashore, hand in hand with Yogiji Maharaj, like a father with his son, while Pramukh Swami Maharaj walked close by. After bathing, he returned to rest.

But at 3:50 a.m., he woke once more. This time, the dream had repeated itself with a slight difference:

Yogiji Maharaj was feeling cold and had wrapped himself in a blanket. Near them, Ramswarup Swami was singing the kirtan "Koti Vandan Kariye Yogiji..." in a soft and emotional tune, called Karun Rāg. Even in Swamishri's dream, tears filled Ramswarup Swami's eyes as he sang, his voice full of heartfelt devotion.

title: Dreaming of Gurus
text:
Later that morning, while eating breakfast, Swamishri reflected on all three dreams:

"Two days ago, in the dream, Yogi Bapa felt hot... Then this morning at 2:30 a.m., he was comfortable. And later in the early morning at 3:50 a.m., he was wrapped in a blanket because he felt cold, otherwise it was the same scene each time…"

Swamishri reminisced in wonder, "...exactly the same."

For Swamishri, these dreams were not just passing images but divine encounters, meaningful moments with his guru, surrounded by the sounds of devotion and the presence of the people he loved.

title: Sanctifying the Water
text:
After a long journey with multiple delays, Swamishri finally arrived in Melbourne late into the night from Singapore, a seven-hour flight covering 6,200 kilometers.

It was around 2:30 a.m. when Paramchintan Swami entered Swamishri's room carrying a bottle of water. He hoped it could be sanctified as prasad for the hundreds of devotees who had fasted that day in devotion to Swamishri's arrival.

Swamishri was already in his bed, just moments away from sleep after the exhausting day of travel. But without hesitation, he sat up immediately, blessed the water, and then lay back down. At 2:40 a.m., he finally closed his eyes to sleep.

title: Caring for Others
text:
When he awoke the next morning, his first words were not about his own fatigue, but about the well-being of Tyagratna Swami, who had accompanied him on the journey.

"Tamne ungh avi? — Did you get enough sleep?"

Despite the exhausting night, Swamishri was ready for his morning puja at 7:25 a.m. He was sharp and serene. In fact, according to Singapore time, it was 5:25 a.m., which perfectly aligned with his usual schedule.

As soon as his puja finished, swamis brought in his breakfast. But Swamishri immediately reminded them, "Arti baki chhe" — "The arti is yet to be done." In the fatigue of travel and the haze of jet lag, everyone had unintentionally forgotten about the arti. But Swamishri did not. With awareness and devotion, he ensured the arti was performed first. Only then did he sit down for breakfast.

Each small gesture revealed the same truth: Swamishri's thoughts were always for God and for others.

title: Bhagwan Sau Nu Bhalu Karo
text:
After completing breakfast, Swamishri shared, "Since I went to bed early last night, I had rested enough by 2:30 a.m."

Then, pointing to the sevak seated beside him, he added, "But I was happy remaining in my bed so that he could rest peacefully."

He then described what he did while lying awake: "We're staying near the beach, so I was praying for the well-being of everyone here — not just those with us, but also all those staying in this area. I kept praying, Bhagwan sau nu bhalu karo — may Bhagwan do good for all… may Bhagwan bring peace and joy to everyone."

Swamishri continued, "That prayer continues within me constantly. We should wish well for everyone, whether or not they reciprocate. The moment we wish even the slightest ill towards anyone, it stains our own mind — and that stain is not easily removed."

title: Bhagwan Sau Nu Bhalu Karo
text:
Swamishri recalled a moment with Pramukh Swami Maharaj: "Pramukh Swami once said, 'Throughout my life, I have never wished ill of anyone.' Just look at the height of his spirituality."

The swamis, grappling to fully understand this mindset, posed a question: "But Swami, some people — they really do deserve punishment!"

Swamishri gently disagreed, "We should still wish only good for them. May God bless him — that is what we need to say. If someone has done wrong, and God chooses to correct him, then even that correction will ultimately be for his benefit. That is how God works."

The swamis responded, "Swami, perhaps we can learn to wish well for most people. But it's difficult to do so for those who have caused us real harm — especially deeper harm. It doesn't sit well in our minds."

title: Bhagwan Sau Nu Bhalu Karo
text:
Swamishri responded with calm clarity: "Then leave them to God. Pray that God blesses them. Even if God corrects them, he will do so in a way that benefits them. But if we take matters into our own hands and try to punish them, it will only damage us.

We may perceive something as punishment from God, but even then, God is acting with compassion. He treats everyone as his own child.

Imagine a father with five sons. If one son goes astray, the father may discipline him, but he does so with love, with the hope that the child improves. In the same way, Bhagwan is that kind of parent, the parent of all parents."

Hearing these final words, the swamis understood that "Bhagwan sau nu bhalu karo" was not a passing gesture but a prayer that flowed through him constantly, for everyone, without exception. This was the secret of his unshakable peace.

title: Bhagwan Sau Nu Bhalu Karo
text:
As Swamishri arrived at the cabin for his morning puja and took his seat on the sofa, a makodo (black carpenter ant) crawling nearby caught his eye. Immediately concerned that the tiny creature might get crushed, he pointed toward it.

Gauging Swamishri's wish, Vednayan Swami carefully gathered the ant with a tissue and transferred it outside to safety.

This gentle gesture offered a vivid glimpse into Swamishri's profound compassion: he never harbors the slightest intent to cause harm to any living soul.

title: Enduring Silently
text:
Following the morning discourse, the Sarangpur Medical Department presented its report to Swamishri. At the end of the meeting, the medical team brought forward a device used for removing corns (kapāsi) to be sanctified. Swamishri sanctified the instrument.

As he did, Swamishri casually remarked, "I also had a corn. It stayed with me for over twenty years."

Later, once Swamishri had retired to his room, an attendant curiously asked, "How was it cured?"

Swamishri replied, "It was never cured. Over time, the skin and the corn just fused into one."

"Did it hurt?" the attendant asked.

Swamishri nodded, "Yes."

For over two decades, he relentlessly traveled and engaged in tireless seva while silently carrying that persistent physical pain. He deliberately kept it to himself—fully aware that speaking of it would have prompted immediate medical attention.

title: Becoming Brahmarup
text:
After his evening meal, Swamishri was scheduled to attend a video recording session in the old Sarvasva Hall. Shortly before departing, he developed a persistent cough. Despite the physical discomfort, Swamishri chose not to cancel the shoot and proceeded to the hall as planned.

Inside, a class was underway, with Atmatrupt Swami guiding the student swamis through the Bhagavad Gita Bhashya. Swamishri sat to observe their studies. Taking the opportunity, Atmatrupt Swami asked, "Swami, the Gita speaks about attaining the brahmarup state. But how does one actually become brahmarup?"

Swamishri replied with unwavering clarity: "One becomes brahmarup only through the association of Brahman—by attaching oneself to the Brahmaswarup Guru. Without that association, even after millions of kalpas (eons), one cannot attain the brahmarup state."

title: Scholarship and Saintliness
text:
Continuing the interaction in the Bhagavad Gita Bhashya class, one of the student swamis posed another question to Swamishri: "Swami, what must we do so that both scholarship (vidvattā) and saintliness (sādhutā) flourish together in our lives?"

Swamishri explained: "The core requirement is attaining the company of a true sadhu—the Satpurush. Once you have that, every problem is resolved. Otherwise, there is always an inner void, a lack of firm grounding. One gets pulled back and forth in different directions, and true balance is never achieved. Through the Brahmaswarup Guru alone, every problem finds its resolution."

Through these words, Swamishri imparted that intellectual mastery and genuine purity naturally harmonize only under the refuge and guidance of the Brahmaswarup Guru.

title: A Sea of Smiles
text:
A massive sea of devotees gathered to celebrate the Janmashtami festival, filling both assembly halls to absolute capacity. After the main evening sabha concluded, Swamishri made a special visit to the lower auditorium to grant darshan. Walking slowly from one end of the stage to the other, he satisfied the eager gaze of every devotee before returning to where he had started.

Suddenly, filled with an overwhelming surge of affection, Swamishri turned to the swamis: "Call the children forward... let them pass by in a line."

At first, the swamis could barely comprehend: "Children? Meaning all of them? From the entire auditorium?!"

Swamishri confirmed with a yes. Like rivers racing joyfully toward the ocean, the children surged toward the stage. Swamishri lovingly placed his hand on the heads of over 200 young children, his face radiating boundless joy, leaving everyone present with an unforgettable, divine smruti.

title: The Art of Smruti
text:
During lunch today, the tumbadis (traditional water gourds) belonging to a few swamis were brought forward for Swamishri to sanctify.

Looking at the gourd, Swamishri fondly reminisced about Yogiji Maharaj: "Yogi Bapa always drank water from a tumbadi. While drinking, he would hold it in such a particular way that his little finger never touched the gourd."

This brief observation revealed how deeply Swamishri had absorbed every action of his Guru decades ago. Shortly after, the attendants showed Swamishri an archival video clip of Yogiji Maharaj drinking water on an iPad. The footage matched Swamishri's description down to the exact detail—Yogi Bapa held the tumbadi with his pinky finger extended, never touching the surface.

He did not simply observe his Guru's physical actions; he imprinted every minute detail into his heart, keeping those divine memories as alive and fresh today as when they first unfolded.

title: Thoughtful Attentiveness
text:
During dinner tonight, Adarshjivan Swami was seated on the floor, writing on a sheet of paper using the carpet beneath him for support.

Swamishri noticed this right away. With a swift, simple gesture, he directed the attendants to place a writing pad underneath the paper, and they promptly handed one to Adarshjivan Swami.

While everyone in the room saw Adarshjivan Swami writing, no one else had thought to offer him a proper writing surface. Swamishri, however, instantly recognized the subtle inconvenience and saw that it was resolved. This quiet moment beautifully reflects Swamishri's deep thoughtfulness and empathy—a virtue marked by an innate sensitivity to the unspoken, everyday needs of those around him.

title: A Cherished Memory
text:
Swamishri sat in a quiet corner of the mandir pradakshinā, enjoying an informal goshthi with the swamis.

One of the swamis asked, "Swami, which memory of Yogi Bapa do you love recalling the most?"

Swamishri replied with a warm smile, "I love them all."

The swamis pressed a bit further: "Swami, is there a specific incident of Yogi Bapa that you especially like?"

Swamishri reflected and shared, "The incident at Ghanshyamcharan Swami's home, where Yogi Bapa squeezed mangoes."

Even after decades, the smallest and most tender moments spent with his Guru remain a living source of joy for Swamishri, revealing how completely his heart is filled with love and remembrance for Yogiji Maharaj.

title: Gātariyu on Fire
text:
While reminiscing about Yogi Bapa during a goshthi in the pradakshinā, Swamishri went on to share another cherished memory:

"Yogi Bapa was performing his morning puja, completely absorbed in devotion. I was sitting nearby, completely unaware that the edge of my gātariyu had drifted too close to the lit divo and caught fire.

The moment Yogi Bapa noticed it, he rose instantly from his seat without needing any support, rushed over, and quickly put out the flames by clapping the burning cloth between his hands. Even while deeply immersed in puja, he maintained such vigilant care for his disciple. Normally, when someone is that absorbed in prayer, no one would expect them to notice what is happening around them."

Through this memory, Swamishri highlighted Yogi Bapa's remarkable balance of total absorption in God and constant, protective care for those under his wing.

title: Sleepless for a Devotee
text:
A devotee from Himmatnagar, Rupabhai, had appealed for help: his wife, Lakshmiben, was gravely ill with a heart condition, and after two failed surgeries the doctors had decided her valve would have to be replaced. He had only been able to raise the matter on the last day of Swamishri's visit, so Brahmavatsal Swami had promised to convey every detail at the first opportunity.

That night, the sevaks shared the entire situation. Even while lying down, Swamishri became completely absorbed. He fell silent, reflecting deeply.

After a moment, he said to Shrutipriya Swami, "We must help them."

"Yes, Swami," he replied. "Tomorrow we will gather all the details, what assistance is needed, and report back. Then we will arrange everything as you wish."

Swamishri closed his eyes.

title: Sleepless for a Devotee
text:
Early the next morning, Swamishri asked again, "What happened to that devotee?"

"We've made further inquiries," they reported. "Their situation is genuine, and he truly needs help. But it was late last night and too early this morning to reach him again. We will call shortly and learn the full details."

Swamishri nodded. Then, in a quiet voice, he added, "Last night, for an hour, I kept thinking about this. From half past two until half past three."

The sevaks were startled. "Swami, you didn't sleep? You were awake, praying for them?"

"Yes."

In the days that followed, calls were made and support began to take shape. To this day, whenever Rupabhai and Lakshmiben remember Swamishri's care, their eyes fill with tears, knowing that even in the darkest hours of the night, Swamishri had never left their side.

title: The Power of Samjan
text:
To mark the inauguration of the Yuva Shibir, Swamishri performed the deep prāgatya (lamp-lighting) and shared a guiding message with the youth: "Nishkulanand Swami writes, 'Sakhi samjanmā ghanu sukh chhe'—there is boundless joy in understanding. With the right understanding, any conflict can be resolved in a single second."

Elaborating, Swamishri explained: "Samjan is the ultimate solution to every problem. When the mind and heart become one, genuine samjan takes root, and from that comes everlasting happiness."

Connecting this to spiritual identity, he added: "The entire essence of samjan is captured in the mantra 'Aksharam Aham Purushottama Dāso'smi,' because Maharaj-Swami are above all. This mantra should be firmly established in our hearts."

Swamishri concluded: "Chant this mantra daily—not just once, but continuously. Contemplate its meaning, and your life will be filled with pure joy."

title: Perfection
text:
Swamishri was asked about his sharp attention to detail:

"You always pay great attention to detail, even in the smallest things. For example, when you hang up your dhotiyu and gatariyu to dry, you make sure all four corners are straight. When you spread a bedsheet, you never leave a single crease. How is such precision connected to ekantik dharma?"

"It brings us closer to God."

"How does this bring us nearer to God?"

"Because perfection is something God loves."

In just a few words, Swamishri revealed a profound truth: that even the most mundane tasks, when performed with care and precision, become a form of devotion that draws us closer to Bhagwan.

title: A Standard of Cleanliness
text:
After breakfast, Swamishri attended an important meeting where an urgent decision needed to be made. Following the meeting, he went to the restroom.

While there, Swamishri pointed toward the pair of socks he was wearing and asked, "Are these socks washed every single day?"

Uttamyogi Swami assured him, "Yes."

Swamishri was satisfied with the response.

This simple moment reflects Swamishri's instinctive preference for purity and hygiene. Even in the smallest, everyday habits, he naturally values cleanliness and encourages those around him to uphold the same mindful standard.

title: Praying for Akshardham
text:
On the morning of Jal-Jhilani Ekadashi, Swamishri completed his personal puja and addressed the devotees. He then offered arti to Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj, seated in a beautifully decorated boat. As it was also the final day of the Ganesh Chaturthi festival, Swamishri performed the pujan and arti of Shri Ganeshji before the murti was immersed in water.

Then Shrutipriya Swami took the microphone: "Late last night, Anandswarup Swami and Narayanmuni Swami made a heartfelt request: 'Swami, the rain is slowing down the seva. Please pray that we overcome this, and may the Robbinsville Akshardham inauguration happen in the best possible manner.'

Then Swamishri sat down to do mala. The swamis nearby began to feel sleepy, but Swamishri continued chanting without pause. I glanced at the clock; it had already been 51 minutes! Only then did Swamishri hand over the mala and lie down, at 11:45 p.m."

title: Praying for Akshardham
text:
Shrutipriya Swami had shared how Swamishri stayed up late chanting mala for the smooth progress of Robbinsville Akshardham. Soon after, another attendant revealed that this intense prayer was far from an isolated incident:

"This wasn't a one-off event. Swamishri continued performing mala the next night, from 11:15 p.m. to 12:06 a.m., and again on the following night, from 10:50 p.m. to 12:05 a.m. Despite his hectic daily schedule, his prayers continued right up until the opening of Akshardham on October 8."

This quiet dedication illustrates the depth of Swamishri's spiritual stewardship. While hundreds of volunteers poured their physical energy into construction during the day, the Guru worked tirelessly through the night—carrying the burden of the entire project through intense, heartfelt prayer and laying the true spiritual foundation for Akshardham's historic opening.

title: No Creases
text:
Swamishri woke up. At 2:45 a.m., he walked towards his bed, and began making the bed himself. Uttamyogi Swami had already made the bed, but there were small creases that would not go away. Swamishri tried sliding his hands downwards to smooth them, but it didn't work. He kept trying. Then he slid his hands upwards, and the crease disappeared.

The sevak watched silently. He saw how Swamishri would not leave even a few creases and would patiently persevere until everything was just right. He often wondered why Swamishri insisted on such perfection in every task.

title: Thakorji Deserves Perfection
text:
Swamishri was asked, "During Gunatitanand Swami Maharaj's 200th birth anniversary celebration, you were arranging small stones in the landscape. Why were you so particular about placing them all exactly evenly?"

Swamishri replied, "It looks nice that way. If they are all different sizes, it feels as if someone has just piled up a heap of stones carelessly."

"But people don't notice everything with such precision. As long as the stones are arranged, it looks fine. There's no need to go to such lengths."

"No, it's not like that. We are doing this for Thakorji (God), and Thakorji deserves perfection."

title: Thakorji Deserves Perfection
text:
Continuing the conversation on Swamishri's particular observance of perfection, they further asked him: "But Thakorji bhavna bhukhya chhe. Whether it is perfect or not, he only looks at the feeling and intention behind it."

"My sentiment is that I should prepare everything to the best of my ability before showing it to Thakorji. So I keep working until I feel satisfied."

"But doesn't it ever get frustrating?"

"When we truly do it for God, it never gets frustrating."

Swamishri executes every endeavor with precision solely to please Bhagwan. His unwavering dedication to excellence, especially in guiding us toward spiritual purity, serves as a guiding light, motivating us to strive to be ideal disciples.

title: Quiet Consideration
text:
From February 3 to April 16, 2018, Swamishri undertook a 73-day vicharan of the Asia-Pacific region. His schedule was fast-paced: moving from Singapore to Melbourne, Auckland, Wellington, Brisbane, Sydney, Adelaide, the Gold Coast, back to Sydney, then on to Perth, Singapore again, and then arriving in Bangkok, the capital of Thailand.

The next morning, Swamishri awoke at around 2:45 a.m. Still adjusting to the time difference, he woke earlier than usual. As he began to get ready, the attendant sitting nearby had dozed off, tired from the heavy travelling. Not wishing to disturb him, Swamishri spent the next hour absorbed in reading the Swamini Vato and Vachanamrut.

Only at 5:00 a.m., when it was time to leave the room for puja, did he gently clap his hands to wake the attendant.

title: Tireless Dedication to Duty
text:
During the Sant Shibir, Swamishri maintained a remarkably demanding schedule. Alongside the shibir sessions, he diligently continued his daily routine of personal exercise, meetings, and writing letters.

A look at his routine for the day reflects his extraordinary discipline. After taking soup and fruit, Swamishri wrote a letter, completed light exercise, and then attended two urgent meetings before the Sant Shibir. He then enriched the sadhus with his guidance before proceeding to dinner. Following dinner, he participated in two more meetings before concluding his day with the nightly cheshta.

Even at the age of 93, Swamishri carries the vast responsibilities of the fellowship with steadfast enthusiasm, all while flawlessly fulfilling his personal daily ahniks. When he sits for the cheshta, there is not the slightest trace of mental weariness—his awareness naturally centers on Bhagwan.

title: A Healer's Compassion
text:
After breakfast today, Swamishri was informed that one of the sadhus was experiencing a physical health issue. Genuine concern was visible on Swamishri's face. He lovingly blessed the sadhu, reassuring him, "Everything will be fine. You will recover completely."

Afterward, Swamishri retired to his room to rest. Yet even as he went to lie down, his mind remained entirely intent on relieving that sadhu's discomfort.

While settling down, Swamishri asked for Shrutipriya Swami to be called. When he arrived, Swamishri instructed him, "There is a red homeopathy book. Near the beginning, there is a section covering allergies. Please give him the remedy mentioned there."

By prescribing the appropriate remedy, Swamishri directly eased the sadhu's suffering while also revealing his remarkably deep knowledge of homeopathy—a study he undertook solely to lovingly serve and care for the sadhus and devotees in times of need.

title: Embracing Hardship within Hardship
text:
During lunch, Anandpriya Swami shared an incident while talking with Swamishri:

"In 2015, during Swamishri's visit to London on the day of Jal-Jhilani Ekadashi, Swamishri had observed a complete waterless fast (nirjala upvas). Having woken up early in the morning, he remained awake and active throughout the entire afternoon. Seeing this, I humbly requested him, 'Please retire to rest a little early tonight.' He kindly agreed. However, until 11:40 p.m. that night, he stayed up writing an encouraging letter to the youth for the Become Adarsh magazine. Finally, at 12:00 a.m., he went to rest. He upheld all of his daily spiritual disciplines and, by willingly embracing hardship within hardship, granted spiritual benefit to everyone."

Even after a strict waterless fast and a demanding schedule, he placed the spiritual encouragement of others above his own comfort.

title: Katha Itself Is Rest
text:
Swamishri's sleep broke at 1:45 a.m. Not wanting to disturb anyone, he stayed in bed until 3:00 a.m., and when sleep still wouldn't come, he spent the next half hour listening to the biography of Bhagatji Maharaj.

At 4:10 a.m. he asked the sevak, "Did you enjoy listening?"

"Yes," the sevak replied.

Swamishri smiled. "So much joy, joy, joy!"

During breakfast, the sevak requested, "Please eat something and get some proper rest. The Divya Sannidhi Parva isn't until eleven, and you were awake almost the whole night."

"I was resting!" Swamishri countered.

"But when? You woke up at 1:45 a.m. and never went back to sleep."

"Katha itself is rest," he said matter-of-factly.

The sevaks fell silent. For most, rest meant sleep. For Swamishri, it was found in devotion, not in comfort or rejuvenation, but in listening to spiritual talks, in katha.

title: Katha Itself Is Rest
text:
That night, as he was about to rest again, Swamishri requested, "I want to relisten to the biography of Bhagatji Maharaj. There was a part that mentioned him washing his face, but I don't remember what came just before or after. I'd like to hear it again."

"We will listen to it ourselves and tell you in the morning," the sevak offered.

"No, please listen to it now and tell me. It was in the part about brahmavidya."

They searched through the chapters he had heard that morning until one of them spotted the heading: 'Brahmavidya's Single Point: Conquering the Mind.' Reading through it, they found the passage exactly as Swamishri had described. Even at 91, his memory impressed them all, for they had listened that same morning yet could not recall it so clearly.

title: Katha Itself Is Rest
text:
At Swamishri's request, the sevaks replayed the section covering Bhagatji Maharaj's incident: 'After saying shripatim, he rose, came down to have his meal, and lay down for a short rest. At three o'clock, Bhagatji woke up, washed his face, drank water, and sat up…'

Swamishri asked, "Was this at night or during the day?"

"It was during the day. After lunch, he rested for a while."

"I thought it said he woke up at three in the morning."

Only then did everyone understand why the detail mattered to him. That morning, Swamishri too had woken at 3:00 a.m. to listen to Bhagatji Maharaj's life, thinking in his heart, "Bhagatji Maharaj too would rise at three in the morning to reflect on spiritual truths." He held each detail of these sacred texts in his mind and reflected on it with care.

title: Cleanliness Can Never Wait
text:
Swamishri visited the sadhus' dining hall and lovingly served the sadhus a variety of sweets.

Afterward, as Swamishri sat in his wheelchair, his eyes caught a few stray drops of dudhpāk that had spilled onto the floor during the serving. He immediately pointed to the spill, gesturing that it should be cleaned up right away.

The sadhus responded, "We will clean it up right after you leave."

Swamishri, however, was not one to postpone cleanliness. He persisted, keeping his finger pointed toward the spill to make sure it was handled on the spot. Seeing his resolve, a sadhu promptly wiped the floor clean, and only then was Swamishri truly satisfied.

This simple moment reflects a principle ingrained in Swamishri's life since the very beginning: an unyielding insistence on cleanliness and immediate action, never allowing even the smallest mess to be brushed aside.

title: Steadfast Through the Night
text:
On the night of May 11, after a taxing day of video recordings, Swamishri returned to his residence for dinner. Following the nightly Cheshtā, he retired to bed.

It had been a rigorous, demanding day, and the physical toll was evident. Compounding the exhaustion, an upset stomach kept Swamishri awake, forcing him out of bed six times through the night. He hardly had any opportunity for restful sleep.

Yet, promptly the next morning on May 12, Swamishri rose at his scheduled time without a trace of hesitation. He prepared for the day, performed his morning puja in his room, and arrived right on time at the mandir for the next filming session.

This simple morning showed Swamishri's remarkable self-discipline and quiet resilience. Refusing to let bodily distress derail his commitments, he carried forward his service with unbroken focus, punctuality, and grace.

title: An Artist's Eye
text:
While seated for breakfast, Swamishri was shown the murtis at Gondal mandir across three consecutive days. They were shown at a relatively fast pace, featuring the daily chandan (sandalwood paste) vāghā adorning Akshar-Purushottam Maharaj.

Once breakfast concluded, Swamishri gestured for the murtis to be shown again. He clearly wanted to point out a specific detail.

Pausing on one of the days, Swamishri observed, "In this chandan vāghā, Maharaj's stomach appears slightly heavy. The sandalwood layer should be applied thinner there so the proportions look natural and slim, rather than protruding."

Even during a rapid glance, Swamishri's sharp eye caught what others missed in seconds. Having personally sculpted chandan vāghā for the Gondal murtis during Yogiji Maharaj's time, his keen aesthetic sense and devotion instantly recognized how to present Thakorji with the utmost grace and beauty.

title: Finding Peace in His Lap
text:
A small white rabbit was gently placed in Swamishri's lap.

The sadhus noted that this particular rabbit was normally spirited and restless, rarely staying still for long. Yet the moment it settled into Swamishri's lap, an immediate stillness took over. Swamishri lovingly stroked its fur, his touch so soothing and affectionate that the once-fidgety creature relaxed completely and drifted off to sleep right there.

This simple moment reflects the innate aura of tranquility surrounding Swamishri. Just as a restless creature found calm in his embrace, anyone who approaches the Satpurush experiences that same deep reassurance, comfort, and peace.

title: Everything Is Divine
text:
While riding in a glass-enclosed cart from the Prarthana Mandir back to his residence, Swamishri noticed a covered drain along the path. Pointing toward it, he asked, "What is that?"

Uttamyogi Swami answered, "That's a drain."

Without missing a beat, Swamishri remarked, "Even that is divine."

A little later, Brahmavatsal Swami followed up, curious: "How is a drain divine?"

Swamishri explained with calm conviction, "Everything within the Akshardham campus is divine."

Through this simple exchange, Swamishri revealed his elevated divyabhāv. Where worldly eyes perceive mere infrastructure and utility, the Satpurush sees the entire sacred campus sanctified, viewing every single corner through the lens of pure divinity.

title: The Joy of Firm Conviction
text:
As Swamishri was leaving the assembly, he traveled along an elevated walkway constructed to lead him directly back to his residence. Along the ramp, Bhadresh Swami met him. Even though Swamishri was high up on the raised platform and Bhadresh Swami stood on the ground below, Swamishri reached all the way down, caught Bhadresh Swami's hand, and shook it warmly with immense joy.

Later in his room, an attendant asked, "Why did you bend down so far just to hold and shake Bhadresh Swami's hand?"

Swamishri replied with deep spiritual pride, "Because the entire assembly had centered on talks of nishthā (firm spiritual conviction)."

Time and again, whenever the theme of nishthā arises, Swamishri's entire demeanor transforms. His spirit surges with unmistakable energy—truly embodying the saying, "chade chogano rang"—as his zeal for pure conviction radiates through every word and action.

title: The True Source of Virtues
text:
After lunch today, Anandchintan Swami gave a brief update regarding the bāl, kishore, and yuvak karyakars of the West Region. He then asked, "Swami, do you have a message for these karyakars?"

Swamishri expressed his clear wish: "They should read the Jivan Charitra (spiritual biographies) every single day."

Curious, Anandchintan Swami asked, "What benefit will they gain from that?"

Swamishri replied, "Through that, all spiritual virtues and qualities will naturally develop."

Swamishri has always placed immense value on daily reading of the Gurus' biographies, seeing it not merely as study, but as the most direct and effective way to transform one's life and absorb their divine virtues into daily life.

title: The True Virtuous Deed
text:
As today was Swamishri's 92nd birthday, an intimate question-and-answer session took place right after his morning puja.

Opening the dialogue, Atmatrupt Swami asked, "On your birthday, Yogi Bapa once blessed us saying, 'On the birthday of a great person, one should perform virtuous deeds (satkarma).' Which specific satkarma should we perform?"

Swamishri answered directly: "Everyone should genuinely understand each other's greatness (mahimā) and bow down to one another. Not casually or half-heartedly, but properly touching each other's feet—that is where true progress begins. And then, remain completely steadfast in nishthā (firm conviction) and āgnā (spiritual commands), constantly leaning in that direction."

Swamishri's message highlighted that true virtuous action begins with genuine humility and respect for one another, anchored in firm conviction and obedience.

title: His Birthday Wish
text:
During the reflective question-and-answer session on Swamishri’s birthday, the sadhus made a heartfelt spiritual request.
Atmatrupt Swami noted, “Swami, Yogi Bapa once said, ‘Mahant Swami is a soul of the highest spiritual stature. Whatever resolve he makes is fulfilled without fail.’ Since today is such a great day, please make an auspicious resolve (sankalp) for us all.”
Swamishri folded his hands and offered a heartfelt prayer: “My only prayer is that every single devotee becomes brahmarup and attains the ultimate ekāntik state.”

title: Yogi Bapa Did It All
text:
Continuing the birthday question-and-answer session, the sadhus reflected on Swamishri’s unbroken spiritual bond with the lineage of Gurus.

Atmatrupt Swami asked, “Swami, Yogi Bapa once said in his blessings, ‘Look how spiritually resolute Mahant Swami is; he offered continuous service, thus pleasing Shastriji Maharaj, and perfected his spiritual work.' Similarly, if we also perfectly ‘join’ our vrutti, we can attain your spiritual state. So Swamishri, please tell us how you managed to join your vrutti so deeply?”

Swamishri replied with characteristic humility: “It joined naturally on its own. In truth, Yogi Bapa did everything. On the outside it might seem like I accomplished it, but it was purely Yogi Bapa who united my mind to God.”

title: The Natural Path to Humility
text:
During the morning question-and-answer session honoring Swamishri’s birthday, the conversation turned toward cultivating inner saintliness and freedom from ego.

Atmatrupt Swami asked, “Yogi Bapa often said of you, ‘Mahant Swami possesses an eternal brahmic state; he is the very embodiment of saintliness and true humility.’ Swami, we also wish to become humble like you. What practical steps must we take to cultivate that?”

Swamishri shared a foundational truth: “That state arises naturally; you won’t have to struggle for it. Simply make two things firm in your life: Maharaj’s āgnā and upāsanā. When those two are firm, everything follows effortlessly.”

title: Beyond Temporary Pleasure
text:
Question: “When we see people who don't follow any rules enjoying worldly pleasures, the thought crosses our minds: shouldn't we indulge and enjoy ourselves too? Is that thought justified?”

Swamishri firmly replied: “It is not right. The moral disciplines (niyams) and righteous codes (dharma) you follow grant you a constant state. Those who disregard rules might appear happy on the surface, but in the long run, it leads only to [spiritual and moral] loss.”

“Often, the spiritual vows we take last only three or four days before we slip back into old habits. How can we sustain our progress?”

Swamishri explained: “When a doctor says something, we do it. We pay out of our own need and strictly follow the prescription. In Satsang, it is Bhagwan Himself giving the guidance. The real question is: Have we genuinely accepted God in our lives? When you truly accept Him, no questions remain, and all the work happens well.”

title: His Vision, My Mission
text:
Following the morning blessings, Swamishri was presented with a reflective question:

“Shastriji Maharaj’s wish was Sarangpur mandir. Yogiji Maharaj’s wish was Delhi Akshardham, and Pramukh Swami Maharaj’s wish was Robbinsville Akshardham. What is your wish? Please write it for us.”

Without hesitation, Swamishri wrote: “Pramukh Swami Maharaj’s wish of completing Robbinsville Akshardham is also my wish.”

Swamishri’s simple yet profound response revealed the pinnacle of gurubhakti. Rather than projecting an independent desire or carving out his own legacy, he aligned his will entirely with that of his Guru, Pramukh Swami Maharaj—demonstrating that true spiritual greatness lies in fulfilling the Guru's vision with total surrender and devotion.

title: Balancing Life and Satsang
text:
During a question-and-answer session with Swamishri, karyakars brought forward an everyday dilemma: “Swami, if we prioritize Satsang, then worldly duties have to take a back seat. If we prioritize worldly affairs, then Satsang has to become secondary. How can we strike the right balance and live an ideal householder life?”

Swamishri gave a straightforward formula: “You don't need to do anything else—just keep leaning toward Satsang, and sooner or later, everything will fall into place. Satsang instills the exact wisdom that anchors you close to Maharaj. Without that, one easily gets lost in the world. When Satsang is deeply rooted within, everything else is taken care of. But we do not practice Satsang completely, so problems come. But if you practice it firmly, then no problem will remain.”

title: Total Faith
text:
“We struggle to develop an interest in reading [satsang books]. What should we do?”

Swamishri advised: “Deepen your Satsang, and the taste for reading will follow naturally. As you engage more, you will encounter topics and stories that resonate with you, and step-by-step, you will progress in that."

Then, referencing the shibir's central motto, they requested: “This entire shibir has been organized with the theme ‘Dhanya Dhanya Mam Jivan’. Please bless us so that this deep feeling of fulfillment stays with us forever."

Swamishri concluded with empowering words: "For that, you must pray. You will not get it for free. What is free, goes for free. You will also have to make an effort. First of all, keep firm faith in Maharaj that everything He has said is the absolute truth.  If faith comes, everything follows. There is a lack of faith currently, but when complete faith comes within, life becomes truly blessed.”

title: Lean Towards Satsang
text:
“Will everyone's difficult phases turn into auspicious times?” Swamishri said yes, and blessed everyone.

Swamishri: "Problems are bound to come; this world is dependent on problems. In such times, lean toward Satsang, and every challenge finds a resolution. If we sideline Satsang and fail to understand its glory, we will end up wandering aimlessly. External hurdles will never cease, but give priority to Satsang. Even the toughest obstacle dissolves because Satsang grants the understanding needed to rise above it. Outwardly you may appear weak, but your inner strength will be immense. Satsang is bound to Bhagwan. With Bhagwan by your side, your problems untangle. And this understanding needs to be done; otherwise how can we be called satsangis? With genuine spiritual understanding, we connect directly with Maharaj; He remains with us always. You will then transcend all problems, and your understanding will keep increasing.”

title: Navigating Up’s and Down’s
text:
As the session progressed, the attendees asked for guidance on emotional resilience and digital discipline.

“Swami, often we cannot tolerate criticism or actions from others, and we end up reacting. How can we prevent this?”

Swamishri offered a reassuring perspective: “Right now, you are in the formative, growing stage of your spiritual life. Ups and downs are completely natural. But as you stay the course, a stage will come where you become spiritually enlightened, and these problems will simply disappear.”

Next, they asked: “On social media, we often see many things. What awareness should we keep so we don’t get carried away?”

Swamishri highlighted obedience: “Have faith in Bhagwan. He has instructed us to stay away from all of this. When a doctor tells us which medicine to take and avoid, we listen without question. When Bhagwan instructs us for our own well-being, how can we not follow?”

title: Precision of Memory
text:
The evening blessings that day were to be delivered from the book Purushottam Bolya Prite. Swamishri had spent time reading from it in his room beforehand.

Later, when it was time for the blessings in the assembly, Uttamyogi Swami approached to help Swamishri put on his microphone. At that moment, Swamishri looked at him and said, “23.”

No one else nearby understood what the number meant. Swamishri was recalling the exact page number in Purushottam Bolya Prite where the passage he had read earlier was located, indicating that they were to open to page 23.

Uttamyogi Swami quickly opened the book to that page and handed it to Swamishri, who then delivered that discourse directly from it.

Swamishri’s sharp recall at his advanced age reveals a mind entirely clear and deeply focused. His ability to retain such minor details shows that every action he undertakes is done with total presence and mindfulness.

title: The Pursuit of Perfection
text:
Today, when Swamishri arrived for cheshta, before sitting down on the sofa, he noticed a few creases on the sheet spread over it. While still standing, he gestured toward the sheet and said, “Locho!”—indicating that it was improper and needed to be straightened properly.

The attendants immediately understood his intention. They carefully removed every crease and neatly smoothed the sheet. Only after it had been arranged to perfection did Swamishri sit down.

Swamishri’s sharp focus and perfectionism reveal that he never settles for anything less than complete excellence. His meticulous nature shows us that every endeavor should be performed with total awareness, demonstrating that true spiritual devotion expresses itself through absolute precision and care in even the most minor tasks.

title: The Fire of Seva
text:
After lunch today, Swamishri appeared physically tired and had a cough. Before resting, one letter still needed to be written. However, seeing Swamishri's condition, Shrutipriya Swami said, “We can write it later. Let him rest.” As Swamishri was being helped to lie down, his facial expression immediately changed, as if asking, “What is happening?”
The attendants replied, “It is time to rest.”
Swamishri firmly responded, “The letter has to be written.”

“We will write it after you wake up.” Swamishri was clearly displeased. They explained, “There is no evening assembly or program today, so there will be plenty of time later.”

Swamishri was not satisfied. His hands were beneath his blanket. He forcefully pushed it aside, bringing his hands out to express his determination that the letter must be written immediately. Nevertheless, they gently helped Swamishri lie down and turned off the lights so that he could rest.

title: The Fire of Seva
text:
After a short while, Swamibapa began moving both of his hands. Whenever he feels warm, he sometimes makes similar gestures, so Shrutipriya Swami asked, “Swami, are You feeling hot?”
Absorbed in that moment, Swamibapa replied, “That heat…”—referring not to physical warmth, but to the fact that they had postponed the letter writing. In other words, what was troubling him was not the temperature, but the delay in completing the seva.
Seeing Swamibapa’s intense eagerness to fulfill this responsibility, the sadhus helped him get up, seated him in a chair, and completed the letter-writing seva.

title: Precision of Devotion
text:
At around 7:25 p.m., Swamishri arrived to perform the pujan of the 20-foot murti of Tapomurti Nilkanth Varni installed in front of the mandir.

Because the pujan had to be offered at the charanarvind (feet) and the murti was placed quite far back, Swamishri’s hand could not reach them physically. To assist him, a rose flower was prepared by dipping its stem in chandan before being handed to him.

Swamishri offered the flower toward the charanarvind. Remarkably, it landed precisely on Nilkanth Varni’s toe, and the chandan-coated tip touched it directly, leaving a perfect sandalwood mark.

Swamishri performed the pujan with extraordinary precision and mindfulness. At his advanced age, his sharp perception and flawless accuracy reveal a mind entirely absorbed in the moment. When every action is performed with heartfelt devotion, even the simplest offering becomes a profound expression of divine connection.

title: Quiet Endurance
text:
This morning, a filming session for the Fuldol celebration was taking place. Swamishri first applied color to Thakorji, after which Thakorji colored Swamishri.

Following this, devotees began coming forward, and Swamishri lovingly applied color to each of them. The sun was shining directly onto Swamishri’s face, creating a naturally intense and glaring heat. Yet, Swamishri did not utter a single word of complaint.

Noticing this, Kalpeshbhai Bhatt apologized and asked, “You must be feeling the heat of the sun quite a lot.”

Swamishri initially indicated “No.” However, when he was repeatedly told, “If we are feeling it, then surely you must be feeling it too,” Swamishri finally replied, “Slight.”

Swamishri’s natural disposition to quietly endure teaches us to bear minor discomforts without complaint, ensuring our words bring comfort rather than burden or guilt to others.

title: The Universal Compassion
text:
This morning, Swamishri visited Yagnapurush Nagar, where a filming session was scheduled.

The first activity was a tree-planting ceremony. Anandswarup Swami, assisting Swamishri, was seated near the pit where the tree was to be planted. As he prepared to place the sapling into the ground, he noticed a small black insect inside the pit. Remembering a cherished teaching from the life of Pramukh Swami Maharaj, he immediately began trying to gently move the insect to safety.

Seeing this, Swamishri was deeply pleased. Through gentle gestures, he encouraged the effort to ensure the insect was safely moved out of harm’s way.

Only after the tiny creature had been relocated did Swamishri proceed with planting the tree.

Swamishri’s instinctive concern for a small insect reveals a heart brimming with universal compassion. His reverence for life reminds us that true spirituality extends to every corner of creation.

title: The Right Mindset
text:
As it was Bal Din, a few balaks asked Swamishri questions after he had completed his morning puja.

One of the balaks asked, “I know how to perform garba really well, and I really want and would love to go to garba. So, should I go or not?”

Swamishri responded, “There was once a grandfather who brought his young grandson to sabha. Navratri came, and the grandfather went to the garba whereas the grandson attended sabha. Everything is because of the mind. We have done all sorts of things [in past lives]. The only thing left in this life is to please Swamibapa. If we do the other things, then we may experience a little happiness, but afterwards, there will be misery. Zerna ladva…?”

Hearing this, a balak immediately completed the Swamini Vat: “Zerna ladva khata sara laage, pan ghadik pachi galu zalay.”

Swamishri added, “And everything is poisoned ladvas.”

title: Brand New Vision
text:
This afternoon during lunch, Adarshjivan Swami was seated in front of Swamishri. A footrest stood before him, with two cushions resting on top.
Although Adarshjivan Swami was able to have clear darshan of Swamishri, Swamishri could not see him properly. After a brief moment, Swamishri gestured to remove one of the cushions so that his view would remain unobstructed.

In this way, the Guru himself seeks darshan of his disciple. While taking his meal, Swamishri regularly casts his gaze toward the swamis seated for darshan to ensure he sees them clearly. 

Based on the incidents, the attendants reflected: “When we were in Nenpur, Swamishri would do this every single day. Once, Gurumannan Swami asked him, ‘When you look toward the swamis from time to time, what thoughts pass through your mind?’

Swamishri replied, ‘I simply remember everyone as muktas (liberated souls).’”

title: Brand New Vision
text:
Continuing to reflect on the prasang from Nenpur, the attendants continued:

“The swamis then asked, ‘Swami! You see the exact same individuals every day and think the same thing about them—does it still feel new to you?’

Swamishri nodded and said, ‘Yes, it feels new every day—brand new.’ He further explained, ‘If we see from a physical perspective, it may seem old. But if we see the soul as a mukta, then it feels new every time.’”

Such a vision, where the Guru beholds his disciples with such reverence and spiritual glory, is truly rare to witness anywhere else. Swamishri’s life invites us to transform our own vision. When we learn to view others not through the lens of human flaws and physical labels, but as divine souls, our relationships and our service become sources of unending joy and spiritual elevation.

title: Ahmedabad
text:
During the first Yuvak-Yuvati Bharat Yatra, Yuvaks had an opportunity to perform a skit in front of Swamishri during the evening program. During the program, various interactions were completed with Swamishri. During one such occurrence, Swamishri was asked “Often times even though small, the problems we encounter seem to be as large as the Himalayas.  Amārā jivanmā koi pan prashna āve tyāre kevi rite prāptinā bale hatāsh thayā vinā himmat rākhi shakie? When these problem arise in our lives, how can we remain courageous and avoid becoming disheartened?
 
Swamishri responded, “Maharaj Swami Sarvopari chhe, karta chhe, eh samjan rakhi ne agad tapo.  karanke Badhuj saachu chhe, khotu hoy paisa pacha.  Pan saacha chhe, etle tame jya juo tya sikho vagshe.”  
 
In these few words, Swamishri reaffirmed that everything will work out if we have firm faith in Maharaj and Swami.

title: His Sinh Santano
text:
Before going to rest tonight, Swamishri was shown a video of a lion that had entered Shatrunjaya Hill and run away with a pilgrim’s bag. Swamishri watched with genuine surprise.

Seeing his reaction, Uttamyogi Swami playfully asked, “The number of lions in India has increased. Would you like to keep one?”

Swamishri pointed toward the swamis nearby and replied with pride, “There are already so many lions here. Why would we need another one?”

Swamishri’s lighthearted yet profound response reveals how he views the swamis and devotees around him. To him, they are not ordinary individuals, but lion-hearted souls—courageous, fearless, and utterly steadfast in their devotion to Bhagwan. His vision reminds us that true spiritual strength lies not in physical might, but in the fierce courage to remain loyal to our faith and Satsang against all odds.

title: The Source of All Desires
text:
After the afternoon discourse, Narayanmuni Swami outlined the schedule for tomorrow’s events. As Swamishri had instructed, the grand procession of the Vachanamrut was set to take place simultaneously across the country and around the world.

Atmatrupt Swami remarked, “Everyone thinks that when you go inside to rest, you are simply resting. But sitting inside, you are shaking (inspiring) everyone!”

Swamishri agreed with a smile, adding that such continuous inspiration is necessary, otherwise things would come to a standstill.

Narayanmuni Swami then noted, “You constantly have new spiritual resolves.”

Bhadresh Swami added, “Resolves certainly arise, but your unique distinction is that you never have any worldly desires. All your resolves are purely spiritual, and there is never any show or pretense involved.”

Hearing this, Swamishri immediately responded, “What show? If something is done for show, it equals zero.”

title: The Source of All Desires
text:
Continuing the conversation revolving around Swamishri’s divine resolves, Atmatrupt Swami continued, “Swami, your regular administrative tasks alone are so numerous that they could fill the entire day. Yet, you carry the deep inner wish to accomplish even more, which is why these new resolves keep emerging.”

Swamishri quietly replied, “They just keep emerging.”

Bhadresh Swami asked, “Do you consciously think about them, or do they happen naturally?”

Swamishri answered, “They happen naturally. Where is the time to sit and think?”

As Nishkulanand Swami describes in the Chosath Padi, divine words and noble thoughts flow effortlessly from the heart of a true devotee without requiring deliberate thought. Through Swamishri, it is truly Shriji Maharaj Himself who initiates all these divine resolves and brings about the spiritual upliftment of everyone.

title: The Weight of Sincere Effort
text:
After lunch and a bath, Swamishri  wanted some medicine. While he took his medicine, two attendants hurried toward a jug kept in the room, while another two ran to fetch water from a jug placed near the meal bag. The first group arrived first, so a swami from the second group said, “Savji Kadiyo took the credit!”

Before Swamishri could ask what was meant, a swami from the first group explained the situation and added, “I told them that because they went toward the jug and brought the water, they earned the same rājīpo.”

Swamishri agreed, “Yes... if effort is made, the fruit received is proportional. It may appear as ‘first rank’ or ‘second rank,’ but the fruit is equal! Everything is included in what is done for the sake of rājīpo.”

An attendant said, “So, even if less is achieved, you look at their effort.” Swamishri nodded yes.

title: Global Compassion
text:
After Swamishri finished his fruits and soup this afternoon, he was informed that a 7.8-magnitude earthquake had struck the Philippines. As soon as he heard the news, he exclaimed, “Oh dear!” His expression changed instantly, and looking deeply serious, he began praying silently for those affected.

Later that evening, when Swamishri went for darshan at the Pramukh Swami Maharaj Smruti Mandir, he specifically performed dhun for the people of the Philippines. He earnestly prayed that they would recover from this calamity as quickly as possible and that everyone affected would receive the strength, courage, and resilience needed to endure such a difficult time.

title: The Forgotten Child
text:
Towards the end of the assembly, dignitaries came for darshan. Once the curtains closed, Swamishri shifted into a serious mood and said, “If children come with the dignitaries, they should be garlanded too. A child looks up, thinking, ‘They are going to garland me,’ and then gets overlooked—how bad that must feel. You may not realize it, but it hurts them deeply.”

Shrutipriya Swami responded, “Swami, we will inform Kothari Swami about this.”

Vednayan Swami then reminded him, “Swami, when we were in Anand, a dignitary came with a child, and you had a chocolate given directly into the child’s mouth.”

Swamishri became engrossed in the memory and said, “A garland. Not a chocolate. How does it look when an adult gets a garland and the child is just handed a sweet?”

title: Constant Current of Prapti
text:
At around 3:00 a.m., Swamishri woke up and had no wish to return to sleep. Instead, he reached for a whiteboard in the room and read aloud the quote written upon it:

“No matter what yesterday was like, birds always start the new day with a song.”

Holding the board in his hands, Swamishri paused thoughtfully and said, “A satsangi should reflect every morning on their bhavya prāpti—the extraordinary gift of God’s presence in their lives.”

Taking a pen, he wrote beneath the existing quote:

“Therefore, since every satsangi has met Maharaj, Swami, and the Satpurush, they should start each day by remembering and appreciating this prāpti. — Sa. Ke. (Sadhu Keshavjivandas) 3 a.m. 11.6.20”

Turning to Uttamyogi Swami, Swamishri spoke softly in Hindi: “Kyā sonā sonā sonā... bhavya prāpti ko khonā khonā khonā.” (“Why snooze, snooze, snooze... and lose, lose, lose your bhavya prāpti?”)
